1. Primeiros passos

Da folha em branco à sua primeira peça para a impressora 3D, em cinco minutos, sem conta e sem instalar nada.

layerling é um programa de modelagem para impressão 3D que roda direto no seu navegador. Você monta uma peça a partir de formas simples, abre furos nela, arredonda as arestas e manda para o seu fatiador. Não há nada para instalar nem cadastro para fazer. O que você cria fica no seu computador.

Criando um projeto

Abra layerling.com. Na página inicial, clique em “Criar novo projeto 3D”. O editor abre com um plano de trabalho vazio, a grade sobre a qual tudo toma forma.

Se você já tem um arquivo para continuar, use “Abrir um projeto ou importar geometria”. Isso funciona tanto para projetos do layerling (.lyl) quanto para arquivos STL, OBJ, 3MF, STEP ou SVG.

Depois, todos os seus projetos aparecem na página inicial com uma miniatura. Eles ficam guardados no seu navegador e são salvos automaticamente a cada alteração, por isso não há botão de salvar. layerling não se responsabiliza pelos projetos guardados no navegador. Um navegador pode falhar, ou uma atualização pode causar problemas, então faça backup dos seus projetos de vez em quando com “Fazer backup de tudo” na página inicial, ou salve-os como arquivos. Para restaurar um backup, use “Restaurar backup”. Como juntar projetos num arquivo e passá-los adiante está em Arquivos e salvamento. Se quiser um lembrete, ative “Perguntar antes de fechar a aba” nas configurações (a engrenagem na barra de opções): o navegador pergunta antes de fechar ou recarregar uma aba com um projeto aberto.

Conhecendo o editor

  • No topo fica a barra de opções. Ela é organizada por tarefa: “Área de transferência”, “Histórico”, “Formas”, “Visibilidade”, “Combinar”, “Modificar”, “Organizar” e “Arquivo”; “Ajuda” fica acima dela, na barra de título, e a casinha ao lado das abas leva de volta à página inicial. Quando a janela é estreita demais para todos os grupos, os menos usados se recolhem num botão com o nome deles, com uma pequena seta na cor do grupo pendurada embaixo: aponte para o botão ou toque nele, e as ferramentas do grupo se abrem logo abaixo. “Histórico” recolhido é a exceção: o botão dele é o próprio “Desfazer”, e só a seta embaixo abre “Refazer” e o resto. Se preferir, a tachinha no canto superior direito, à esquerda da lupa, mantém todos os grupos abertos. Passe o mouse sobre um ícone, mesmo que esteja acinzentado, para ver o nome dele. Com a “Ajuda interativa” (o ponto de interrogação na área “Ajuda”, ou Shift+F1), você pode clicar em qualquer ícone para saber o que ele faz e acessar a seção correspondente deste guia. O pequeno ponto de interrogação, por exemplo nas configurações de uma forma, na biblioteca de formas ou nas janelas de ferramentas, leva direto ao capítulo correspondente deste guia. O grupo “Modificar” é dividido em quatro seções, cada uma com o nome acima das ferramentas: “Espelhar e padrão”, “Dividir e moldar”, “Arestas e paredes” e “Superfície”. Um ícone em cinza diz também o que falta, por exemplo “Selecione uma só forma” ou “A seleção está bloqueada: desbloqueie-a primeiro”. Não encontra uma ferramenta? Pressione Ctrl+K e digite o nome dela; um projeto vazio lembra disso na parte de baixo da vista.
  • No centro fica o plano de trabalho. É aqui que você posiciona as formas, dá forma a elas e vê o resultado.
  • À direita fica o painel de propriedades, com as configurações da forma selecionada: cor, dimensões, posição e tudo o mais que compõe a forma. Digitar números é mais exato do que arrastar.
  • À esquerda fica a barra de visualização, com o cubo de visualização acima dela. Eles levam você pela cena; mais em Vista e plano de trabalho.
  • Ao lado da barra de visualização abre a lista de objetos (Ctrl+U), com todas as formas do projeto.
  • À direita do cubo de visualização aparece a mensagem de status quando o layerling tem algo para te dizer, por exemplo o que uma ferramenta espera de você. Quando não há nada a dizer, ela não aparece.
  • Janelas de ferramentas abrem sobre o plano de trabalho quando você inicia uma ferramenta como “Arredondamento”, “Padrão” ou “Vazar”. Arraste-as pela barra de título quando cobrirem algo.
  • Bem no topo você alterna entre “Editor 3D” e “Esboço”, renomeia o projeto e escolhe o idioma e o tema de cores.

Os botões em volta da área de trabalho

Passe o mouse sobre um botão para ver o nome dele. Se não tiver certeza do que um botão faz, clique em “Ajuda interativa” na área “Ajuda” (Shift+F1) e depois no botão. Estes são os botões que mais geram perguntas.

Colar

“Colar” (Ctrl+V) adiciona ao projeto o que você copiou com “Copiar”. “Duplicar” copia e cola num só passo. Ao colar, cada peça fica um pouco ao lado de onde estava. Peças que vêm de outro programa podem cair longe da mesa; para elas existe “Colar no meio e baixar” nas configurações, em “Aparência”: ao colar, as peças vão juntas para o meio do plano de trabalho e baixam até ele.

Excluir

“Excluir” (Delete) exclui as formas selecionadas. “Desfazer” as traz de volta.

Desagrupar

“Desagrupar” (Ctrl+Shift+G) desfaz o grupo de união selecionado, separando as formas que o compõem.

Configurações da área de trabalho

“Configurações da área de trabalho” abre as configurações da área de trabalho: unidade, tamanho da mesa, impressora, grade, cores, luz e mais. Mais em Vista e plano de trabalho.

Tema

“Tema”, bem no topo, escolhe a aparência do layerling: igual ao sistema, claro, escuro ou grafite.

Renomear projeto

“Renomear projeto”: o lápis ao lado do nome, bem no topo. Digite o novo nome e pressione Enter.

Nome do projeto

O nome do projeto (“Nome do projeto”) fica bem no topo. Clique nele, digite o novo nome e pressione Enter para confirmar.

Opções de visibilidade

Em “Opções de visibilidade”, na seta ao lado do ícone de olho, você encontra o que pode mostrar ou ocultar: a lista de objetos, tudo o que você ocultou, as anotações e as saliências da impressão. Mais em Selecionar e organizar.

Ocultar selecionados

“Ocultar selecionados” (Ctrl+H) oculta as formas selecionadas. Elas continuam no projeto e na lista de objetos; “Opções de visibilidade” as mostram de novo.

Pesquisar comandos

“Pesquisar comandos (Ctrl+K)”: digite o que você procura, uma ferramenta, uma forma ou uma configuração, e clique no resultado.

Ocultar a barra de visualização

“Ocultar barra de visualização” recolhe a barra de visualização à esquerda e dá mais espaço à área de trabalho; “Mostrar barra de visualização” os traz de volta.

Grade de encaixe

“Grade de encaixe”, no fim do painel de propriedades, define o incremento usado ao mover e redimensionar as formas. Ao lado, a pequena chave mm | in troca a unidade. Mais em Vista e plano de trabalho.

Unidade: milímetros ou polegadas

A chave mm | in ao lado de “Grade de encaixe” troca a unidade, a grade da mesa e o incremento de encaixe, para este projeto.

Rodapé

No rodapé você encontra: “Apoie o projeto”, que leva à página onde você pode apoiar o projeto; “Guia do usuário”, que abre este guia; “Discussões”, o lugar para perguntas, ideias e relatos de erros (as discussões no GitHub; em alemão, o fórum do drucktipps3d); “Relatar erro”, que cria um ZIP para um relato de erro; “Mais no GitHub”, que leva ao projeto no GitHub; e o número da versão, que abre as notas da versão. Os links para as informações legais e a política de privacidade são de quem mantém a cópia do layerling que você usa.

Sua primeira peça

Por exemplo, vamos montar um cubo com um furo.

  1. Clique em “Adicionar forma” na barra de opções e escolha “Caixa”. A forma agora fica presa ao ponteiro do mouse. Um clique no plano de trabalho a coloca ali.
  2. No painel de propriedades, defina as dimensões, por exemplo 40 mm de comprimento, 40 mm de largura e 20 mm de altura.
  3. Coloque um “Cilindro” no centro do mesmo jeito, com 14 mm de diâmetro e 30 mm de altura. Ele deve ser mais alto que o cubo, para atravessá-lo de ponta a ponta.
  4. Selecione o cilindro e clique em “Buraco” no painel de propriedades. Ele fica transparente: o sólido virou uma ferramenta que tira material.
  5. Selecione as duas formas e clique em “Grupo de união”. Agora o cubo tem um furo.

É assim que se fazem furos, rasgos e cavidades. O capítulo Sólidos e buracos explica isso em detalhes.

Novidades desde a sua última visita

Quando você abre o layerling de novo depois de uma atualização, um cartão na página inicial lista o que foi adicionado desde a sua última visita: cada versão desde então, a mais nova primeiro. Depois de muito tempo sem abrir o layerling, você rola a lista dentro do cartão. Abaixo da lista, “Mostrar versões anteriores” acrescenta também as versões de antes da sua última visita. Feche o cartão com “Entendi” e ele não aparece mais até a próxima atualização. “O que há de novo?”, no rodapé da página inicial, mostra as últimas novidades de novo a qualquer momento. O navegador lembra a última versão que você viu, e nada sobre você sai dele.

Numa cópia do layerling no seu próprio computador ou servidor, o aviso "Atualização disponível" tem um botão, “Prévia: o que a atualização traz?”, que lista o que a atualização traz antes de você instalá-la. A lista só é buscada no GitHub quando você clica no botão.

Do projeto à impressão

Quando a peça estiver pronta, clique em “Exportar”, escolha STL ou 3MF e baixe o arquivo. Abra-o no seu fatiador, por exemplo Bambu Studio, PrusaSlicer, OrcaSlicer ou Cura. Se você escolher sua impressora nas configurações, dá para ver enquanto modela se a peça cabe na mesa de impressão. Mais em Impressão.

Dica: Se você vem do Tinkercad, vai se achar rapidinho: a mesa, as formas, sólido e buraco, agrupar, alinhar e espelhar funcionam quase igual. As novidades são principalmente chanfro e arredondamento, vazar, roscas e esboços. Seus próprios projetos do Tinkercad também podem vir junto, veja Arquivos e salvamento.

2. View and workplane

Moving around the scene, looking straight on, and placing new shapes on any surface you like.

Este capítulo ainda não foi traduzido para o português. Segue o texto em inglês.

Moving around

With the mouse:

What you doWhat happens
drag with the right buttonrotate the view
click the right buttonon a body, a menu with the most used commands: duplicate, hole or solid, group, hide, lock, delete and more; on empty space Paste and Select all
drag with the middle buttonmove the view
mouse wheelzoom in and out
hold Ctrl / Cmd and drag with the left buttonalso moves the view (on a MacBook trackpad: hold Cmd, press and drag); on a Mac, holding Control instead turns the view, as Control-click is the Mac's right click
double-click on empty workplane or beside the platemoves the view so that the spot comes to the middle; the view then turns around it

How fast the wheel zooms is set with “Velocidade do zoom” in the settings, under “Aparência”: a slider from 1 to 14, 5 to begin with. It sets the wheel and the trackpad only: the buttons and the keys + and − always zoom in the same small steps. One notch of a mouse wheel zooms alike in every browser, a trackpad zooms with how far you stroke.

Mouse buttons as in your slicer. If you are used to Bambu Studio or OrcaSlicer, set “Botões do mouse” in the settings, under “Aparência”, to “Como no Bambu Studio e no OrcaSlicer”. A left drag on empty space then turns the view, the right button shifts it as the middle one does, and Shift with a left drag draws the selection box. A drag on a body still moves it, and a short right click still opens the menu. In a sketch the right button shifts the view too.

3D mouse. A SpaceMouse or another 3D mouse turns, shifts and zooms the 3D view: push the cap away to zoom in, slide it to shift the view, tilt it to tilt the view and twist it to turn the view round. In the settings, under “Aparência”, click “Conectar mouse 3D” and choose the device in the window the browser opens; it remembers the choice, so this is needed only once. This works in Chrome and Edge, which can reach such devices; Firefox and Safari cannot. If a direction feels the wrong way round, tick it under the button: shifting sideways, shifting up and down, zooming, tilting or twisting.

On a tablet or phone, two fingers zoom (spread and pinch) and move the view (slide together). One finger on empty space turns the view, and a tap there clears the selection; on a shape or a handle it works on the design, just like the left mouse button. To turn the view with a finger that starts on a shape too, switch on “Girar a vista com um dedo” in the view bar. That switch shows on devices with a touch screen.

A graphics tablet with a pen behaves like a mouse: the tip is the left button, the barrel button on the pen the right one, for turning the view and for the menu. The tablet's hotkeys can be set in its driver to layerling's keyboard shortcuts.

On a tablet, work with a stylus if you can. Its tip is far finer than a fingertip and does not cover what you aim at, so small points, thin lines and handles in a sketch, measuring points and edges are hit exactly, and longer work is less tiring. layerling already lets a finger reach a little further to points, lines, handles and edges than a mouse pointer does, but a stylus remains the more precise way. This holds for a pen that the tablet knows as a pen (an S Pen, an Apple Pencil and the like). A plain stylus with a rubber tip counts as a finger for the screen and is not finer than one.

There is no right mouse button on a tablet: hold a finger still on a shape or on empty space for half a second, and the menu opens that a right click opens, with Select all on empty space. Select multiple in the same menu stands in for Shift on a tablet: each tap on a body then adds it to the selection or takes it out again, until you tap empty space or press Esc; a finger on empty space still turns the view. The handles around a selected shape can be caught by a finger from a little beside them.

The view cube

The cube in the top left shows where you are looking. A click on one of its sides jumps to the straight view from top, bottom, front, back, left or right. A click on a corner of the cube looks at the model diagonally from that corner, and a click near an edge looks from that edge, between two sides; the spot lights up while the pointer is on it. The number keys 1 to 6 give the straight views too. Hold Shift with them and the view also zooms to the selection, as Shift+F does.

Drag the cube to turn the view around, just like dragging with the right mouse button. With nothing selected, the arrow keys turn the view as well: 15° a press, 90° with Shift. They turn the model the way they point - → turns its front to the right, ↑ tilts its front upwards. With Ctrl held, the arrows slide the view across the screen instead: a tenth of the picture a press, half of it with Shift as well. The model moves the way they point. If something is selected, the arrows move it; click on empty space first to turn the view. On a touch screen this works with one finger, without switching on “Girar a vista com um dedo”.

The view bar

At the left edge is a narrow bar. From the top:

  • “Visão inicial” brings the whole scene back into view. The key is Home; F does it too when nothing is selected.
  • “Centralizar a vista na seleção” zooms to the selection (F or Shift+F); with nothing selected it brings the whole scene into view, as F does.
  • “Aproximar” and “Afastar” zoom step by step, as do the keys + and −.
  • “Vista ortográfica” switches to a flat view in which parallel edges stay parallel. For measuring and lining up edges that is often more comfortable than the perspective view. O switches back and forth, and a second click returns.
  • “Abrir uma segunda vista” opens a second view of the design in a window of its own, described below. A second click closes it.
  • “Show scrollbars” puts a scrollbar along the bottom of the view and one down its right edge. Drag a bar to slide the view smoothly, click an arrow at its end to move it a little (hold it to keep going), or click beside the bar to move by most of the view. Nothing turns, and unlike the arrow keys the bars work while a part is selected - handy close up on small details. A second click hides them; “Abrir o editor com barras de rolagem” in the settings decides whether a design opens with them. This browser also remembers the switch.
  • “Ocultar plano de trabalho” (the eye over a grid) hides the plate with its grid, so you can look at the underside of a design from below. Only the view changes: new shapes still land on the workplane. A second click shows it again.
  • “Posicionar plano de trabalho”, the tape measure and the framing square are tools of their own, covered below and in Measuring and notes.

The small arrow at the very top of the bar hides it if it gets in the way. That same button, dragged, moves the bar anywhere in the editor, in a sketch too; a double click puts it back. The 3D preview of a revolved sketch moves by its title in the same way.

A design opens the way you left it: the angle, zoom and position of the view are kept with it in this browser, so you continue where you stopped, also after going Home or closing the page. A saved file (.lyl) carries the view along, so it opens in it elsewhere too. The view is not part of the undo history.

You can also keep four views of your own in each design. Shift+7, Shift+8, Shift+9 or Shift+0 saves the view exactly as it is - angle, position, zoom, and flat or perspective - under that key, and the key alone (7, 8, 9 or 0) brings it back. A message at the bottom confirms the save; saving again under the same key replaces the view. Like the view above, the saved views stay with the design in this browser and travel in a saved file (.lyl), and they are not part of the undo history.

A second view in its own window

“Abrir uma segunda vista” opens a window that shows the same design through a camera of its own, so you can see it from two sides at once - from the front, say, while you work from above. Every change you make in the editor shows there straight away; the design is only changed in the main window, and the handles stay there too. In the second window the mouse and the view cube turn its view as they do here, and so do the keys: 1 to 6, F, Home, O, + and −, the arrow keys to turn and Ctrl with the arrows to slide. F there zooms to what is selected in the editor. The design's four saved views work there too: 7, 8, 9 and 0 bring them back, and Shift with one of these keys saves that window's view under it - for both windows. Its own view bar has “Visão inicial”, “Centralizar a vista na seleção”, “Aproximar”, “Afastar”, “Vista ortográfica” and “Ocultar plano de trabalho”, and they act on that window alone. The window opens where you left it, at the same size, and closes with the editor. On phones and tablets the button is not shown.

Looking inside: the section view

“Vista em corte”, the last button in the bar (the cut tool), cuts the view open along a plane so you can check walls, cavities and parts that fit into each other. Nothing is cut for real: the design, its files and every export stay whole. Where the plane goes through a solid, the cut is filled with the colour of the body a little darker, and a hole inside it stays empty, so you can tell solid from hollow; the filled face appears a moment after the plane stops moving. Under “Face do corte” you choose how the cut looks: “Hachurada”, the start, hatches it like a drawing, and a body that lies inside another is hatched the other way, so the two stand apart; “Preenchida” fills it plain; “Aberta” leaves it open, and you look into the skin of the body. The choice holds for every design.

  • Choose the axis the plane stands across: X (width), Y (depth) or Z (height), as in the position fields. The plane starts in the middle of your design.
  • “Eixos de referência” sets what these axes follow. “Projeto” takes the design's axes. “Plano de trabalho” takes the workplane's: Z then cuts parallel to it, X and Y square to it, and the position counts from its origin. With the workplane on a sloped face you cut parallel to that face, and the cut moves along when you move the workplane. “Vista” turns the plane to face the screen: it takes away what lies in front, and the slider pushes it deeper into the design along your line of sight, for example to reach a buried part and click it. After turning the view, click it again and the cut follows the new view.
  • “Aproximado” moves the plane across the whole design, “Fino” moves it a little either side of where it stands, for tenths of a millimetre. You can also type the position.
  • The button beside the axes shows the other side of the cut, “Centralizar” puts the plane back in the middle, and “Mostrar plano de corte” hides the blue plane.
  • You can click and select what the cut lays open, inner walls included.
  • “Plano de trabalho aqui” puts the workplane on the cut. It lies on the plane of the section and faces out of the body that stays, like the face a cut leaves. If you then switch to the sketch, it starts exactly there, and the faint outline shows the cut, which you can draw along and snap to. That is how you sketch a lid that fits the cavity you opened with the section, for example. The button beside the axes chooses which side stays, and with it which way the workplane faces. You put the workplane back on the base plate as usual.
  • “Esboço a partir do corte” starts a new sketch right on the cut, with the cut's outlines already in it as lines: a hole comes in as a true circle, a rounded corner as an arc. Change them, delete what you don't need, draw more, and finish: the body grows out of the cut towards the side that is cut away, so a part that has to fit another one, such as a lid, an insert or a gasket, starts from that part's own outline. The button beside the axes chooses that side. As for the SVG, only visible bodies count and holes are already taken off.
  • “Medir” measures right on the cut: the outline shows in blue, and two clicks on it give the distance, plus its parts along the plane's two axes. Both points snap to the outline, corners first. When the second click lands anywhere on the opposite wall, it snaps square to the first point - so you read wall thickness, gaps and clearance without aiming exactly. A third click starts the next measurement, Esc ends measuring. Moving the plane clears the measurement. On a round outline, such as the cut through a cylinder or a hole, a small cross marks the centre and the centre snaps too. Click a point on the circle, then go near the point across from it: the second click lands exactly across the centre, and the number reads Ø, the diameter. From the centre to a point on the circle you get R, the radius.
  • “Corte como SVG” saves the outlines on the cutting plane as an SVG at 1:1, for a laser, a plotter, a template or a gasket. An X cut is seen from the right, a Y cut from the front, a Z cut from above. As in the export, only visible bodies go in, holes are already taken off, and bodies of the same colour are joined into one outline. Each colour stays its own path without a fill, so laser software keeps them apart as layers.

The tool window hangs on its button. If it covers something, drag it by its title bar anywhere on the workplane; it opens there next time too. Double-click the title bar or drop it at the button to put it back.

The X and Esc close the tool window; with a measuring running, Esc ends it first. The cut stays until you switch it off with “Corte ativo”, click its button in the bar while the window is open, or go back to the design overview. While it is on, its button stays highlighted. Anything you place on the side that is cut away only shows once you switch the cut off. A tablet has no Esc, so there the tool window has two more buttons: “Voltar” ends the measuring if one is running and otherwise closes the tool window, and “Fechar” closes the tool window in one step. A computer does not show them.

The workplane

New shapes align with the workplane. At first that is the base plate with the grid. But you can put it on any surface, to place something on a side or a sloped face.

  1. Press W or click “Posicionar plano de trabalho”.
  2. Move the mouse over a face of a body. It lights up.
  3. A click puts the workplane there. Everything you add now sits on that face.

Click on the empty plate instead, and the workplane lies flat at the spot you clicked, on the snap grid. New shapes and a finished sketch, a revolved one too, then appear there rather than in the middle of the plate. While the workplane lies flat on the plate like this, the plate shows only its outline: two grids in the same plane would make a flickering pattern.

On a face the origin of the workplane otherwise snaps to the grid. Click close to a corner of the face and it sits exactly on that corner. Close to an edge it lies on the edge, and the grid lines up with it; that is how you choose the angle of the grid on purpose. Without a corner or an edge, the grid on a lying face runs parallel to the body, so on a turned box it is turned with it.

A click beside the plate or Esc returns the workplane to the base plate. Quicker still is “Plano de trabalho de volta à base”: the button with the downward arrow sits in the view bar below the eye while the workplane lies on a face. Shift+W puts it directly on the currently selected face. Alt+W puts it back on the base plate at any time, whether something is selected or not. If you hold Shift while clicking, the plane points the other way.

While a workplane sits on a face, an eye appears next to “Posicionar plano de trabalho”. It hides the workplane without dropping it, for a clear look at the design: new shapes still land on that face, and rotating still turns about it. A click on the eye shows it again, and so does setting a new workplane. A box's size handles follow a workplane that stands on one of its sides too: the corner and edge handles lie on that face, and each one changes the box's own width, length or height that runs along it. The handle in the middle of the face changes the size across it.

To look straight at the workplane, press P or click “Olhar de frente para o plano de trabalho” next to “Posicionar plano de trabalho” in the view bar. The view turns until you see the workplane square, from the side new shapes grow towards, with its origin in the middle. On the base plate that is the view from above.

Build plates

When a design holds more than one plate can print, a box with its lid and inserts for example, it can have several build plates. Click “Build plates” in the “Organizar” group, or choose “Onto plate…” in the menu of a right click on a body. A bar appears at the foot of the view with one button per plate; the number on it says how many bodies stand on the plate.

  • Every plate is as large as the workplane, and the plates lie side by side to the right of the first one, 20 mm apart. A body belongs to the plate the middle of its footprint stands on, so dragging it across puts it on the other plate. A design holds up to 12 plates.
  • A click on a plate in the bar looks at it, and new shapes and imported files then land on it. “Show all plates” looks at all of them. A double click on a plate, or “Rename plate”, gives it a name such as "Lid", which is written on the plate.
  • “Move plate left” and “Move plate right” change the order, the bodies moving with their plate. “Remove plate (its bodies go onto the first plate)” takes the active plate away; its bodies go onto the first plate at the same spot.
  • “Arrange on plates” lays the selected bodies, or all of them, out row by row on the plates, the largest first, 5 mm apart, and adds plates while they are needed. A body larger than a plate stays where it is.
  • With a printer chosen, every body is checked against its own plate, and the build height counts from the lowest body on that plate. A plate with a body that does not fit shows its number in red.
  • In the properties, X counts from the middle of the body's own plate.

The export window then offers “Plates”: all plates in one file, side by side as in the design; one file per plate, packed in a ZIP (STL, 3MF and OBJ); or a single plate, set where the first plate is. A slicer opens every file as one plate, so to print the plates one after another, take the files per plate. Moving bodies between plates and arranging them can be undone; adding, naming, ordering and removing plates is kept with the design but not undone.

Grid and snapping

The grid shows the size of the plate. At the bottom right is the snap step: moving and scaling snap in steps of that size, for example 1 mm. Make it smaller for fine work and larger for rough arranging. “Encaixar na grade” in the ribbon moves the selected shapes afterwards onto the nearest grid crossing. While moving, shapes also snap to other shapes, see Selecting and arranging. Without the mouse: Alt+1 to Alt+0 pick that entry of the menu (Alt+1 turns snapping off), and , and . make the step one size finer or coarser. This works in a sketch too. A short click with the middle mouse button, without moving the mouse, opens the snap step menu right at the pointer, in a sketch too; holding the middle button and dragging still moves the view.

Tip: Stop rotating the view when you fit parts together exactly. Use the number keys to go to the straight view from top or front and press O for the flat display. Then you see at once whether two edges are really flush.

The settings window

The cogwheel in the title row (“Configurações da área de trabalho”) opens the settings. On the left are five areas: “Aparência”, “Medidas”, “Plano de trabalho”, “Padrões das formas” and “Histórico”. A change counts at once. “Tornar padrão” at the bottom saves the current settings as the default, so that a new design starts with them. A file you open brings its own settings; “Usar minha configuração padrão” next to it puts your saved colours, grid and the rest on the open design, keeping its units. If your default has a printer, that printer comes along with its plate size; without one the design keeps its plate and printer. “Fechar configurações” at the top right closes the window. This part goes through the settings one by one.

“Export settings” next to it saves the settings of the window in a file (layerling-settings-<date>.json): the colours, grid, shadows, camera and shape defaults, together with the theme, toolbar size, view cube corner, shape colours and the play of each printer. On another computer, or after the browser lost its data, “Import settings” reads the file again: it becomes your default for new designs and goes onto the open design like “Usar minha configuração padrão”. Your own keys from the keyboard shortcuts go along too.

Appearance: theme, toolbar and view cube

“Tema” sets the colour scheme of the whole program: “Sistema” follows your computer, the others are “Claro”, “Escuro” and “Grafite (escuro neutro)”. You can also change it at the top right of the editor.

“Tamanho dos controles” makes the buttons of the ribbon on top, its shape menu, the view bar on the left and the properties panel on the right smaller or larger: “Pequeno”, “Médio” (as it always was) or “Grande”. Small leaves more room for the workplane on a laptop; large is easier to hit on a big screen or with a finger. With large buttons the groups of the ribbon go onto a second row when the window is too narrow for them. The size sits in the “Ribbon” tab of the settings, is kept in this browser and holds for every design.

“Cor das formas” puts the colour a new shape starts with on the pictures of the shape library (the colour of its kind, or the one you saved with “Salvar como padrão”). Switch it off if you prefer grey pictures; your browser remembers the choice.

“Posição do cubo de visualização” puts the view cube in another corner of the workplane: “Superior esquerdo” (as it always was), “Superior direito”, “Inferior esquerdo” or “Inferior direito”. In any corner but the top left, the view bar moves up into the spot the cube left. In the bottom right the cube stands just above the “Grade de encaixe” control. While the properties of a shape are open on the right, a cube on the right steps to the left of them. The corner is kept in this browser and holds for every design. On a narrow window, such as a phone, the setting is hidden and the cube stays in the top left.

Appearance: buttons in the ribbon

“Buttons in the ribbon” takes the groups and buttons you never use out of the ribbon. Click a group to open its list: “Show this group” takes the whole group out, the tick next to a button just that button. “Show all” brings everything back. A group with no button left disappears and the others move up, so more of the ribbon fits in one row.

What you take out only leaves the ribbon: the command search (Ctrl+K) still finds it, and its key still runs it. The arrows next to a group move it up or down the list, and so along the ribbon; “Reset order” brings back the order it came with. The arrows beside a button move it the same way inside its group; in “Modificar” it stays within its named section. The Shapes group and Help always stay, and Shapes keeps its place after the first two groups. The choice is kept in this browser and goes into the file of “Export settings”. It applies to the 3D editor; the sketch has a bar of its own.

Appearance: fast mode

“Modo rápido” is for slower computers. It turns off shadows, edge lines on all bodies and the camera's inertia, and draws the view at screen resolution only. Your own settings are kept for later, and the switches it overrides say “Desligado no modo rápido” while it is on. More about what helps on a slow computer is under "When layerling feels slow" below.

Appearance: colours of the work area and the sketch

The colours of the work area are set under “Aparência”: “Fundo da janela (tema claro)” and “Plano de trabalho sob a grade (tema claro)” for the light theme (the dark themes keep their own), next to the grid colour under “Plano de trabalho”. Each colour is a button that shows the colour. A click opens a small window with the colour field, a row of ready colours, a field for the hex value and an arrow that puts the colour back to what layerling started with. Enter takes a typed hex value, and so does a click outside the window.

The sketch view has its own colours: “Esboço: fundo da janela (tema claro)” for the window round the sheet, “Esboço: área sob a grade (tema claro)” for the sheet under the grid, and “Esboço: cor da grade (tema claro)”, all for the light theme. “Esboço igual à área de trabalho” takes over the work area's three colours in one click.

“Visual clássico” sets the work area up as Tinkercad shows it: white ground, a pale blue millimetre grid with a darker line every centimetre, black edge lines, light from above with soft shadows. Every value can still be changed on its own afterwards. All of them start as layerling always looked, and what suits you depends on your monitor.

Appearance: axis arrows and edge lines

“Setas dos eixos” (on by default) draws three arrows at the back left corner of the plate: X in red to the right, Y in green to the back and Z in blue upwards, the way the position fields count. That is the right-hand rule Tinkercad, CAD programs and the slicers use too. With the workplane on a face they follow it. Switch them off here if they are in your way.

“Linhas de aresta em todos os sólidos” draws an outline on every body, in the colour of “Cor das linhas de aresta” (black to begin with, as in Tinkercad): it helps when dark colours run into each other. It is off by default, and very large imported meshes are left out.

“Destacar os buracos” draws holes in a darker grey, less see-through and with a dark line round them. It helps when a hole is hard to find among see-through bodies. Unlike the edge lines it stays on in fast mode.

Appearance: light and shadows

“Mostrar sombras” switches the cast shadows on and off. Two sliders set how the bodies are lit. “Intensidade da sombra” says how dark the cast shadows are, and “Contraste do sombreamento” moves light from the even ambient light to the main light: towards "punchy" the shaded sides get darker and the shadows show more, towards "soft" everything gets flatter. At the top end the contrast gets very strong, so shaded sides and shadows turn really dark. “Suavidade da sombra” makes the edges of the shadows soft instead of crisp. “Direção da luz” turns the main light round the plate (0° from the front, 90° from the right), and “Altura da luz” lifts it; at 90° it stands straight above the plate as in Tinkercad, and the shadows fall right under the bodies. “Luz suave” brings most of the light from where you look, turning with the view: no face is left dark, and a face of a dark colour that points up is no longer burnt out to white. The main light stays a little for the shadows, and the contrast slider still works. If a bright reflection still shows with the light set low, lift “Altura da luz” to 90°: it then looks like Tinkercad. “Restaurar luz e sombras” puts everything back.

Appearance: measures on the workplane

“Mostrar dimensões do deslocamento” shows by how much you move while dragging or with the arrow keys, “Mostrar distâncias até a origem” the distances of the selection to the origin of the plate, also with several bodies selected. With “Dimensões sempre visíveis” these measures stay visible permanently, and not only while you drag. While a turned body is selected, its angles show below it on the workplane; “Mostrar os ângulos de sólidos girados” switches that off. More in Measuring and notes.

Appearance: selecting and moving

“Selecionar antes de mover”: a body then has to be selected first, and only the next drag moves it. That helps when children or hurried hands touch bodies, and on a touch screen.

“A direção da moldura define a seleção”: a frame dragged to the right selects only what lies completely inside it, one dragged to the left everything it touches (drawn dashed), as in SketchUp.

“Clique duplo abre o esboço” decides whether a double click on an extruded sketch opens the sketch again, as in Tinkercad, and “Clique duplo abre um grupo de união ou um conjunto” whether a double click on a group or a bundle opens it for editing. “Clique duplo no plano de trabalho centraliza a vista ali” decides whether a double click on empty workplane moves the view to that spot.

“Encaixar em outras formas ao mover” lets the edges and the centre of a shape snap to other shapes while you drag it; the grid menu at the bottom right has the same switch. “Cruise ao adicionar formas novas” makes a new shape hang on the mouse pointer and land on the face under it, like Cruise in Tinkercad; switched off, a new shape appears in the middle of the plate. More in Selecting and arranging.

Appearance: the view

“Abrir o editor na vista em perspectiva”: the editor then opens in the perspective view, not in the flat one.

“Abrir o editor com barras de rolagem”: a design then opens with the view's scrollbars shown. It is saved with the design and with “Tornar padrão”.

“Vista inicial” sets the angle a new design opens in and “Visão inicial” goes back to. Turn and zoom the view the way you like it, then click “Usar a vista atual”; “Padrão” brings back the usual view from the front right. It holds for every design in this browser. A design you open again still opens the way you left it.

“Velocidade do zoom” is a slider from slow to fast: how fast the wheel and the trackpad zoom; the zoom buttons and keys keep their own small steps. “Inércia da câmera”: after you let go of the mouse the view turns on for a moment and slows down gently. Switched off, it stops at once, as in Tinkercad and Fusion 360.

“Marcar saliências a partir de {angle}°” is the angle from which a face counts as an overhang when you switch on Show overhangs in the visibility menu: those faces are hatched red and white. 30° is careful, 70° counts on good cooling of the print; 45° is the usual start. While they are shown, a line under the view says the steepest overhang and how many cm² need supports.

“Cortar malhas importadas de até” limits how many triangles an imported mesh may have when you cut, merge or intersect it, because that is calculated in your browser. A mesh above the limit is not processed; simplify the mesh first, or raise the limit if your computer can take it. A higher limit can freeze the editor for a few seconds.

Measurement: units, scale and snap steps

Under “Medidas” you set the “Unidades”, the unit that measures are shown in (“Escala”: millimetres, centimetres or metres in metric, inches or feet in imperial), how many decimal places a number shows (“Precisão”), the “Grade de encaixe” that moving and resizing snap to and your own snap steps under “Grades de encaixe personalizadas”.

Under “Medidas” in the settings you set the “Unidades”. With “Imperial”, layerling shows every measure in inches, on the shape, in the properties panel, on the tape measure and the ruler. The snap grid then offers steps from 1/64 to 1 inch, and the grid on the plate is drawn in inches (1/8 to 1 inch, 1/4 inch by default) with a stronger line on every whole inch. Under “Mostrar polegadas como” you choose whether inches appear as fractions like in Tinkercad (1 5/8, rounded to 1/64 inch) or as decimals (1.625) with as many decimal places as set under “Precisão”. You can type either, "1 5/8" included. A quick way between millimetres and inches is the small switch mm | in beside the “Grade de encaixe” at the bottom of the properties window: it changes the unit, the plate's grid and the snap step as the settings do, for this design.

Under “Grades de encaixe personalizadas” in the same place you add snap steps of your own: a name and a size in millimetres, for example "Pin pitch 2.54 mm" for the spacing of DIP chips, pin headers and perfboard holes, or "MX Key Unit" with 19.05 mm for the spacing of keyboard keys. The snap step menu then offers that measure whole, halved and quartered (1 ×, ½ × and ¼ ×), so shapes can be moved by one pitch, half a pitch or a quarter pitch. If you want just the measure itself, untick “Também metade e quarto” beside it; the menu then has only that one step. Custom steps are kept with the design and go along with “Tornar padrão”.

“Começar novos projetos com um esquadro na origem”: every new design in this browser then starts with a framing square at the origin, see Measuring and notes. Designs you already have stay as they are, and a square you remove from a design stays removed.

Workplane: plate and printer

“Impressora” sizes the workplane to the build plate of your printer and flags bodies that reach past it, see Printing. “Textos na mesa” writes the design's name on the plate, and the printer's name and build volume when a printer is chosen.

“Printer play” is the room per side a printed pin needs to turn in a printed hole on your printer. “Make fit test” puts the fit test that measures it on the plate, and new lids, dovetails, snap-fits, nuts and the clearance check then start from it, see Printing. It is kept in this browser, not in the design.

“Tamanho do plano de trabalho” gives the plate a size of your own, with “Largura” and “Comprimento” in millimetres or the unit you chose. The grid always runs through the origin, so the stronger lines lie on the axes whatever the plate measures.

Workplane: grid

“Mostrar grade” shows or hides the grid on the plate. “Tamanho do bloco da grade” sets the spacing of its lines, and “Linha mais escura da grade a cada” whether the darker line comes every 5 or every 10 grid steps; “Cor da linha mais escura” gives that line a colour of its own, and the centre cross and the plate border take it too. “Cor da grade” is the colour of the ordinary lines.

Every line of the grid grows wider as you zoom in, as in Tinkercad, and stays visible as you zoom out. If that is too much for you, switch off “Linhas da grade engrossam com o zoom” and the lines stay one pixel wide at every zoom, as in the sketch.

If the grid has disappeared, say because a colour was set to that of the plate, “Restaurar grade” at the end of the “Plano de trabalho” area brings its visibility, colours, spacing and line weight back to the standard, here and in the default saved with “Tornar padrão”.

Shape defaults

Under “Padrões das formas” you choose a shape with “Forma” and set how it starts when you add it: its width, length and height. “Usar padrões do app” takes the shape back to what the app starts it with. Shapes with settings of their own show them under “Detalhes da forma”. The values apply to new shapes, not to those already on the plate. “Limite de tamanho personalizado” sets a ceiling of your own for how large the handles and the properties may make that shape; left blank, the usual limits stay.

Saved history

Under “Histórico” the slider “Histórico salvo” sets how many completed actions stay available for Undo after you save or reopen a design. The default is 100 actions in a design. A lower limit permanently discards the older undo steps of the design.

When layerling feels slow

layerling calculates and draws everything in your browser. On an older computer, with a weak graphics card or on several large screens the view can therefore feel sluggish. This helps:

  • “Modo rápido” under “Aparência” turns off at once everything that costs the view a lot: shadows, edge lines on all bodies and the camera's inertia. It also draws the view at the screen's own resolution only, which on high-resolution screens is up to four times fewer pixels. Your own settings are kept and apply again as soon as you turn it off.
  • The camera keeps turning: When you let go of the mouse after turning, the view turns on for a moment and slows down gently. That is on purpose, not stutter. If you are used to Tinkercad or Fusion 360, turn off “Inércia da câmera” under “Aparência”, and the view stops at once.
  • Single switches: Without fast mode you can also turn off just “Mostrar sombras” or “Linhas de aresta em todos os sólidos”.
  • Use the graphics card: In Chrome open chrome://gpu (in Edge edge://gpu). Next to "WebGL" it should say "Hardware accelerated". If it says "Software only", hardware acceleration is off in the browser's settings. On Windows you can also pick "High performance" for the browser under Settings → System → Display → Graphics, so it uses the real graphics card and not the weaker one in the processor.
  • Simplify large imported meshes: A model of many hundred thousand triangles slows any view down. How to thin it out is in the chapter on files, under "Simplifying an imported mesh".
  • Close other tabs: Every open layerling tab and every other 3D page shares the same graphics card.

3. Placing and adjusting shapes

The shape library, dimensions by number and by handle, colour, rotating, tapering and twisting.

Este capítulo ainda não foi traduzido para o português. Segue o texto em inglês.

Every part in layerling starts with a shape. From them you build everything else: shapes complement each other, cut each other out or are joined into a new shape.

Adding a shape

Click “Adicionar forma” in the ribbon. The shape library opens.

The library is one list in sections, from “Basic shapes” to “Helpers”, each with the number of shapes in it. A click on a section's name folds it away, and the browser keeps what you folded; the first time, all of them are open. On top, “Recently used” holds the last four shapes you put in. The search field finds a shape by its name and by other words for it, in English and German too: "USB" finds the “Abertura de conector”. While you type, only the sections with a match show; an empty field brings your folded sections back as they were. “Formas personalizadas” on top is a single line until you keep a shape there.

The library closes after each shape you pick. Its title bar moves it, so you can put it where it does not cover the spot you are aiming at, over the properties panel for example; a double-click on the title bar puts it back under its button, and where you left it is kept in the browser. The pin in the title bar keeps the library open while you put several shapes one after the other. Its edges and corners pull its size, as wide and as high as your screen allows; the size is kept in the browser too, and a double-click on an edge sets it back. Pulled narrow, the library leaves out the names and shows only the pictures; the name appears when you point at a shape.

Pick a shape. It now hangs on the mouse pointer and lands where you click. Move it over a body and it lies down on the face under the pointer, sloped ones too, like Cruise in Tinkercad; over the empty plate it lands on the workplane. Esc cancels placing. A tool that waits for a click, such as the tape measure, the framing square, a note, “Posicionar plano de trabalho”, “Deitar sobre a face” or the edge tools, is switched off when you pick a shape, so the click places the shape. The other way round, switching one of those tools on puts the shape down again. If you would rather have the shape appear in the middle of the plate, you can switch off placing by click in the settings (area “Aparência”, switch “Cruise ao adicionar formas novas”).

On a face the shape snaps to the middle of that face when the pointer comes near it, as a corner or an edge snaps; hold Alt to set it down anywhere. Dragged from the library onto a face instead, it always lands in the middle of the face, or with Alt where you let go.

What the library offers:

  • “Basic shapes”: “Caixa”, “Caixa arredondada”, “Cilindro”, “Cápsula”, “Elipse”, “Polígono” (three to twenty-four sides), “Rampa”, “Esfera”, “Cone”, “Cone curvo” (its side bends inward into a trumpet like a pseudosphere or outward into a dome; “Diâmetro do topo” and “Curvatura” set it, and it can be hollowed out and filleted like any exact body), “Pirâmide” (with three to twenty-four sides, so three-sided too), “Telhado arredondado”, “Meia esfera”, “Paraboloide” (a dome that narrows to a rounded tip, its height falling with the square of the distance from the axis) and “Toro”.
  • “Vessels, tubes & transitions”: the “Transição” from one outline to another, say from square to round, the “Tubo”, the “Tubo curvado”, made of up to twelve straight pieces with bends in between, and the “Vaso”.
  • “Holes & cut-outs”: the “Rebaixo” and “Escareado” for screw heads, the “Furo em gota” for horizontal holes and the “Abertura de conector” for USB, HDMI, DisplayPort and RJ45 sockets.
  • “Connections”: “Rosca” (threaded rod, screw, nut and tapped hole), the “Arruela de acabamento” under a countersunk screw, the print-in-place “Dobradiça” and the “Rabo de andorinha”. More in Threads and mechanics.
  • “Enclosure parts”: the “Screw boss” for heat-set inserts and self-tapping screws, the “Snap-fit” with its catch and the “Rib” or gusset. More in Threads and mechanics.
  • “Mechanics & moving parts”: “Mola”, “Engrenagem”, the “Junta Hirth” and the “Polia GT2”.
  • “Systems & templates”: “Gridfinity” bins and baseplates, and the “Placa SBC”, a single-board computer true to size to build a case around.
  • “Lettering & signs”: “Texto”, also along a circular arc, the “Etiqueta de nome”, the “Etiqueta de ícone” and the “QR code”. More in Text.
  • “Decorative outlines”: “Estrela”, “Coração”, “Meia-lua” and the “Serrilhado” for grips.
  • “Helpers”: the “Régua”, which is only a measuring tool and never shows up in an export.

You get a triangle in two ways: the “Polígono” with three sides is an isosceles triangle, the "Roof" of Tinkercad, and the “Rampa” is a right triangle. Both are true triangular prisms. For a triangular hole, copy the shape, make the copy smaller, mark it as a hole and line it up with “Centralizar no plano de trabalho” or “Alinhar”. Both work with the shape's bounding box, the smallest box that encloses it, so a halved square still counts as a whole square. The command search (Ctrl+K) also finds both shapes under "triangle" or "roof".

The “Cápsula” can be narrower at one end than at the other, say for a guard over a belt between two pulleys. Under “Propriedades” set “Ponta menor (diâmetro)”; the large end is as wide as the capsule, and the sides run straight from one arc to the other. “Distância entre centros” is the distance between the two arcs' centres, that is how far apart the pulleys are. Change the small end and the centre distance stays, the capsule getting longer or shorter. The tapered capsule stays an exact body too, for fillets and STEP.

The shape's settings

As soon as a shape is selected, its settings appear on the right. At the top is the name; the pencil beside it (“Renomear”) lets you type a new one. Enter keeps it, Esc cancels, and an empty name brings back the shape's default name. Further right, the padlock locks the shape against accidental moving and the eye hides it. The arrow on the far left folds the settings down to their title bar. The cards below fold open and shut with a click on their title (“Propriedades”, “Posição”, “Rotação”, “Afunilamento”, “Torção e inclinação” and the cards of the special shapes); layerling remembers which ones you left open, for the next shape and the next visit.

The settings sit docked at the right edge. If they cover something you want to see, drag them by their title bar and they float wherever you drop them; they stay there for the next shape too. Drop them back at the top right, or double-click the title bar, and they dock again. While they float or are folded down, the snap step moves from the bottom of the settings to the bottom right of the workplane.

  • “Sólido” or “Buraco”: A solid stays, a hole takes material away. A click on “Sólido” opens the colours; colours of your own that you mix there wait under “Usadas recentemente” afterwards, the last eight. More in Solids and holes. The pin in the row “Guardadas” keeps the colour you have chosen for good: it stands in a row of its own, newer colours never push it out, and the same pin lets go of it again; up to 21 colours are kept in this browser.
  • “Transparente”: Lets you see through the body, for example to spot a shape behind it.
  • “Multicor”: For a group or a bundle; Shift+M switches it. Switched on, every part of the group shows in its own colour, also in a group that was cut with holes into one body (the walls a hole leaves take the colour of the body they were cut into). Picking a colour for the group switches it off and colours the whole group; the parts keep their own colours underneath, so switching it on again brings them back. A bundle has it switched on to begin with, and when it is switched off the bundle shows and exports in one colour. A group of solids only that you make starts with it switched off and shows as one body; groups made before keep showing their parts' colours. In a 3MF export every part keeps its colour, so the slicer can map the parts onto filaments; OBJ carries the colours on its points, so the border between two colours is a little rougher there.
  • “Propriedades”: The dimensions and everything that belongs to this shape. For a cylinder the diameter, the height and the number of sides. For a round tube or ring the “Diâmetro externo”, the “Diâmetro interno” (for a bushing on a shaft of a known size) and the wall thickness: any two give the third, in whatever order you type them. The outer diameter keeps the bore and changes the wall, the inner diameter keeps the outer one and changes the wall, and a bore wider than the tube makes the outer diameter grow by the wall. The tube's length is its height. A tube that is not round, after you pulled one of its sides, has the sides Length and Width instead of the one outer diameter; there the wall stays when you change the width. For a gear the teeth, for a spring the turns. A value you have moved away from its default gets a small arrow next to its name: a click takes just that value back, whatever else you did since, unlike Undo. A double click on a slider does the same, here and for the sliders in the workspace settings. Dragged with the mouse, the slider of a length snaps to the snap step, so a height comes out in whole millimetres (not with the grid off, and not on short sliders); a typed value and the arrow keys on the slider stay exact. “Salvar como padrão” at the bottom makes the current values the start values of this kind of shape (the same as “Padrões das formas” in the settings), and “Restaurar padrões” goes back to the app's own. With “O furo corta como vazio ao agrupar” the bore counts as a hole once the tube is grouped: it then also cuts the wall of what the tube is grouped with, so two tubes in a T-junction open into each other. A bent tube with an opening has the same switch.
  • “Transformar em elipse”: Only on a cylinder. A cylinder is always round: it has one diameter, and every handle changes both sides together. For an oval, click this and it becomes an “Elipse” - the same body, whose length and width you then set one by one. A cylinder with a chamfer, a fillet or a wall, or a turned or grouped one, cannot be changed this way; take the “Elipse” from the start for those.
  • “Afunilamento”: Different sizes at the top and bottom, for example for a slope or a funnel. With “Manter proporções” switched on, Length and Width of the same end change together in the ratio they have, so a square top stays square; top and bottom stay separate.
  • “Torção e inclinação”: Twists the top against the bottom or shifts it sideways. That gives twisted columns and leaning towers.
  • “Inclinação no comprimento”: Runs the top down towards one end. “Extremidade mais baixa” picks the end, “Altura na ponta” or “Inclinação (°)” how low it goes, and “Curvatura (%)” whether the top runs straight (0), bulges up (above 0) or sags (below 0). The other end keeps the body's height. Once it is set, an orange dot sits on the top of the lower end; drag it up and down like the height. That gives a roof whose height runs down along its length, a ramp or a slanted pipe end.
  • “Afunilamento no comprimento”: Seen from above, runs both long sides in evenly towards one end, so that end stays in the middle. “Extremidade estreita” picks the end, “Largura na ponta” its width (0 makes a point), “Começa em (%)” where along the length the narrowing begins (0 % at the wide end, 50 % in the middle), and “Curvatura (%)” whether the sides run straight (0), bulge out like a boat's bow (above 0) or are drawn in (below 0). Its orange dot sits on the side of the narrow end and moves across. Together with “Inclinação no comprimento” it makes a bow or a ridge that runs down and in at once.

Taper and twist work on almost every shape. Only the gear, thread, spring, Gridfinity, hinge, pyramid, bent tube, teardrop, port opening, the screw-head cutters and the ruler leave them out: they have fixed measures of their own or, like the pyramid, a top of their own already.

“Salvar como padrão” keeps what you changed on this shape as the start of every new shape of its kind: the sizes, the settings of the shape and its colour. Colour a cylinder green, press the button, and every cylinder you add from then on is green; the other kinds keep their own colours. “Restaurar padrões” takes the kind back to what the app starts it with. The kinds that have defaults of their own are marked in the settings under “Padrões das formas”. A new design that you start from the start page begins with them too; the values are kept in this browser.

A tapered or leaning box, cylinder, ellipse, polygon, tube or ring keeps its exact shape, and so do the capsule, star, heart, crescent, dovetail a rounded box without rounded top and bottom edges, and a straight or round knurl (its chamfered ends narrow with it): chamfers and fillets work on it as on the plain shape, and the STEP export writes it. The same holds for a twisted shape: its section turns exactly as it rises, and the sides wind evenly from bottom to top.

“Inclinação no comprimento” is offered on the box, rounded box, cylinder, ellipse, polygon, tube, ring, wedge and round roof. The wedge and the round roof lie along their depth, so they slope to the front or the back only. The sloped body keeps its exact shape, so chamfers, fillets and the STEP export work on it as on the plain shape; only a rounded box with rounded top and bottom edges, and a slope together with a taper, a twist or a lean, stay on the display mesh.

“Afunilamento no comprimento” is offered on the same shapes except the tube and the ring, whose wall would get thinner across than along. A narrowed box, and a wedge or round roof narrowing, sloping or both, keep their exact shape in the same way. For now the display mesh only covers the rest: a narrowed cylinder, ellipse, polygon or rounded box, and a box that slopes and narrows at once. Chamfers, fillets and the STEP export then work on that mesh rather than on an exact body.

Typing is more exact than dragging. All number fields take millimetres, but also percentages: type "50 %" into a width of 40 mm and you get 20 mm. They calculate too: "15*3", "120-2*4" or "(40+2)/2" give 45, 112 and 21; x works instead of *. The field remembers the calculation, in the properties panel as well as in the dimension boxes around the selected body: click into it again later and the formula stands there instead of the number, as long as the value still matches it, and you change it in place, "(140+2)/2" becoming "(40+6)/2". Drag the body by a handle or scale it and the formula no longer fits, so the field shows just the number again. In a number field you have clicked, the mouse wheel and the keys ↑ and ↓ change the value by one step, with Shift a larger step and with Alt a finer one. In a size or position field Shift steps by the snap grid instead, and by ten steps when the grid is off. It also works without clicking into a field: hold the mouse button down on the name of a value, say "Width", and drag left or right; the value changes as you drag, with the same keys as the wheel.

Choosing colours

A click on “Sólido” in the properties of a body opens the colour card, headed “Cor da forma”. On top it shows the hex value of the colour the body has now. Under it are the ready colours of the palette; a click on one colours the body and closes the card.

“Personalizada” opens the colour picker of your browser, for a colour of your own. What it offers depends on the browser: in Chrome and Edge it has a colour field, a slider for the hue, an eyedropper that takes a colour from anywhere on the screen, and the value as HEX, RGB or HSL, which you switch with the arrows beside it. The colour counts when you close the picker or click outside it.

A colour of your own that you mix there waits under “Usadas recentemente” afterwards, the last eight. The pin in the row “Guardadas” keeps the colour you have chosen for good: it stands in a row of its own, newer colours never push it out, and the same pin lets go of it again; up to 21 colours are kept in this browser. The pin is for colours of your own, the ones of the palette are always there. With several colours selected, or with a hole, there is no single colour to keep.

The colours of the work area in the settings have a simpler picker of their own, with a colour field, a row of ready colours and a field for the hex value; see The settings.

How round is round? The side count

Round shapes such as cylinder, cone, tube, ellipse or the bores have the switch “Lados acompanham o tamanho” and the slider “Lados” in their properties. The “Toro” has two sliders: “Lados do anel” around the ring and “Passos do tubo” around the tube. They follow the size there too until you hold them, so a large torus shows no facets. The reason: for the view and for STL, 3MF and OBJ, layerling draws a circle as a polygon of many small sides. The more sides, the smoother it is, and the more triangles it takes.

The “Espessura do tubo” sets how thick the tube is seen from above. The height only squashes or stretches the tube, so a flat ring keeps its hole; at half the outer size the hole closes. Dragging the handles scales the tube along. Only a torus whose tube is as thick as the torus is high stays an exact body for chamfers, fillets and STEP.

Where the side count matters

  • In the export for the slicer (STL, 3MF, OBJ). A cylinder with few sides arrives there as a polygon.
  • When bodies and holes are combined. A bore cut by a hole with few sides is angular in the finished part. That includes screw holes.
  • In the view. Many very fine shapes slow the editor down.

Where it does not matter

  • For the STEP export. It writes the round shape, not the polygon.
  • For chamfers and fillets (“Chanfro”, “Arredondamento”) as long as the shape stays round. That is the case when you have not set a side count, when the count is at least the shape's default, or when the polygon strays at most 0,05 mm from the circle. The default is 96 sides for cylinder, ellipse, tube and cone, 64 for the “Telhado arredondado”, 24 steps for the “Esfera”, 32 for the “Meia esfera” and the “Paraboloide”, 96 sides and 24 steps for the “Toro”, and a “Qualidade” of 32 for a round “Tubo curvado”.
  • For a thread, a spring or a helical or herringbone gear. The edge tool and the STEP export take its exact body; its “Qualidade” only sets how finely it is drawn.

Where it matters again

  • For chamfers and fillets on a shape with few sides. If you set the side count below the default, the edge tool takes the shape as it is drawn: a cylinder with 6 sides stays a hexagonal bar, and the fillet runs round its six edges. That is how you can build, for instance, a nut pocket with rounded corners. For a round shape, leave “Lados acompanham o tamanho” on.

How to use it

  • Leave “Lados acompanham o tamanho” on. Then layerling picks the side count from the diameter so that the polygon strays at most 0,005 mm from the true circle, far below what a printer resolves. Small shapes get at least 24 sides, large ones more.
  • Fewer sides you take when you want a polygon on purpose (but there is the “Polígono” for that) or when the editor gets slow with very many round shapes.
  • More sides you hardly ever need. Only on very large round parts, when you see edges in the STL.
  • For parts you only treat with edges or hand on as STEP, the side count does not matter.

Working with the handles

Besides the settings there are handles on the shape itself:

  • The corners and edges make the shape larger or smaller. Drag one past the opposite side and the shape keeps growing there, on the other side of that edge. The arrow on top does the same below the base. Hold Shift while dragging a corner to scale width, depth and height together and keep the proportions; hold Alt to scale from the center instead of the opposite corner. Without a keyboard, or if you do not want to hold a key, switch on “Manter proporções” at the top of the properties: then the corners always keep the proportions, and typing one of width, depth or height scales the other two by the same factor. The setting is remembered.
  • The black arrow above the shape lifts or lowers it; with Alt held from the start, a copy is made where you let go, so you can stack. The handle on the top face changes the height. The handles that change one measure carry the colour of its axis, as the curved arrows do: the middle of a side (width red, depth green) and the top (height blue); the corners change two measures and stay white.
  • The red and the green arrows on top move the shape along X or along Y only. The shape then follows the mouse along that line, even when you look at the plate from low down, where a free drag runs off far. It snaps to other shapes as a drag does, and afterwards you can click the distance moved and type the exact value.
  • The curved arrows rotate it.
  • The numbers beside the shape show the dimensions. A click on one opens a field in which you type the number you want. With Enter the shape grows from the edge opposite the number, as when you drag; with Alt+Enter it grows round its middle, so a shape that was aligned with another stays aligned. With “Manter proporções” ticked in the properties, or with Shift+Enter, the other two dimensions follow by the same factor. That holds for width and length; the height always grows upward from the underside. The fields in the properties on the right keep the middle without a key. Tab keeps the number and opens the next one (width, depth, height); Shift+Tab goes back. In a field of the properties that you have clicked, the mouse wheel changes the value as well: a unit a notch, ten times as much with Shift (in a size or position field the snap grid), a tenth with Ctrl and a hundredth with Alt. A field that you have not clicked leaves the wheel to the panel, which scrolls.
  • A click on a corner (without dragging) opens width and depth together. Type the first, press Tab for the second and Enter to apply both. Esc cancels.

Once a shape is turned by right angles, for instance laid on its side with “Deitar sobre a face”, the fields in the properties are named after the direction each measure runs in now: “Altura” is what goes up, “Largura” runs along X and “Comprimento” along Y. Typing the height of a shape lying down therefore changes the vertical measure, and its underside stays on the plate. A shape tilted at any other angle shows its own measures in the fields, and a note below says so.

Without the mouse, use the keyboard: the arrow keys move the selection by one snap step (0.01 mm when the grid is off), with Shift by five, or by ten if you set “Linha mais escura da grade a cada” to “10 incrementos da grade” in the settings under “Aparência”: as far as the next darker line, as in Tinkercad. They follow the view: → moves to where the screen's right is, ↑ away from you, even after turning the plate. Push a shape out of the picture and the view moves along. Ctrl+↑ and Ctrl+↓ raise and lower it. A run of arrow presses is one step in the history: as long as the next press follows within a second and a half, Undo takes back the whole run, not a press at a time. R rotates by 45°, Shift+R by 22.5°. D drops the selection onto the workplane.

The handles pull a shape as large as your plate, at least 220 mm wide and deep. Typing a number in the properties goes beyond that, and a shape made that large does not shrink back when you grab it again. A ceiling of your own per shape is set in the settings under “Padrões das formas” with “Limite de tamanho personalizado”.

The snap step is at the bottom right of the editor and can be changed at any time.

Copying and duplicating

“Copiar”, “Colar” and “Duplicar” are in the ribbon (“Área de transferência”). Ctrl+D duplicates a selection. layerling remembers how you last moved or rotated the copy and applies the same again on the next duplicate. That produces a row of holes or steps in a few key presses. For regular arrangements there is also the pattern, described in Selecting and arranging. If you also resized the copy, every further copy grows by the same factor again, as in Tinkercad. A shape you gave a name of your own gets a copy that is called after it, "Holder (copy)", then "Holder (copy 2)" and so on, so the object list stays readable; a shape that only has the name layerling handed out ("Box") keeps it.

Tip: If a shape refuses to take the size you want, it is often the limits for new shapes. Under “Padrões das formas” in the settings you decide how each shape starts and how large it may get.

Custom shapes

A holder, a grip or a base plate you need again and again goes into the “Formas personalizadas”. They sit at the top of the shape library, above the “Formas básicas”, and fold away with their arrow.

  1. Select one or more bodies, holes, groups or an imported model included.
  2. Open the shape library and click “Salvar seleção”. Enter a name and confirm with “Salvar”.
  3. In any design, a click on the tile inserts the shape, like any other shape. You can also drag the tile onto the workplane; it then lands where you let go. The shape then hangs on the pointer, like any other: it follows it, also over the faces of other bodies, and a click sets it down; Esc puts it away.

Several bodies come back together, placed as they stood to each other, and stay selectable one by one. Notes pinned to the saved bodies go along and come back closed, pinned to the inserted ones; free notes and reference points stay in the design. The pencil on a tile renames it, the bin removes it after asking. Shapes already inserted into designs stay as they are.

The “Formas personalizadas” live in this browser, apart from the designs, and are there again the next time you start. “Fazer backup de tudo” on the start page backs them up with the designs, and opening the backup brings both back. To take only the shapes to another browser, “Fazer backup das formas personalizadas” (the arrow pointing down) saves them as a ZIP file and “Carregar formas” (the arrow pointing up) brings them back there. “Carregar formas” also takes single .lyl designs; each one becomes a shape. Shapes already there are not added twice.

Folders

Many custom shapes sort better into folders. “Nova pasta” (the folder with the plus, next to “Salvar seleção”) asks for a name and makes a folder at the top; the folder with the plus on a folder, “Nova subpasta”, makes one inside it. Folders go three levels deep: a folder on the third level holds shapes but no further folders. Folders sit above the shapes that are in none, in the order of their names, and open and close with their arrow; the number on a folder counts the shapes in it and in the folders inside it. When saving, choose the folder in the list next to the name; “Sem pasta” keeps the shape at the top.

The folder with the arrow on a tile moves that shape into another folder, or back out with “Sem pasta”. The pencil on a folder renames it, the bin deletes it after asking, together with the folders and shapes in it. A folder itself cannot be moved: make the new one where it belongs and move the shapes over. A backup keeps the folders, and loading it puts the shapes back in the same place.

Custom shapes on the server

With the shared server store switched on, the section shows two groups: “No servidor” and “Neste navegador”. When saving you choose where the shape goes; the server is chosen to start with. There it lives in the folder Custom shapes, as a .lyl file of its own with a picture, ready on every device that reaches the server; its folders are folders inside Custom shapes. Each side has folders of its own, and a shape moves between the folders of its side. The cloud on a browser tile puts that shape on the server; it is then no longer kept twice.

The Custom shapes folder shows on the start page as well. Open a shape there like a design, change it, and it is saved automatically like any design on the server; the next insert takes the new version. As the server store has no login, everyone who reaches the server sees the same shapes.

Wrapping around a cylinder

Should a pattern, a logo or lettering go onto a cup, a can or a tube? First lay it flat on the plate, as an imported SVG or as text for example, the way it should look from above. Then wrap it around a cylinder in the shape's settings under “Envolver em um cilindro”:

  1. Open “Envolver em um cilindro” and enter the “Diâmetro” of the cylinder wall, such as the outside diameter of your cup. Tenths of a millimetre work too, such as 63.5.
  2. Click “Envolver”. What ran from left to right now runs around the cylinder, the back edge becomes the top, and the thickness stands out of the wall.
  3. Select the wrapped shape and the cylinder and centre both, left to right and front to back. The middle of the wrapped shape is the cylinder's axis, so it then sits right on its wall.

Every body can be wrapped, a shape from the library too: a round roof, say, that should sit on the wall of a round tower. Lay it on the plate the way it should look on the wall, its round top at the back.

For an engraving, switch on “Para dentro (gravação)”: the thickness then goes into the wall. Make the shape a hole, centre it and group it with the cylinder.

A shape that is wrapped already is a mesh of the wrapped thing and cannot be wrapped again: undo the wrapping, or wrap the flat original once more with another diameter.

The result is a mesh like an imported model. Undo lays the shape flat again; for another diameter, undo first and wrap again. It cannot go further than once around the cylinder; then layerling names the smallest diameter that fits.

A surface texture

Grooves, knurling, honeycomb or bumps on a body, for a better grip or for looks: open “Textura de superfície” in the shape's settings. The button “Textura de superfície” in the “Modificar” group at the top does the same: it opens and closes the card for the selected body and stays lit while the card is open.

  1. Choose the “Padrão”, its “Espaçamento” and its “Profundidade”. “Direção” says whether it goes into the body or stands out of it. For “Saliências”, “Formato da saliência” chooses between “Meia esfera”, “Cone (pontiagudo)”, “Suavemente arredondado” and “Topo plano”. Under “Disposição” they sit “Desencontradas”, every other row half a spacing along, or in “Fileiras retas”.
  2. Under “Modo de aplicação”, take “Em volta de um eixo” for round bodies such as a cup, a knob or a handle. The pattern runs round the “Eixo”, and the spacing is rounded a little so that a whole number of grooves or cells goes round: the pattern closes without a seam. “Por todos os lados” suits bodies that are not round, “Plano, na direção do eixo” a lid or a plate seen from above. Leave it at “Automático” and Layerling chooses for you: “Em volta de um eixo” on round bodies and on angular ones standing upright such as a box - the pattern then follows the outline and runs round the edges without a seam, a pattern standing out bending round them -, “Por todos os lados” on other angular ones.
  3. Click “Aplicar textura”. A large body takes a few seconds; you can keep working meanwhile.

To give the pattern to only some faces, say only the top of a box, click “Escolher faces” and then the faces in the view: the top, the bottom or a side. A face reaches up to the body's sharp edges; on a cylinder the mantle is one face, and the top and the bottom are one each. Picked faces light up, a second click takes one out again, and “Voltar a todas as faces” gives the pattern the whole body again. Only the picked faces get the pattern; all others stay as they were and keep few triangles. On a top or a bottom the pattern lies flat; on a round top, grooves, rope and knitting run in rings round the middle, like a tree's year rings. “Direção no topo e na base (°)” turns the pattern on the top and bottom: at 0° the rows run along the front edge, at 90° along the side edge. “Estilo no topo e na base” switches grooves, rope and knitting there between rows and rings; on an angular body the rings follow its outline. “Aresta do topo e da base” says what happens at the edge between the side and a patterned top or bottom: “Termina na aresta” lets both end at the edge. With “Lateral sobre o topo” the side's pattern bends round the edge and takes the whole top: rows of rope, knitting and level grooves run on as rings, upright and slanted grooves as rays almost to the middle. “Dobra curta” does the same as a rim only; inside lies the top's own pattern, as “Estilo no topo e na base” sets it. “Moldura” lays a border round the edge for every pattern – a cord, a cast-off chain or a round bead.
