Cada pino se apoia num pequeno ressalto num encaixe da placa; depois de impresso, balance cada um até que se solte, como o pino do teste de encaixe.
  • “Clearance per side” é a folga entre um pino e o seu furo. Depois que você mediu a folga da sua impressora com o teste de encaixe (no capítulo sobre impressão), ele parte desse valor, senão de 0,2 mm.

“Dovetail” une as metades sem cola, como o corte em rabo de andorinha do OrcaSlicer: uma lingueta que se alarga ao se afastar da face de corte fica de pé na metade cujo nome termina em menos e atravessa a face em linha reta, de borda a borda; a outra metade recebe a ranhura correspondente, aberta nas duas pontas. Deslize as metades uma na outra pelo lado, ao longo da lingueta; depois de encaixadas, elas não podem mais ser separadas no sentido transversal ao corte. As linguetas seguem o lado comprido da face de corte, e quando um sólido encontra o plano em vários pedaços, todas vão no mesmo sentido, para que uma metade entre num só movimento. “Per cut face (0 = automatic)” é o número de linguetas lado a lado em cada pedaço; 0 deixa isso pela largura do pedaço, uma a cada seis larguras de lingueta, pelo menos uma. Ao lado do seu topo largo, uma lingueta mantém metade da própria largura e mais 1,2 mm de material até a borda da face de corte, e duas linguetas o dobro disso entre si. Um pedaço estreito demais para uma lingueta, ou curto demais no sentido dela, não recebe nenhuma, e uma lingueta fica de fora onde a outra metade é mais fina do que a profundidade da sua ranhura. Contornos brancos no plano mostram onde elas vão ficar: a faixa preenchida é o pé da lingueta, a linha em volta o seu topo largo.

  • “Width at the cut face” é a largura da lingueta onde ela sai da face de corte, 6 mm para começar.
  • “Depth into the other half” é quanto ela se projeta da face de corte para dentro da outra metade, 4 mm para começar. A ranhura é 0,3 mm mais funda, para que as metades fechem por completo.
  • “Flank angle” é quanto cada flanco se inclina para fora em relação à perpendicular da face de corte, de 5° a 30°, 15° para começar. Quanto maior, mais largo o topo da lingueta e mais firme ela segura.
  • “Direction (0 = lengthwise)”: 0 deixa as linguetas no comprimento, 90 atravessadas na face de corte, e um ângulo intermediário as gira esse tanto.
  • “Clearance per side” é a folga de cada lado entre a lingueta e a sua ranhura, do seu teste de encaixe como para os pinos. As pontas da lingueta são chanfradas em volta para que ela encontre a ranhura, e a ranhura tem um chanfro na boca.

Para imprimir, apoie a metade com a ranhura sobre a sua face de corte e imprima a metade com a lingueta ao contrário, com a face de corte para cima: assim os flancos da lingueta se inclinam para fora só pelo seu ângulo, o que se imprime sem suportes.

Furos são divididos sem conectores.

As metades são malhas simples: configurações como os lados de um cilindro ou as letras de um texto se perdem, então ajuste isso antes. Ctrl+Z traz o original de volta num só passo. Objetos bloqueados e ocultos não podem ser divididos.

Uma malha importada precisa de uma superfície fechada para ser dividida, agrupada ou recortada. Se ela tiver aberturas, como os olhos de uma figura deixados abertos ou uma rachadura num escaneamento, layerling as fecha antes com uma tampa plana e diz quantas fechou. Ele fecha qualquer abertura pequena e qualquer abertura plana, seja do tamanho que for; uma abertura grande cuja borda não está toda no mesmo plano fica por sua conta, e a mensagem avisa. Feche-a no programa de onde o modelo veio, ou com uma ferramenta de reparo de malha, e importe de novo.

Separando peças

Se uma forma é composta de vários pedaços separados, como um texto feito de letras soltas, “Separar peças” a divide em formas independentes. A opção também está no menu que aparece com um clique direito na forma.

Dica: Faça os buracos sempre um pouco mais compridos que a peça que eles devem atravessar. Se o buraco termina exatamente rente à face, às vezes sobra uma película finíssima. Um milímetro a mais garante o corte.

6. Breaking edges and hollowing bodies

Chamfer and fillet on chosen edges, walls of equal thickness for boxes, cups and cases.

Este capítulo ainda não foi traduzido para o português. Segue o texto em inglês.

Chamfering and filleting edges

Sharp edges rarely look good on a printed part, and they are not particularly strong either. A chamfer cuts the edge off at an angle, a fillet rounds it. Both act on the edges you click.

  1. Select the body (or the group).
  2. Click “Arredondamento” or “Chanfro” in the ribbon, press B for the fillet or Shift+B for the chamfer, or right-click the body and pick it from the menu.
  3. The body's edges light up. Click those that should be affected. Another click takes an edge out again. With Shift you add or remove a single edge.
  4. Set the size and confirm with “Aplicar” or Enter. Afterwards the window stays open on the new body with the same size, so the next fillet or chamfer can follow at once; “Concluído”, Esc or the cross closes it. With Shift or Ctrl a click on “Arestas de cima”, “Arestas de baixo”, “Arestas verticais” or “Arestas horizontais” adds those edges to the ones picked instead of replacing them.

The tool window sits at the top right. If it covers edges you want to click, drag it away by its title bar; it opens there next time too, and so do “Vazar” and “Padrão”. Double-click the title bar to put it back.

Picking a shape from the shape list while the tool window is open closes it without applying anything, and the edges you clicked are forgotten. The click then places the new shape instead of picking edges.

In the tool window you find:

  • “Todas as arestas vivas” selects every edge at once, “Limpar” empties the selection.
  • “Raio” for the fillet. For the chamfer you set “Distância” or “Ângulo”.
  • “Raio variável” (fillet only) lets the radius change along one edge: small at one end, larger at the other, evenly in between, as where a straight wall meets a slanted one. Click a single edge, then set “Raio no início” and “Raio no fim”. Which end counts as the start follows from how the edge was built; if the larger radius comes out at the wrong end, “Trocar as pontas” turns it round. It works on one edge at a time, so round several edges one after the other. “Editar” brings both values back.
  • “Côncavo (escavar)” (fillet only) turns the fillet round: instead of rounding the edge off, it cuts a quarter-round scoop out of it, like the notched corners of a box. The scoop is a cylinder of the chosen “Raio” lying along the edge, so it works for any angle between the faces, but on straight edges only, and not together with “Raio variável”. “Editar” brings it back.
  • “Limite de aresta viva” decides which edges count as sharp at all. A value of 25° treats only clear kinks as edges and leaves flat transitions alone.
  • “Arestas verticais” picks the edges that stand straight up, such as the corners of a box: one fillet then rounds all the vertical corners at once.
  • “Arestas de cima” picks only the edges along the very top of the body. It is the quick way for a cookie cutter: build the outline in a sketch as a stroke, then chamfer the top edges. “Ângulo” sets how steep the chamfer is; it cannot reach further than the wall is thick.
  • “Arestas de baixo” picks only the edges along the very bottom of the body, the mirror of “Arestas de cima”. It is the quick way to round or chamfer only the foot of a part.
  • “Chanfro com arredondamento”, chosen at the top of the chamfer window next to “Chanfro”, makes the printable foot of a part: a chamfer at the plate that blends tangentially into a fillet toward the wall, so the first layers need no support and the edge still ends soft. “Distância” is the height the foot takes up, “Ângulo” (15° to 75°) the steepness of the chamfer at the plate. Pick the edges with “Arestas de baixo”.
  • “Só arestas visíveis” hides the edges that lie behind the body from where you look. By default every edge shows through the body, which gets confusing on a busy part; with the switch on you see, and can click, only the edges facing you. Turn the view to reach the others. An edge drawn in red (see below) always shows.
  • “Um clique também escolhe arestas que continuam suavemente”: a click then also picks edges that flow smoothly into each other, for example all edges around a face with rounded corners. The switch only decides what a click picks: the CAD kernel always carries a chamfer or fillet on along such smoothly continuing edges. The tool window tells you along how many more edges that happens.
  • “Manter o tamanho da aresta ao redimensionar” keeps the chamfer or fillet as large as it is, even if you scale the body later.
  • “Qualidade da prévia” (“Rascunho”, “Padrão” or “Fina”) decides how finely the preview is calculated. For difficult parts “Rascunho” is faster.
  • The window keeps its settings in this browser, one set each for chamfer, fillet and chamfer-fillet: size, angle, threshold, preview quality and the switches stay as you left them after “Aplicar”, after an undo and the next time you open the tool. A size the body cannot take gives way to the one worked out from the body. Only “Um clique também escolhe arestas que continuam suavemente” starts anew: on for a body's first chamfer or fillet, off after that.

While you adjust the size, layerling recalculates the preview. It can take a moment. You may keep adjusting; the last value you chose is what gets calculated.

If the size is too large for the edge, layerling says so and suggests a smaller value. Often one or two millimetres less will do. At sharp angles a fillet needs more room than its radius suggests. On a small screen the tool window scrolls down by itself so the message is in view.

When a selection that worked fails after you click one more edge, that edge turns red and is drawn wider: it is the one that cannot be treated together with the others at this size. Click it again to take it out, or make the size smaller. If you click more edges while the message stands, the first one stays red. When there is no earlier selection that worked - the very first click, or a size you just raised - the edges that fail even on their own turn red, or all of them if it is only their combination.

A fillet along a curved edge has one more limit. Where the edge bends round the outside of the body tighter than the radius, as at the tip of a drop drawn in a sketch or brought in as an SVG, the rounding cannot follow the bend. layerling then says how tight the tightest bend is and draws the edges that have it in red. Choose a radius smaller than that, or draw the bend rounder. A sharp corner is no such bend: two edges meet there, and each is rounded on its own. So round the top edges before you round a corner with a small radius: the rounded corner would be a tight bend for the top.

Before it gives up, layerling tries once more with the short edges at the ends of the picked ones, up to twice the size long. One sits where an earlier chamfer ends on a wall that is still sharp: a short slanted edge in the corner, and the corner cannot be treated while it stays sharp. If that helps, those edges are picked as well, and a message says how many were taken along. And where the picked edges meet in a sharp inner corner, as two discs of a cloud do, a fillet has no room at any size: layerling then rounds those corners first, at the same size or a smaller one, and the message says how many and how much (a chamfer chamfers them).

The edge under the pointer is drawn wider too, so you can see which one a click will pick.

A hole takes “Chanfro” and “Arredondamento” as well, and so do “Vazar”, “Deslocamento” and “Excluir face”: it stays a hole and cuts with its new shape. Rounding the four upright edges of a box hole cuts a pocket with round inside corners, and a hole grown with “Deslocamento” cuts with that much more room. To break the edge where a hole meets the part, treat the finished group instead: that edge belongs to it.

Taking an edge treatment back

A treated body can always be treated again. Select it again and open the tool - Fillet, Chamfer or Hollow, each shows the list: under “Desfazer um tratamento de aresta” you see what is already on it. “Desfazer” takes back a single treatment. Note: if newer treatments lie on top, they go with it, and the tool window tells you how many.

Next to a chamfer, a fillet or a hollowing there is also “Editar”. It takes the treatment back the same way, but opens the tool again at once with the same edges and the old value. You change the value and apply it again: a 3 mm fillet becomes a 5 mm one without clicking the edges once more. If newer treatments lie on top, they go with it here too. This holds for edge treatments you make from now on; older ones only offer taking back, and so do single parts of a group.

On a group, say a cylinder with a hole, the treated edge belongs to the finished body, not to one of its parts. So the group becomes a single body. “Desagrupar” still works on it: it takes the edge features back first and then dissolves the group, in one step that Ctrl+Z undoes. Take the treatment back as described above and the group returns with all its parts. The easiest way is to treat edges last. That goes for threads too: the edge tool takes a thread as its exact body, so a block with a tapped hole in it gets its edges rounded with the thread in place. Working out a thread's edges takes longer than for a plain shape, a few seconds for an M6 and about half a minute for a G1/2 pipe thread.

Good to know: layerling works with real CAD geometry for fillets and chamfers, not just a triangle mesh. That is why a rounded edge is still a rounded edge in the STEP export.

A part imported as STEP keeps its CAD geometry too: chamfers, fillets and hollowing work on the body from the file, however finely the part is drawn on screen. STL, OBJ and 3MF bring only triangles, and a finely drawn part can be too dense for the edge tool. If a part is also available as STEP, import that. “Make exact” turns such a part into an exact body with real planes and cylinders first, see Files, saving and sharing, "Making an imported mesh exact".

Hollowing bodies

Boxes, cups, cases and covers have one thing in common: they are empty inside, with walls of equal thickness. That is exactly what “Vazar” does.

  1. Select the body and click “Vazar”, or right-click the body and pick it from the menu.
  2. Set the “Espessura da parede”.
  3. Under “Lados abertos”, switch on the sides that stay open: “Em cima”, “Embaixo”, “Frente”, “Trás”, “Esquerda” or “Direita”, as many as you like - “Frente” alone makes a slot for a drawer, “Esquerda” and “Direita” a tunnel. With no side switched on the body stays closed all round, with a cavity in the middle. “Fechado (cavidade interna)” switches every side off in one click. “Em cima” is already on when the tool window opens; a click on it closes the top again. A body closed all round looks unchanged from outside: the section view shows the cavity.
  4. Decide whether the “Arestas internas” should be “Arredondadas” or “Vivas”.
  5. Click “Vazar”.

The walls grow inward. The outside stays as it is.

The “Arestas internas” only matter where the inner walls move apart - at a step in the body or around an opening. The corners of the cavity of a plain box are always sharp, with both settings. For a rounded inside, round the outside edges of the body first (see above), then hollow it: the inside follows with the radius minus the wall thickness. If the rounded inside cannot be built, which can happen with an outline made of very many short straight pieces such as a traced drawing, layerling builds the same hollow body with sharp inner corners instead.

For every open side, the body needs a flat face at its very edge on that side. Spheres and free-form shapes therefore cannot be hollowed this way. If the wall is too thick for the body, layerling tells you and asks for a thinner one. A rounded box whose top and bottom edges are rounded as well is such a case: its wall has to be clearly thinner than that rounding, or set the rounding to 0 first.

A body with a pocket - a block with a hole that does not go all the way through, made by grouping a box with a raised hole - can be hollowed too, with the top open: the walls round the pocket are hollowed as well, so a ring of cavity stays between the outer wall and the pocket, open at the top, and a thin cavity lies under the pocket's floor.

Bodies that end in a point, such as a cone or a revolved triangle, have no flat face on top that could stay open. A fully closed cavity does not work there either, because a point cannot be offset inwards: even with a 1 mm wall you get the message that the walls cannot be this thick. Draw the wall into the profile before revolving instead: duplicate the outline, scale the copy down evenly, put it in the middle of the large outline and cut the large one with it, then revolve the whole (chapter Sketches, section Revolve). The distance between the two outlines is the wall thickness.

If you resize a hollowed body later, layerling hollows it again at the new size right away. The wall stays as thick as you chose, round bodies included. A cylinder you pull further one way than the other becomes an ellipse. Fillets and chamfers you laid on it after the hollowing go on again at the same edges.

Tip: With a 0.4 mm nozzle, 1.2 to 2 mm of wall is a good start: thin enough to save material, thick enough for a sturdy part.

A lid for an open body

“Lid” makes the lid for a body that is open at the top: a box you hollowed with its top open, a pot, a tray. Select the body and click “Lid”. In the window you choose the kind:

  • “Push in”: a plate as large as the body with a lip below it that goes into the opening.
  • “Over the top”: a plate a wall wider than the body with a rim below it that goes over the outside.
  • “Both sides”: a plate a wall wider than the body with both: a lip into the opening and a rim over the outside. The body's wall sits in a groove between them, like on a food container.
  • “Flat”: only the plate, to lay on top or glue on.
  • “Screw on”: a cap that screws on like a jar's lid, for a round body; more about it below.
  • “Screw in”: a plate with a threaded plug that screws into the opening of a round body; more about it below.
  • “Bayonet”: a twist lock for a round body, a cap pushed down over lugs and turned; more about it below.
  • “Slide-in”: a plate that slides into a box through one wall, like a wooden pencil box's lid; more about it below.

Then you set the “Lid thickness”, the “Fit” (the “Gap per side” between lid and body: 0.1 mm tight, 0.2 mm normal, 0.3 mm loose, or any value up to 1 mm) and how deep the lip or rim reaches down and how thick its wall is. Click “Make lid”: the lid lies beside the body, turned over with its plate down, so it prints without support. The body stays as it is. The lid follows any outline, round or angular, because it is taken from the body itself just below its rim. A body without an opening at the top only gets a flat lid; for the others, hollow it with the top open first. For a body that is an exact CAD body, such as a rounded box hollowed with Hollow, the lid is one too, with round corners that stay round: round or chamfer its edges with the edge tool like any other. Other bodies, and lids with posts for the magnets, get a lid made of triangles.

Tip: How tight a lid sits depends on the printer. Print a small box with its lid first; if the lid is too tight, take the next looser fit.

Tick “Magnets in the corners” and the lid holds by four round magnets instead of a tight fit. Pick a “Magnet” (6 × 2, 8 × 3 or 10 × 3 mm) or set its “Magnet diameter” and “Magnet height”, and the “Play round the magnet”: 0.1 mm to press the magnets in, 0.2 to 0.3 mm to glue them. Layerling cuts a pocket into each corner of the body's rim and one facing it into the lid's plate, a little deeper than the magnet, so it never stands proud. Where the wall is too thin for a pocket, a post fills the corner from the bottom up to the rim, and the lid's lip goes round it. The body is grouped with its pockets and posts: ungroup it and you have it back as it was. The plate must be at least the magnet's height plus 0.8 mm thick; switching the magnets on makes it so.

Tick “Hinge” and the lid swings open about a pin along a straight side of the body: the back, or the side you pick under “Hinge side” (as in the starting view, where the back faces away from you). Knuckles take turns along it, the outer ones on the body and those between on the lid, “Hinge clearance” apart, and a hole for the pin goes through them all: with a “Pin diameter” of 1.75 mm a piece of filament is the pin; tick “Print the pin too” for a thicker one printed apart. The pin sits tight in the body's part of the hinge, so a piece of filament pressed in stays put, and turns in the lid's: “Pin play (per side)” is its room there on each side, 0.2 mm to begin with; give it more if the lid turns stiffly. In the body's part a printed pin has 0.15 mm on each side, as it comes out at its full width: it still sits firmly, but it can be pressed in. The body's knuckles stand on a 45° slope, so the body prints upright without support; the lid's are flush with its top, so it still prints turned over. “Knuckles (0 = automatic)” at 0 gives about one knuckle per 10 mm. A hinge goes with a lid that pushes in or a flat one; a rim round the outside would hit the back wall as it opens. On a round side, a pot or a tube, the hinge runs where the wall stays within a knuckle's radius of the hinge's line, and the body's knuckles stand on a small block that reaches in to the wall. “Teardrop pin holes (no droop when printed)” (on to start with) gives the pin's holes a point on top as each part is printed, so they do not droop; a printed pin lies on a small flat. Under “Hinge type”, “Flush” puts the knuckles into the wall instead of behind it: the box keeps its size, each part is notched round the other's knuckles, and the lid opens to about 140°. “Pivot pins” makes a lid that lies in the opening on a small ledge and turns on two pins through the side walls, to about 95°; the box keeps its size there too. Both need a straight side and go without magnets.

For a “Flush” hinge, tick “End plugs” to close the pin's hole at both ends, so the pin stays hidden and cannot slide out. The last 4 mm of the hole at each end are then square, standing on a corner so that they too have a point on top and print without drooping, and just large enough for the pin to pass: push the pin in first, then press a plug into each end. The square plugs cannot turn and sit as tight as the pin does in the body; each is cut flush with the outside of the box, rounded corners included (on such a box the hinge runs on into the corners, with plugs or without). They come out beside the lid, lying on a flat side. The pin is shorter by them, and the status bar says how long.

Tip: Press the magnets into the body first. Then set one more magnet on each of them, where it snaps on the right way round, and press the lid down onto them (with a drop of glue in its pockets if they are loose): each magnet goes into the lid facing its partner, so they attract.

Tick “Click bumps” and the lid clicks shut: small round bumps on the outside of its lip (on a lid that goes over the top, on the inside of its rim) snap into dimples that Layerling cuts into the body's wall at the same places, one in the middle of each straight side of 12 mm or more, two on a side over 80 mm, four round a round opening, and none on the hinge's side. “Bump height” is how far each bump reaches into the wall, 0.4 mm to begin with: less for a small box or a stiff lip, more for a firmer click. Under “Handle”, “Pull tab” gives the plate a tab 6 mm out from its front edge (or the edge opposite the hinge), as thick as the plate, so the lid still prints turned over, and “Finger notch” cuts a recess for a finger into the body's front wall just below the lid's edge, always leaving 0.8 mm of the wall; neither goes with a pivot lid, nor do the bumps with a flat one.

Pick “Screw on” and the lid screws on like a jar's: the body gets a thread on the outside of its top, and the cap the same thread inside its rim. This needs a round body, such as a cylinder, a tube or a round pot hollowed with its top open, with a wall at least 0.8 mm thick; a box or an oval is refused. A rim that is rounded or chamfered, as on a vessel revolved from a line with round ends, can stay as it is, for this lid and for “Bayonet” below: the thread or the lugs go on the straight wall under the rounding, and the cap reaches over it. The thread is added to the outside of the wall rather than cut into it, so even a thin wall keeps its strength, and it is grouped with the body: ungroup it and you have the body back as it was. “Thread pitch” is how far the thread climbs in one turn, 3 mm to begin with, as on a jar; the thread is three tenths of that deep (at most 1.5 mm), its flanks at 45°, so the body prints upright and the cap on its plate, both without support. “Turns” is how many times it goes round, and with the pitch how far the cap's rim reaches down. The “Gap per side” is the thread's room on each side, measured across the radius as for a nut; if the cap turns stiffly, take a looser fit. Turn the cap clockwise to close it. Cap and thread are made of triangles, and magnets, a hinge, click bumps and a handle do not go with a screw lid.

Under “Thread” you can pick, instead of “Custom”, the thread of a standard bottle or jar: PCO 1881 is the 28 mm neck of most water and soft-drink bottles, PCO 1810 the older one with a taller thread, GL 45 the thread of laboratory bottles (DIN 168), Mason 70 and Mason 86 the regular and the wide mouth of mason jars. The cap is then made to the standard, so it fits such a bottle or jar from the shop; the standard sets the pitch and how far the cap reaches down, and the “Gap per side” is the room all round its thread. The body gets the neck's thread only if its top is that neck: round, and as wide as the neck under its thread, which the window tells you (24.94 mm for PCO 1881); a cap from the shop then fits the body too. Any other body stays as it is and only the cap is made, as the status bar says. To make a cap for a bottle you have, select a cylinder about as wide as its neck, click “Lid”, and pick “Screw on” and the bottle's thread. A standard's flanks are steeper than the 45° of the custom thread, so the thread's underside on the body and the ridges inside the cap hang over more as they print; they are only about a millimetre deep, but print one cap first to see how your printer manages them. The thread of mason jars has no published drawing, and its sizes are measured ones: try the cap on your jar.

Before you click “Make lid”, the window measures your body's top and says whether it is the neck: how wide it is, how wide the neck must be under the thread, and whether the body gets the thread or only the cap is made. If it is not the neck and the body is a cylinder, a tube or a hollowed cylinder standing upright, “Fit the body to the neck” makes it as wide as the neck, in the middle of what counts (65.85 mm for Mason 70), and keeps its height; a hollowed body keeps its walls as thick as they were. “Make lid” then gives it the neck's thread, and one undo takes the fitting back. For any other body, such as a group or an imported mesh, the window says how wide to make its top.

Pick “Screw in” and the thread goes the other way round, for a pen holder, say, whose outside should stay smooth: the body gets the thread inside its opening, like a nut, and the lid is a plate as large as the body with a plug below it that has the same thread and screws in until the plate rests on the rim. The body and its opening must both be round, with the same middle, such as a cylinder, a tube or a round pot hollowed with its top open, with a wall at least 0.8 mm thick; a box, an oval or a square opening is refused, and so is an opening too narrow or not deep enough for the plug. Here too the thread is added to the wall rather than cut into it: the wall keeps its strength, the outside stays as it was, and the opening is only the thread's depth narrower near the top. “Thread pitch”, “Turns” and the “Gap per side” work as for a screw lid; pitch and turns also set how far the plug reaches down. The plug is hollow, a ring with a “Plug wall” of 1.6 mm to begin with (0.8 mm at least), and stays solid where the opening leaves no room for a hole. The body prints upright and the lid on its plate with the plug standing up, both without support. Turn the lid clockwise to close it. As with a screw lid, lid and thread are made of triangles, and magnets, a hinge, click bumps and a handle do not go with it.

Pick “Bayonet” for a twist lock, as a light bulb sits in its socket, to join the sections of a lamp or close a round box: the body gets lugs standing out of the outside of its top (“Lugs”: three to begin with, two to four), and the cap an L-shaped slot inside its rim for each. Set the cap on with its slots over the lugs, push it down and turn it clockwise until it clicks, 40° with three lugs (45° with two, 30° with four): a ledge in the cap then lies under each lug and holds it down, and a stop ends the turn. “Turn (0 = automatic)” lets you set the turn yourself, up to a quarter turn of 90°, for example for a cap with two lugs that goes on with a 90° twist; at 0 it is the turn the lugs give. Each lug's slot, its turn and a stop before the next slot must fit round the body: with more lugs or on a small body, a turn that does not fit is held to what fits, and the status bar says so. Two lugs reach 90° on all but the smallest bodies; four turn about 65° at most on a body 40 to 80 mm across. Like a screw lid it needs a round body with a wall at least 0.8 mm thick, and the lugs are grouped with the body. They are sized from its diameter, standing a fortieth of it out of the wall (1.2 to 2.5 mm); their undersides and the ledge slope at 45°, so the body prints upright and the cap on its plate, both without support. “Rim depth” is how far the cap reaches down, 8 mm to begin with; below the lugs it guides the cap along the wall. The “Gap per side” is the room round the lugs and along the wall, and starts from your printer's play once you have measured it; “Gap in height” is the room above the ledge, how far the locked cap can lift, 0.3 mm to begin with. “Detent height” is how far a small rib behind each locked lug reaches into its way: the lug clicks past it, so the cap does not turn back by itself. Take less if the cap turns too hard, 0 for none. To open it, turn the cap back and lift it off. Cap and lugs are made of triangles, and magnets, a hinge, click bumps and a handle do not go with a bayonet lid.

Tick “Tether” with a screw or bayonet lid and the cap stays with the body when it is open, as on a drinks bottle. The tether is one part, lying flat beside the cap: two open rings joined by a strap. The larger ring snaps onto the cap from below and sits under a collar round its top, held there by a bead. The smaller one goes round the body just below the cap, on a bead the body gets there, and the thread or the lugs above keep it on: open it a little and push it on over them, or from below over the bead. Both rings turn freely, so the cap still turns on and off, and the strap is long enough for the open cap to hang beside the neck. Print the tether in PETG or TPU; in PLA it takes only a few bends. The beads slope at 45°, so cap and body still print without support, and the rings keep the “Gap per side” round what they turn on. The tether needs a few millimetres of the body below the cap, round and as wide as at the top, and a cap rim about 4 mm deep; where that is missing, the tool says so.

Screw lids and bayonet lids can be flip-tops, as on a bottle of shampoo or ketchup: tick “Flip-top” and the cap's plate gets a round opening in its middle (“Opening”: its diameter, 8 mm to begin with) with a flap in it that closes it, flush with the top. The cap stays on, and you open only the flap. A cap prints on its plate, so a flap folded over from beside it would lie upside down, its plug against the bed; that is why the flap is printed in the opening itself, the “Gap per side” all round it, and is its own plug. Its edge narrows at 45° just below the top, so it rests on the plate and cannot be pushed in, and at the front a catch reaches under the edge of the opening, so it clicks shut. At its straight back a strip 0.4 mm thick and 3 mm long, lying flat on the bed, joins it to the plate and bends as its hinge, so the flap never comes off; under the strip, flap and plate lean towards each other in a V. Nothing slopes more than 45°, and the cap prints in one piece without support. To open the flap, put a fingernail in the groove across it and lift; to close it, press it down until it clicks. Print a flip-top in PETG or PP: in PLA the strip breaks after a few bends. The plate must be at least 1.8 mm thick (with a gap of 0.2 mm), and the opening and its hinge have to fit inside the body's opening; an opening too large is refused with the largest that fits.

Screw caps and bayonet caps can have their top rim rounded or chamfered: under “Top edge” pick “Rounded” or “Chamfer” and set “Edge size”, 1 mm to begin with, at most as much as the plate is thick. The edge is made with the cap, because afterwards cap and thread are one mesh with far too many triangles for the edge tool. The cap prints turned over, so this edge lies on the bed: a chamfer prints cleanly, and a rounding of 1 or 2 mm does too.

Pick “Slide-in” for a lid that slides in like a wooden pencil box's: a plate in the opening, its top flush with the rim, whose edges run in grooves in three walls. The fourth wall, the one picked under “Slides in from” (the front to begin with, as in the starting view), is cut down to the lid's underside where the lid passes, so it slides in over that wall, and the lid's end fills the cut, flush with the wall's outside. A box set down turned on the workplane takes one too: the wall picked is then the one facing most nearly that way. This needs a box with upright, straight walls, rounded corners included; a round body is refused. The grooves go as deep as the “Lid thickness” allows, a little under 1 mm for a 2 mm lid and up to 1.5 mm for a thicker one, always leaving 0.8 mm of the wall behind them; their tops slope at 45°, so the box prints upright and the lid on its top, both without support. If the walls or the lid are too thin for the grooves, the window says how thick they must be. The “Gap per side” is the lid's play in the grooves on each side; if it slides stiffly, take a looser fit. Walls inside the box are cut down under the lid too. Tick “Click bumps” and a small bump under the lid's end clicks past the cut wall, so the lid does not slide out by itself; “Bump height” is how far it reaches below the wall's top. Under “Handle”, “Finger notch” gives the lid four grooves across its top near that end, for your thumb, and “Pull tab” a pull tab there. The grooves and the cut are grouped with the box as a hole: ungroup it and you have the box back as it was. Magnets and a hinge do not go with a slide-in lid.

To sink the lid below the rim, set “Frame above the lid” (0 to begin with). The lid and its grooves then sit that much lower, and the walls keep their full height above them, a frame round the lid. The wall it slides in through is then not cut down either: it keeps its full height, with a slot through it where the lid passes, and the lid's end fills the slot, flush with the outside. Above the lid the slot leaves the same play as at its sides (“Gap per side”), and with “Click bumps” the bump's height more, so the lid can bow up over its bump on the way out; at least 1 mm of the wall must stay above it, and a lower frame is refused with the frame needed (1.2 mm with a gap of 0.2 mm). The box still prints upright: the slot's top is the one place printed over air, a short, level bridge across the lid's width, which most printers bridge without support. The thumb grooves then sit just behind that wall, and a pull tab stands out of the slot.

A cable channel through a body

“Cable channel” runs a round tunnel through a body for a cable or an LED lead, from where it goes in to where it comes out, and finds the way itself. Select the body and click “Cable channel”, then click on the body where the cable goes in (“Entry”) and where it comes out (“Exit”). The way starts and ends straight along the surface, runs straight where it can and bends where it must, never tighter than “Smallest bend”, and keeps as far from the outside as it can, never closer than “Least wall”. A cable pushes through a bend of about five times its diameter; “Diameter” is the channel's own.

While the panel is open the body is seen through, with the channel inside it and a mark on each end. The panel says how long the channel is, its tightest bend and its thinnest wall, and in red when a bend or the wall had to be smaller than asked; a smaller value for “Smallest bend” or another entry or exit helps then. “Set again” moves an end. “Make channel” cuts the channel in: it becomes a “Tubo curvado” as a hole, grouped with the body, so the body stays exact, and after ungrouping the tube can still be changed. A bent tube has at most eleven bends; a way that needs more asks for another entry or exit.

Offsetting bodies

Every face of a body can be moved by the same distance, out or in. That is what a press fit, a lid or a snap joint needs: a gap of 0.1 to 0.3 mm all round while the features stay where they are, which scaling cannot give you.

  1. Select one body and click “Deslocamento”, or right-click the body and choose it there.
  2. Choose “Aumentar” or “Diminuir” and set the “Distância”.
  3. The “Cantos externos” decide the outer corners: rounded keeps the offset surface round there, sharp lets the faces run on until they meet.
  4. Tick “Manter o original e adicionar o sólido deslocado como buraco” to keep the part as it is and get the grown body as a copy that already is a hole. Group that hole with the mating part and it cuts exactly the clearance you chose.
  5. Click “Deslocar”.

Tick “Só os lados: as faces planas de cima e de baixo mantêm a altura” when only the outline should grow or shrink: the sides move by the distance, while every flat top and bottom stays at its height. A sign gets a border all round, a base gets wider, and the body does not get taller. On a stepped body each step keeps its own height. A text that is offset through its outlines keeps its height then too.

Without the tick the body itself is offset. It becomes a fixed exact body, like after a chamfer: the list at the top of the tool window takes the offset back, and “Editar” opens the tool again with the old distance. Only bodies that are exact CAD bodies can be offset - boxes, cylinders and the other shapes, groups of them, imported STEP parts. A body that is only a triangle mesh, such as many STL imports, often cannot be. A distance that is too big for the body, for example a shrink beyond its thinnest wall, is refused.

A text whose letters the kernel cannot offset as a body - in some fonts an A, B, M, N, W or 9 - is offset through its outlines instead: it gets the fill “Mais largo (base para impressão multicolorida)” by the distance (narrower when it shrinks) and grows by as much at the top and the bottom. It stays a text you can go on editing. This works for a text with filled letters and no rounding; one that already has a fill mode is refused as before.

Deleting faces

A fillet in the way, a hole in the wrong place, a boss you no longer need: “Excluir face” takes it off the body again, without building the body anew.

  1. Select the body and click “Excluir face”, or right-click the body and pick it from the menu.
  2. Click every face of what should go: the faces of a rounded edge, the wall of a hole, the side and the top of a boss. A picked face lights up; another click takes it out again. The tool window counts the faces.
  3. Click “Excluir” or press Delete. Esc closes the tool without changing anything.

The faces around the deleted ones grow until the gap is closed. A box with rounded top edges gets its sharp edges back, a hole is filled, a boss is gone. The body stays exact, so it can be filleted and chamfered again and the STEP export keeps its true faces. Ctrl+Z takes the deletion back in one step. It is also listed under “Desfazer um tratamento de aresta” with the fillets and chamfers, where “Desfazer” takes it back; there is no “Editar” for it. On a group, the result is a single body, as with an edge treatment.

Pick all the faces of what should go, and only those. If the faces around them cannot close the gap, layerling says so and nothing changes: a main side of a box, for example, has no neighbour that could take its place. Deleting only the floor of a pocket turns it into a hole straight through, because the walls of the pocket run on to the other side.

“Excluir face” needs exact faces: it works on parts imported as STEP and on layerling's shapes. Whatever layerling keeps as a mesh has none: an imported STL, OBJ or 3MF, a split, wrapped or simplified body, or a very detailed shape such as a long text. Import a part as STEP if you can. On a detailed imported part, a few faces can be too much for the CAD kernel: after 45 seconds the deletion is stopped and nothing changes. A body resized after an edge treatment while keeping its edge size has no exact faces at its new size until the resize is taken back.

An imported mesh made exact with “Make exact” can keep hair-thin faces where the file's triangles were bad, between faces that lie in one plane, so that one side comes out as strips that cannot be deleted on their own. Such a thin face, too narrow to click, goes with a picked face when it touches it and leads on to another face in the picked face's plane, together with the thin faces joined to it that touch a face in that plane too; the tool window counts them as taken along.

7. Sketches: from outline to body

Draw a flat outline, round or chamfer its corners and pull or spin it into a body.

Este capítulo ainda não foi traduzido para o português. Segue o texto em inglês.

Not everything can be put together from basic shapes. For parts with a contour of their own, such as a bracket, a tooth profile or a vase, you first draw the outline and then make a body from it. That is what sketch mode is for.

Starting a sketch

At the top, switch from “Editor 3D” to “Esboço”. In the “Criar” group of the ribbon, three buttons stand side by side for what the outline should become:

  • “Extrusão do esboço”: The outline is pulled upward, like a cookie cutter.
  • “Revolução do esboço”: The outline is spun about an axis, as on a lathe. That gives vases, cups, cones and everything round.
  • “Varredura do esboço”: The outline is pulled along a path: a cable channel that turns a corner, a conduit, a ring round a shape. See Sweeping along a path below.

The editor then shows a sheet with a grid. That is your drawing surface.

The sketch lies on the workplane. To draw on a face of a body, for an outline that should start higher up, say, first put the workplane on that face with W (see View and workplane), then start the sketch.

Drawing

The ribbon in sketch mode is divided into areas. Below, each tool has a card of its own: what you do, one step to a line, and after an arrow what happens then. The key on the right of a card picks the tool.

Drawing tools

Linha1
  • Click points one after another.
  • Hold Shift to snap the new line in 15° steps, horizontal and vertical included.
  • The length and angle of the new line show at the pointer.
  • To type how long it should be, see Lines by numbers.
  • Every point you click lands on the snap grid set under “Grade de encaixe”. With Shift held the 15° step comes first: the length still goes in grid steps, but the end can lie between the grid lines.
Arco
  • Click the two ends of the arc.
  • Click a third point the arc runs through.
  • Until that third click a preview follows the pointer, and the message names the radius.
  • An end clicked on an existing point joins it, so an arc can close an outline.
  • Esc drops the points clicked so far and goes back to “Selecionar”.
  • Once drawn, the arc is ordinary geometry made of points and curves: move, cut or erase it like any other line.
Curva de Bézier2
  • Click a point and drag in the direction the line should carry on, as with the pen tool in Illustrator or Inkscape.
  • The further you drag, the more it bends.
  • The stretch to the new point bends along while you drag, so you see what you get.
  • Coming from Tinkercad and just want to click points? Take the “Curva suave”.
  • The first stretch only bends at its start if you drag at the first point too. Just clicked, the line leaves that point straight; to bend it later, select the point with “Selecionar” and drag its handle.
Curva suave3
  • Click points one after another.
  • It lays a flowing path through the points you click.
  • At the two ends of an open line the curve heads straight for the next point, so the first and the last stretch bend less than the others. To bend one more, select its end point with “Selecionar” and drag its handle. In a closed outline every point bends alike.
Closing or ending a line
  • To close the outline, click the first point again at the end.
  • To end the chain of lines without closing the outline, right-click without moving the pointer, or double-click the last point.
  • A body comes only from a closed outline.
Freehand5
  • Draw with the pen, a finger or the mouse, as on paper.
  • When you lift it, the line becomes ordinary points: a corner where it turned sharply, smooth points in between, only as many as the shape needs, so each can be dragged afterwards.
  • Zoom in for fine detail: the closer you look, the more closely the line follows your hand.
  • A line that ends where it began closes into an outline that can become a body; an open one stays a line, for “Traço” or as a path to sweep along.
  • Start on lines or on a template picture to trace a picture by hand.
  • Begin or end a stroke at an open end to carry that line on, so a shape can be drawn in several strokes.
  • The stroke does not keep to the snap grid, so that it follows your hand. A point you drag afterwards does snap to it, unless “Grade de encaixe” is switched off.

The digits pick a tool as long as no line is being drawn; while one is, they are its length (see below). With “Selecionar” and lines or points selected, the same keys change them instead: 1 makes lines straight and points corners, 2 turns lines into curves and 3 makes points smooth. With nothing selected they pick the tool as before.

Shapes

Adicionar forma ao esboço
  • Pick a ready-made outline: “Retângulo”, “Círculo”, “Oval”, “Semicírculo”, “Fatia”, “Furos em círculo” (a disc with holes), “Triângulo”, “Hexágono”, a “Polígono” or a “Estrela”.
  • Click it to put it at the origin of the sketch, or drag it from the menu to where you want it.
  • At the bottom of the menu, “Lados / pontas” sets the number of sides of the polygon and of points of the star, and “Medida interna da estrela” how deep the star's valleys reach in towards the middle (10 to 90 percent of the outer radius).
  • Both apply to the next shape you add.
  • Like every sketch shape they are ordinary corner points afterwards, so you can move, round or chamfer them one by one.
  • The rectangle starts with the width and depth set for the box under “Padrões das formas” in the settings, the circle and the ellipse with the width of the cylinder there; without a default of your own, and for the other shapes, they start 20 mm across.
Overlapping outlines
  • Push two closed outlines over each other.
  • They stay two bodies, which merge in the 3D editor; the overlap is not a hole.
  • Moving does not join the lines where they cross, so you can pull the shapes apart again.
  • Draw a line across others instead, and layerling puts a point at every crossing.
  • A hole only comes from an outline lying wholly inside another.

Select and change

Selecionar
  • Click a point or a line and drag it to move it.
  • Click inside a closed outline to select the whole outline; inside a hole it picks the hole.
  • You can drag or resize it straight away.
  • Hold Shift and click to add a point or line to the selection or take it away again, so you can move several together.
  • Drag a box over empty space to select everything in it.
  • Drag a line to move it by its two ends, or all of the selection if it is part of one.
  • The arrow keys move the selection by one grid step, Shift with them by a larger one.
  • Hold Shift while you drag to keep the move on one axis.
The frame round the selection
  • Drag a corner handle to change width and height together; hold Shift to keep the proportions.
  • Drag a side handle to change one direction only.
  • Click the width or height pill to type a new size, also as a sum ("60+12.5") or in percent ("150%").
  • Drag the curved arrows beyond the corners to turn the whole selection about its middle.
  • The figure over the pointer shows the angle; with Shift held it moves in steps of 15°.
  • While you turn, a ring appears: with the pointer inside it the turn snaps to 22.5°, outside it goes in whole degrees, whatever the grid.
  • R turns a whole closed outline by 45° at each press.
The bar above the sketch
  • “Manter proporções” keeps the proportions without Shift: the corners and sides then stretch both ways alike, and a typed width or height changes the other one too.
  • layerling remembers the switch.
  • The X and Y fields show where the middle of the selection lies, in mm from the sketch's origin. Type a value to move it there, for a hole exactly 12 mm from the middle, say. Y counts upwards, as in the 3D editor.
  • With two or more outlines selected, the bar lines them up: left, centred or right, and top, centred or bottom, on the frame round all of them.
  • Each outline moves as a whole and keeps its shape; centred both ways, two circles become a ring.
Locking an outlineCtrl+L
  • Click “Bloquear” in the bar to lock the selected outline, like a locked body in the 3D editor.
  • It can no longer be moved, resized, turned or changed. Its lines turn paler, its points grey, and the frame's handles turn grey and no longer respond.
  • Lines may still start at its corners.
  • When outlines are lined up, a locked one stays where it is and the others line up on it.
  • To free it, click the padlock in its corner while it is selected, or click “Desbloquear”.
Adicionar ou remover pontos4
  • Click a section to add a point.
  • Click a point to remove it.
  • layerling joins its two neighbours, so the outline stays closed.
Apagar
  • Click a point or a line to take it away.
  • Drag a window over several to take away everything inside it.
  • With something selected, the button erases the selection.
  • To get rid of only a piece of a circle, for a rounded corner say, click exactly that piece of arc between two points.
  • The rest stays.
Closing a gap
  • Drag one open end onto the other, for example after erasing one side of a hexagon.
  • It snaps there and the two become one point, so the outline is closed again.
  • At a crossing, such as where a line cuts a circle, the sides that run straight on are joined: arc with arc, line with line, and the circle stays round.
Adicionar imagem
  • Put a template picture under the sketch to trace it, see A picture as template.

Clipboard and history

Copy, paste, duplicate, delete
  • “Copiar”, “Colar”, “Duplicar” and “Excluir” work on the selected points, lines and images, as in the 3D editor; Ctrl+X cuts.
  • Pasted and duplicated geometry lands next to the original with a 10 mm gap, on a free spot where it touches no existing line, so it never gets joined to what is already there.
  • It stays selected, so you can drag it straight into place.
  • “Desfazer no esboço” and “Refazer no esboço” take a step back and forward again.

Notes

AnotaçãoN
  • Click “Anotação” under “Controles da vista do esboço”, then click where the note should go: anywhere, on a line too.
  • Drag the pin to move it; a click on the pin folds the card away.
  • The notes of a sketch belong to its body: in the 3D view they sit on top of an extruded or swept body and on the drawn profile of a revolved one, and they move with it.
  • Opening the sketch again shows all of the body's notes, those placed in 3D too.
  • “Desfazer no esboço” takes back a note like a line, and “Cancelar” discards what changed in the notes.
  • More in the chapter Measuring and notes.

View and dimensions

Moving the view
  • Pan with the middle mouse button, or with Shift or Ctrl plus the right mouse button, as in the 3D editor.
  • With nothing selected, Ctrl and the arrow keys slide it too: a tenth of the view a press, half with Shift as well; the sketch moves the way they point.
  • Home fits the whole sketch in the view, F zooms to the selection (with nothing selected, to the whole sketch), and + and − zoom in and out, as in the 3D editor.
  • With nothing selected, double-click an empty spot to slide it to the middle of the view.
  • “Clique duplo no plano de trabalho centraliza a vista ali” in the settings switches the double-click off.
Dimensions
  • Click a line or a point.
  • The sketch shows the length of the line, or for a point the lengths of the lines that meet there.
  • “Mostrar medidas” on the sketch toolbar hides and shows these dimensions when they get in the way, for example while shaping curves.
  • The “Trena” on the sketch toolbar measures the distance between two points; it keeps working with the dimensions hidden.
Typing a length
  • Click the dimension pill of a straight line and type the length in millimetres.
  • Enter applies it, Esc cancels.
  • The line keeps its direction, its start point stays where it is, and the lines at the other end follow. With an end point selected, that one moves.
  • Alt+Enter grows the line to both sides around its middle instead.
  • On curves the pill only shows the length.

Lines by numbers

Once you have set the first point with “Linha” or “Curva suave”, just type a number: two fields open next to the line, “Comprimento” in millimetres and “Ângulo” in degrees. < or Tab moves to the angle, so "50<30" gives a line 50 mm long at 30°, as in AutoCAD. Enter sets the point, and you can type the next line straight away; Esc closes the fields without ending the line chain.

The angle counts counterclockwise from the right: 0° to the right, 90° up, 180° to the left, 270° down. Leave it empty and the line follows the pointer, so you give only the length and show the direction with the mouse. Sums like "40+12.5" work in both fields. If the point would land off the plate, the field says so and waits for another value.

Curving a straight side

Select a straight line and click “Curvar linha” in the bar that appears: the side bows out into a curve, as in Tinkercad, and shows its two handles. Drag them to shape the curve; the further out a handle stands, the stronger the bend. Under the pointer a handle turns orange, and it also catches a click just beside it, so a template image underneath does not move by mistake. “Linha reta” makes the side straight again. A point you select can be made round with “Curva suave”: it gets handles of its own and the lines next to it become curves. With three or more points selected, “Curva por pontos” in the bar lays one flowing curve from the first of them to the last, through every point in between, the way the “Curva suave” tool draws one; the lines beyond the two ends stay as they are. Other programs call this "Fit curve" or "Fit point spline". The two differ: “Curvar linha” bends each selected side on its own and keeps the corners between them, for an arch on one side; “Curva por pontos” runs one curve through the points with no corners left, for smoothing a jagged traced edge. Click a handle and it lights up: the arrow keys then move it by one grid step, with Shift by a larger step, so you can set a curve precisely.

Values can be typed too. A selected point shows “X” and “Y” in the bar: where it lies, in mm from the sketch's origin, with Y counting up. Click a handle and the bar shows “Alça X” and “Alça Y” instead: where the handle lies from its own point. On a smooth point the opposite handle turns along. Give the matching handle on the other side the same Y and the X with the opposite sign, and the curve comes out exactly mirrored; “Espelhar” mirrors a whole half at once.

Reading and typing angles

Click a corner point where two straight lines meet: next to the lengths, layerling shows the angle between them in degrees, with a small arc. On a closed outline it is the angle inside the shape, so a dent reads above 180°. Click the value and type a new angle. One of the two lines then turns about the corner and keeps its length, and the other stays where it is. The line that turns is drawn dashed; Tab switches to the other one, Enter applies and Esc cancels. What hangs at the far end of the turned line goes with it.

A locked point stays where it is, and a typed value works round it: a length moves the free end of the line, and an angle turns the line whose far end is free. A single point can be locked as well: select it and press Ctrl+L. That way you can make an outline exact one corner after the other: lock a corner, type the length and the angle of the next line, lock its end, and go on.

Moving a point changes three angles: at the point itself and at the two neighbouring corners at the far ends of its lines. So layerling shows those two as well, and each can be clicked and typed. That way you set, say, the bottom left corner to 75.5° while the top left point, which moves for it, is selected. You can calculate here too, e.g. "90-14.5".

A corner shows no angle where a curve meets it, or where more than two lines meet. The “Mostrar medidas” button on the sketch toolbar hides the angle together with the lengths.

Rounding or chamfering corners

Click a corner point and choose “Arredondar canto” or “Chanfrar canto”. A small field appears for the “Raio” or the “Distância”. Enter the size and confirm with the check mark. This works for corners between two straight lines.

Several corners at once work too: select them with Shift and a click each, or pull a frame round them, and choose “Arredondar canto” or “Chanfrar canto” from the bar that appears. All of them get the same radius or distance. Where two selected corners share a side, each takes at most 45 % of it, so a rectangle rounded all round comes out alike at every corner. Points that are not a corner between two straight lines are left out, and the message says how many. A frame round a whole shape, or a click inside it, selects its corners and its lines together, and the bar then offers “Curvar linha” and “Linha reta” for all the selected lines next to the corner tools.

Mirroring

Select points and lines (click, Shift and click, or pull a frame round them) and click “Espelhar” in the bar. Then choose the axis: “Esquerda-direita” mirrors across the vertical axis through the middle of the plate, “Cima-baixo” across the horizontal one, and “Por uma linha” across a straight line of the sketch that you click next. The copy is added on the other side and the original stays; nothing is linked, so you can change either on its own. Points that lie on the axis are shared, so a half outline whose ends sit on the axis becomes one closed outline: draw half of a bracket, select it, mirror it and make the body. A construction line makes a good axis. Esc cancels.

Construction lines

A construction line helps you place points without becoming part of the body. It is drawn dashed and never counts as outline: you can pull it as far beyond the shape as you like and the body does not grow.

  • Switch on “Linha de construção” in the “Desenhar” group. New lines, those typed by measure too, are then construction lines. The button switches back to normal lines.
  • A line you have drawn already becomes a construction line when you click it and choose “Construção”. “Transformar em linha” makes it a normal line again.
  • New points snap to where a construction line crosses another line, a blue ring shows it, and to the ends of the construction line. That is how you put a corner on a middle, at a fixed distance from an edge or on a crossing, without calculating.
  • New points also snap to the middle of every straight line of the sketch, to the centre of every circle and rounded corner, and to the middles of the sides of a body shown underneath (#624). A point that is being dragged ignores the middle of its own lines.
  • A selection you drag snaps with its middle (#1236): the centre of a circle or the middle of a rectangle lands on the ends, corners and middles of the other lines, on the centres of circles, where construction lines cross and on the corners of a body underneath; a blue ring shows where. A shape dragged in from “Adicionar forma ao esboço” lands with its middle on these points too. Hold Alt to keep to the grid only.
  • “Linha a partir do meio” in the “Desenhar” group draws a line from its middle: click the middle first, then the end, and the line runs the same length to the other side. The middle becomes a point of its own. Click the button again to draw normal lines.
  • A construction line does not cut the outline apart where it crosses it. When revolving it may lie to the right of the axis too.

Making a body from it

Click “Concluir esboço”. The outline stands as a body on the workplane. In its settings you change the height, the colour and everything else as with any other shape. When you resize it, layerling builds it again from the sketch a moment later, and the sketch grows with it. So it stays an exact body that takes chamfers and fillets, and the next time you edit it the sketch has the size the body has.

If the workplane lies on the side of a body, you draw the way you look at that side: up in the sketch is up on the finished body too. The faint outline of the body in the sketch view shows where it stands. If the workplane cuts through a body, the sketch view shows the outline of that cut instead, so a hollow body appears as a ring and you can line the sketch up with its walls. A point you set or drag close to a corner of these outlines snaps exactly onto it; a small blue ring shows it. That way you take edges of other bodies into the sketch, even when the workplane does not lie exactly on them. To trace round existing work, switch on “Mostrar no plano do esboço todas as arestas das peças ao fundo” (the layers button in the view buttons on the left): all the edges of the bodies are then drawn on the sketch plane, thin and faint, as if you looked through them, whatever height they lie at. A plane that stands upright, set on a front face for example, shows the front view this way. The choice is kept in the browser.

With “Editar esboço” you can return to the sketch at any time to change it. A double click on the body does the same, as in Tinkercad (a locked body stays closed); “Clique duplo abre o esboço” in the settings switches that off. Edge treatments you already made on the body are lost, though, because the edges are created anew. A body you turned or moved in the 3D editor opens where it stands on the plate, turned as you see it there and on the plate's grid; only a tilted or mirrored body opens in its own frame.

A sketch with several outlines makes one body, and outlines that overlap merge in it. To have every outline on its own, select the body and click “Separar peças”: each outer outline becomes a body of its own, with the holes that lie in it, and keeps the body's height, colour and place. Each part has its own sketch to edit, with the construction lines, so you can raise or lower the parts one by one and join or cut them afterwards. Edge treatments block this, as does a body stretched since: it is then taken apart as a mesh.

Another kind of body from the same sketch: the badge at the top of the sketch says what it becomes, “Esboço de extrusão”, “Esboço de revolução” or “Esboço de varredura”. Click it and pick another, also while you edit an existing body: an imported SVG, which comes in extruded, becomes a vase or a knob when you switch it to “Esboço de revolução”. An outline reaching across the axis moves left until its right edge lies on the axis, so the half cross-section of an SVG turns about its straight side; Ctrl+Z takes the move back. When you finish, the new body takes the old one's place, name and colour, its foot at the same height. Edge treatments go, as with every edit of a sketch.

Revolving

When revolving, you draw half the cross-section to the left of the axis shown in the sketch. Next to it you see a 3D preview of the revolve. It shows at once what the body will look like. You can turn, shift and zoom it with the mouse; the small button in its top right corner, or a double click on it, brings back the first view. The outline must be closed, or you build an open line as a stroke, see below. At the end click “Concluir revolução”. The other bodies of the design are shown from the front, in the same view as the profile, with the axis standing at the middle: draw the profile next to them or above them. The body stands where you drew it, and the horizontal line through the middle of the sketch is the ground: a profile drawn above it gives a body that stands higher, and its lowest point is the foot of the body. For a bigger radius, move the profile further from the axis, past the edge of the plate if need be: the plate grows with the sketch, its grid follows when you let go, and the minus button zooms out until all of it fits.

A revolved body is an exact body, like an extruded one: it takes chamfers and fillets, and you can hollow it, for a cup or a vase. A body revolved with an older layerling is a mesh; open “Editar esboço” and finish it again to make it exact. A profile that reaches across the axis cannot be built exactly and becomes a mesh, as before.

Smoother round faces: “Smoothness”. An exact revolved body is cut into small flat facets for the view, the export and the print, and on a large pot they can show on the print. Select the body and set “Smoothness” in the properties panel to “Fine” or “Extra fine”: the round faces are cut finer, at the cost of more triangles and a slower design. A helix or a mesh revolve has “Lados” for this instead.

One continuous strand: “Passo”. A revolve turns its outline into closed rings. Select the revolved body and give it a “Passo” above 0 in the properties panel, the distance it climbs per turn, and the outline winds up as a helix instead: one continuous strand, like filament on a spool or a coil. “Abertura” then becomes “Voltas”, up to 200; a negative number winds left-handed. Turns closer than the outline is high melt into one body, so a solid core with a fine pitch works too. A helix is built as a mesh, so fillet, chamfer and hollow do not work on it; keep “Lados” low on many turns. A pitch of 0 makes rings again.

Sweeping along a path

“Varredura do esboço” pulls an outline along a path: a cable channel that turns a corner, a conduit, a guard round a belt, a ring around a hexagon. It sits next to “Extrusão do esboço” and “Revolução do esboço” in the “Criar” group.

You draw two things on the same sheet:

  • The cross-section as a closed outline, as usual. Draw it as you would see it looking along the path from its start: across the path is the sketch's left and right, up is up on the finished body. A hollow section, a channel or a tube, is an outline with another one inside it. By default the section is centred on the path. The menu next to the mode badge at the top lets you put its left or right edge on the path instead (“No caminho: borda esquerda”, “No caminho: borda direita”, seen looking along the path), so a rail can sit on one side of the line or follow the edge of a part. The body stands on the sketch plane with the lowest point of the section.
  • The path as a “Linha de construção”: switch it on and draw lines or curves, one chain, open or closed (a closed chain gives a ring). The path lies flat in the sketch plane.

Draw the section near the end of the path where it should start; the path starts at the end nearest to it. Then click “Concluir varredura”. A corner of straight pieces becomes a mitre, a curve stays smooth, and the section stays upright all the way. The body is exact, like an extruded one: fillet, chamfer and the STEP export work on it. If a closed outline or a path is missing, or there are several separate paths, layerling says so. With “Editar esboço” you can return to the sketch and change the section or the path.

Building as a stroke

Normally the area inside a closed outline becomes the body. With “Traço” in the “Concluir” section you build the line itself instead, with a width you set. Tick “Construir como traço” in the stroke window; the sketch shows straight away what comes out.

  • A closed outline becomes a frame. “Posição” says where the wall lies: “Centralizado” on the drawn line, “Interno” within it or “Externo” outside it. Outside is handy for a tolerance: draw the outline of a hole, a dovetail for instance, and give it a 0.2 mm stroke outside to get the gap the print needs.
  • An open line becomes a stripe, centred on the line. “Pontas” sets how its ends look: “Retas”, “Quadradas” (longer by half the width) or “Redondas”.
  • “Cantos” applies to both: “Vivos”, “Redondos” or “Chanfrados”.

The sketch keeps the drawn line. Open it again and you go on changing line and stroke; untick the box and the area is built again. Curves are broken into short straight pieces for it.

In a revolve the stroke is a thin wall: draw the wall of a vase or a cup as one open line to the left of the axis, tick “Traço” and set the width, and the revolve turns that band. What reaches across the axis is cut off at it.

Fill and silhouette

You can set the stroke without opening the sketch too: in the properties of a sketch body, choose “Área”, “Traço externo”, “Traço interno” or “Traço centralizado” under “Preenchimento”, with “Largura da linha” and “Cantos”. The body is built again straight away, where it stands. These match the fill modes of Tinkercad's SVG import: default, outer line and inner line. “Mais largo” keeps the area filled and grows it by the line width all round, with sharp, round or bevelled corners: a base layer under a logo for a multicolour print, which the stroke outside alone would only give as a ring. “Mais estreito” does the opposite: the area stays filled and its edge moves in by the line width all round, holes included (they grow). Use both on copies of one sketch for a fit: the hole at its drawn size, the part that goes through it “Mais estreito” by 0.5 mm, or a wall inside a shape cut from the same outline. A width larger than the outline allows leaves nothing. In the sketch's stroke window the same two choices stand under “Posição”. With a line outside, inside or centred, “Fio de corte” makes the wall sharp on top: its top runs in to that width with a 45° chamfer on both sides, as on a cookie cutter. 0 leaves the top flat; the edge stays when you change the line width.

“Silhueta (sem furos)” leaves out every outline lying inside another: holes and whatever lies in them. Only the outer outline stays. Together with “Traço externo” it makes a cookie cutter: import an SVG twice, once with the silhouette as an area for the base and once with the silhouette and 1 to 2 mm of stroke outside as the wall. The switch is in the “Traço” window in sketch mode as well.

Fillets and chamfers on the edges go when the body is built again, as when the sketch is edited.

Slanted walls, for stamps

An extruded sketch has vertical walls. A stamp, an embossing die or a punch wants slanted ones, outside and inside, with the same wall thickness all the way. Layerling has no draft angle for an extrusion, but for plain outlines the “Afunilamento” gets you there. One way that works:

  1. Draw the outline with the hole it needs and make a body of it. Duplicate the body (Ctrl+D).
  2. On the first body, switch on “Silhueta (sem furos)”, so the hole is filled, and give it a wider bottom than top with “Afunilamento”.
  3. On the copy, open its sketch again and delete the outer outline, so that only the outline of the hole is left. Finish the sketch, switch the body to “Buraco” and give it a narrower bottom than top with “Afunilamento”.
  4. Move the hole into the first body, where the hole was, and group the two.

The walls now slope outside and inside. Taper scales the whole outline, so this is exact for plain shapes, where you can choose the sizes so the walls run parallel, and only an approximation for fine details such as lettering.

A picture as template

With “Adicionar imagem” you put a photo or a drawing under the sketch and trace it, at any time, also before the first line. You can set its size, opacity and position. Once the picture sits right, lock it with Ctrl+L so you do not move it by accident while drawing. A locked image is out of the way: clicks go through it, so you can pick lines and points on top of it and drag a frame over them. The padlock in its corner unlocks it with one click; Alt+click selects it without unlocking it. If its settings at the right edge cover the picture, drag them away by their title bar; a double-click on it docks them again.

Under “Alinhar” you line up a photo that was not taken straight:

  • “Rotação”: Turn the picture about its centre, with the curved arrows beyond its corners or as a number in degrees. With Shift the arrows snap in 15° steps. Inside the ring that appears while turning they snap to 22.5°, outside it to whole degrees.
  • “Para X = 0” and “Para Y = 0”: put the picture's centre on X = 0 or Y = 0. For a revolve, X = 0 is the axis, so the picture then lies symmetric about it.
  • “Calibrar”: Its button sits at the top, right under the preview. Click two points in the picture whose distance you know, the ends of a ruler or a known diameter, and type the real distance. The picture is scaled evenly so that distance is right; the first point stays where it was.
  • “Recortar”: The handles on the frame now crop the picture instead of scaling it; what is cut away stays stored and comes back with “Mostrar imagem inteira” or when a handle is pulled out again.

All four touch the reference only, never the sketch.

“Traçar”, in the picture's settings, sets the points for you: it traces the outline of the shape in the picture – a silhouette, a logo, a word – and shows it in red over the picture, square points for corners, round ones for smooth points. “Forma escura” or “Forma clara” picks which part of the picture is the shape, “Limiar” where dark turns light, “Pontos” how many points the outlines get together (fewer give smoother curves, more follow the picture more closely), “Canto a partir de” from what turn a point is a corner, “Ignorar manchas de até” how small a speck is left out, and “Manter furos” keeps the middle of an A or an O. “Aplicar” puts the outlines into the sketch exactly where the picture lies, at its size, turn and crop, and selects them: they are ordinary points to move, curve or remove, and Ctrl+Z takes them back in one step. It works best with clear contrast; cut a photo with a busy background out first. What falls away – around the outlines, in the holes, what is cut away – the preview covers in the plate's colour, so only what stays shows of the picture. Outlines that lie so close that loose curves would cross get more points by themselves; the card says so. For a border outside or inside the outline, give the sketch body a stroke outside or inside its lines, or offset the finished body.

For a photo – a toy on a white table, say – choose “Objeto” under “Forma”: the background is the colour at the picture's edge, and everything that stands out from it becomes one outline, whatever its colours; “Limiar” then sets how clearly it must stand out. A colourful picture on an even background starts this way. “Escolher áreas” outlines more: click an area in the picture, a window say, and the patch of like colour round the spot is outlined (“Tolerância de cor” sets how like). Holes and clicked areas are listed under “Furos e áreas”; pointing at one shows it in the preview, ✕ takes it out, and with “Recortar” off it is drawn as a construction line instead of a hole. An area that reaches the picture's edge is the background and is not taken. What no threshold and no colour can tell apart – a shadow as dark as the wheels above it – “Cortar fora” takes away: click corners round it (a click on the first corner, a double click or Enter closes it), and the outline runs along the cut; it is listed as “Cut 1”.

The tree beside a house, a figure before a busy background – where no colour tells the shape from the rest, the “Laço magnético” catches it: click roughly along its edge, and between two clicks the line follows the edge by itself, round its bends too; while you move, the preview already shows where it will run. A click on the first point, a double click or Enter closes it, Esc throws it away. It is listed as “Lasso 1”, with the choice “Incluir” (the area joins the shape) or “Cortar fora” (it is taken away); every cut has the same choice. Under “Forma”, “Só o laço” makes the shape only of what you catch this way – nothing else of the picture.

Keys in sketch mode

KeyEffect
Escput the note tool down; otherwise put the tool down (back to “Selecionar”), then clear the selection
Deletedelete the selected element
Ctrl+Ccopy the selection
Ctrl+Xcut the selection
Ctrl+Vpaste
Ctrl+Dduplicate the selection
Ctrl+Zundo
Ctrl+Aselect every point and line
Ctrl+I“Adicionar imagem”
Shiftwhile drawing: snap the line in 15° steps; while dragging: keep movement on one axis
digit, <, Tab, Enterwhile drawing: type and set the length and angle of the next line
Rrotate the closed sketch by 45°
Ctrl+Llock or unlock the selected outline, or the template image
Nplace a note: the next click puts it on the sketch
Shift+Nshow or hide the notes

Tip: Draw as few points as needed. An outline with a few well-placed points gives a smoother body than a tangle of many.

8. Text and curved lettering

Raised or engraved lettering in eight typefaces or one of your own, and if you like along a circular arc, such as on a coin, a lid or a ring.

Este capítulo ainda não foi traduzido para o português. Segue o texto em inglês.

Adding text

Choose “Texto” in the shape library and place it. In the “Texto” field on the right, type what it should say. The settings below:

  • “Fonte”: Eight typefaces are available: Multilanguage, Sans, Serif, Script, Monospace, Rounded, Stencil (letters made of straight lines) and Japanese (Zen Maru Gothic). New text starts in Sans. Accented letters such as ä, ö, ü, é and the € sign are in every typeface, and so are kana, the common kanji and many of the rare ones in names such as 澤, 槇 and 檜: a Japanese name works in every typeface and on a name tag. The Japanese letters are fetched the first time a text needs them (the rare kanji in a second file, only when a text has one), so such a text shows question marks for a moment. They are kept on the computer afterwards, so Japanese also works offline from then on. Fonts of your own come on top, see Your own fonts below.
