  • “Tamanho das letras”: How big the letters are, seen from above; “Altura” sets how thick they are.
  • “Altura”: How far the lettering stands out from the surface.
  • “Bisel”: Rounds the letter edges so they look softer. With “Segmentos” you decide in how many steps.
  • “Borda das letras”: rounds or chamfers the top edge of the letters, as on a name tag: “Nenhuma”, “Arredondada” or “Chanfrada”, with the “Tamanho da borda” (0.4 mm to start with, at most as high as the text). It goes further than the “Bisel”, but only as far as the strokes are wide: where a stroke is thinner than twice the size, the edge ends in a narrower top. The underside stays flat, so single letters can be glued on afterwards. While an edge is chosen it takes the place of “Bisel”.
  • Length: A text takes up to 250 characters. The letters keep their size and the line gets as long as it needs to be; to make it shorter, make the letters smaller. The “Borda das letras” works on a text of up to 40 characters, because on a longer one it would take minutes to build.
  • Size: You set the length and width of the line as with any shape. Drag the handles or type the dimensions.
  • “Espaçamento entre letras (%)”: The space between the letters on top of the one the font has, in per cent of the letter size: 0 leaves it as the font made it, above it the letters stand further apart, below it (down to -50) tighter, which a font of your own often needs. The letters keep their size and the box follows the line, on straight and on curved text. The spacing is not applied to Arabic and Hebrew, whose letters join up.
  • “Esticar as letras até a moldura”: Off at first: the letters keep their proportions and sit in the middle of the frame, so a frame pulled wider or deeper than the word needs stays larger than the letters. Switch it on and the letters are stretched to fill the whole frame in both directions: a capital can be made lower or narrower, as in Tinkercad. It is for straight text; curved text has its own letter size.
  • “Automatic kerning”: Moves pairs of letters that leave too much room between them, such as AY, AV, LT or To, closer, measured from the shapes of the letters, in every font, your own too. New texts start with it on; texts made before it existed have it off, so nothing moves in a saved design. The letters keep their size and the box follows. It works on straight and curved text, not on vertical text, Arabic, Hebrew or Japanese.
  • “Letras de cima para baixo”: Stacks the letters top to bottom, each in the middle of one upright line, for a sign on a door frame or a name down a pen. The box turns upright and the letters keep their size; “Espaçamento entre letras (%)” sets the gap between them. On curved text the letters form a column along the left side of the circle, each one standing upright; “Pelo lado direito” puts the column on the right side.

Text is at first a single body. If you want to treat the letters individually, click “Separar peças”. Then every letter is a shape of its own.

Several lines: A text holds one line. For a sign or a plaque with several lines, open the “Text block” card below the settings: type the lines under “Lines”, choose “Align” (“Left”, “Centre” or “Right”), “Line gap” and “Next line (%)” - at 80 % each line is a fifth smaller than the one above. The button makes every line a text of its own under the one above, in this text's font, height and fill; the first takes this text's place. Afterwards each line can get its own size, font or colour.

The edges of text can be chamfered or filleted too, straight or curved, see Breaking edges and hollowing bodies. Use small sizes such as 0.2 to 0.5 mm, because the strokes of the letters are narrow.

Your own fonts

The list under “Fonte” draws every font in its own letters, with the words of your text, so you see how they will look before you choose. The same goes for the fonts in the window below; the fonts listed from your computer show their names in their own letters. Arrow keys and Enter work in the list, and a letter jumps to the next font that starts with it.

Besides the eight built-in fonts you can use any font of your own: a font file from your computer or, in Chrome and Edge, a font installed on your computer. Choose “Suas próprias fontes …” at the bottom of “Fonte”. The “Suas próprias fontes” window opens.

  • “Escolher um arquivo de fonte …” takes a TrueType file (.ttf), an OpenType file (.otf) or a WOFF file (.woff). You can also simply drag the file into the window.
  • On Windows the installed fonts live in the Fonts folder (C:\Windows\Fonts). The browser's file dialog hides it. Open it in Explorer instead and drag the font into the “Suas próprias fontes” window. Fonts installed for you alone live in %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Fonts, which the file dialog shows too. On a Mac fonts live in /Library/Fonts and ~/Library/Fonts.
  • “Fonte do computador …” lists the fonts installed on your computer. The first time, the browser asks whether layerling may read them. The search field finds a font quickly, a click takes it.

If a text is selected, it gets the new font at once. Otherwise the font shows up under “Fonte” in the “Suas próprias fontes” group, and “Usar” in the window puts it on the selected texts. Fonts of your own work like the built-in ones: text on a circular arc, chamfers and fillets on the edges and the STEP export all work the same. Letters a font lacks are taken from Sans.

Arabic and Hebrew

Arabic, Persian, Urdu and Hebrew are written right to left: the first letter stands on the right, and in a mixed text such as "Name عربي" only the Arabic word runs backwards, digits stay as usual. Arabic letters join their neighbours the way the script asks, and lam-alef becomes a ligature. This needs a font that has these letters; the built-in ones do not. Add one of your own, such as Arial, Tahoma or Segoe UI on Windows, or a free one such as Noto Naskh Arabic, Noto Sans Arabic or Amiri. Vowel marks sit on the letter they belong to. Text on a circular arc, outline, silhouette, layers and name tags work with it as with any other text.

What works in which browser

BrowserChoose a font fileFont from the computer
Chrome and Edge on a computer, the installed layerling app tooyesyes, after the browser asks
Firefoxyesno
Safari on a Macyesno
Tablet and phoneyes, from the device's filesno

Web pages may not simply read the installed fonts. Only Chrome and Edge have a permission for it, and only on secure pages, over https as on layerling.com. When layerling runs over http, say on your own server or as a Docker install in your home network, “Fonte do computador …” is missing; drag the font over from Explorer then. In the other browsers you choose the font file from the fonts folder, with the same result. If you declined the question in Chrome or Edge, allow it again in the site settings, behind the padlock to the left of the address.

layerling cannot read WOFF2 files (there is almost always a TTF or OTF version), font collections (.ttc, several fonts in one file) or colour emoji fonts. From very large fonts, such as Chinese ones, layerling takes the first 8000 characters. A variable font is read in its default setting, usually the regular weight.

Some fonts, script and variable fonts above all, draw a letter from strokes that overlap. layerling merges them into one clean outline when it reads the font, so the body stays printable. Such letters are then made of very short straight pieces instead of curves; it does not show.

Where the fonts are kept

A font of your own stays in this browser on this computer. Another browser or another computer does not know it until you add it there too. Clearing the browser's site data clears the fonts as well. In the “Suas próprias fontes” window the bin removes a font from the browser. Your designs lose nothing by it, as the next section shows.

Passing on designs with a font of your own

A design does not store the font file, only the outlines of the letters its texts use, those in earlier steps of the history included. If a text says "Hello", only H, e, l and o travel with it. That holds for every way a design is saved: in the browser, on your own server, as a .lyl file and in “Formas personalizadas”.

So:

  • The design opens correctly anywhere, also on a computer without the font. The texts look the same and can be moved, turned, scaled and filleted.
  • New letters need the font. If someone without the font types a letter the design did not bring along, layerling draws it from Sans. Under “Fonte” the font is then marked “só as letras do projeto”. Adding the font file brings back every letter.
  • Exports hold geometry only. STL, 3MF, OBJ, STEP and SVG contain bodies and outlines, no font.
  • Older layerling versions do not know fonts of one's own yet and draw such texts in Multilanguage.

Licences: Fonts are protected by copyright, and their licence says what you may do with them. The embedded letter outlines are what PDF files take along from a font, and most licences allow that. Some commercial fonts, though, forbid passing on even single letters. Before you pass on or publish a design with a font of your own, check the font's licence. Free fonts such as those from Google Fonts (mostly under the SIL Open Font License) can be passed on without worry. For a printed part or an exported STL it does not matter: they hold no font any more, only geometry.

Raised or engraved

  • Raised: Place the text on the surface and group it with the body. It grows out as a relief.
  • Engraved: Switch the text to “Buraco”, let it reach a little into the surface and group it with the body. The letters are then engraved.

For lettering on a side face, first put the workplane on that face, see View and workplane.

Stencils: bridges for the middle of letters

Cut through a plate, letters like O, A and B lose their middle: it lies loose inside the letter and falls out. “Pontes de estêncil” holds it to the plate with small bridges, as on a stencil.

  1. Switch the text to “Buraco”, let it reach through the plate and select both, grouped or not.
  2. Click “Pontes de estêncil” in the “Modificar” group of the ribbon, right-click the selection, or find it with Ctrl+K. The bridges show in orange where they will go.
  3. Set “Largura da ponte” and “Pontes por parte”. “Altura das pontes” starts at the plate's thickness; lower bridges sit flush with the bottom, in the middle or flush with the top of the plate, as “Posição” says. On a spray stencil, bridges at the top leave room under them for the paint.
  4. “Criar” groups the bridges with the plate.

Each bridge is an ordinary box: open the group to move one, delete one or add one of your own. If you change the text later, select the group and click “Pontes de estêncil” again; new bridges take the place of the old ones. A text that is engraved and does not go through gets no bridges, as nothing falls out there. For a laser or a plotter, the DXF and SVG export add the same bridges, see Files, saving and sharing.

Outline, silhouette and wider

A text need not be built as filled letters. “Preenchimento” in the properties offers the same choice as Tinkercad:

  • “Preenchido”: the letters as they are.
  • “Contorno”: a line along the outline of the letters, half inside and half outside it.
  • “Linha externa”: a line round the outside of the letters.
  • “Linha interna”: a line on the inside of the letters.

With a line chosen, two settings appear right under the list: “Largura da linha” sets how thick the line is, “Cantos” how it goes round the corners (“Redondos”, “Chanfrados” or “Vivos”). The rarer settings are under “Mais”: “Silhueta (sem furos)” leaves out the holes in O, A or e, and “Mais largo (base para impressão multicolorida)” keeps the letters filled and makes them thicker by the line width all round; letters that touch grow into one piece.

With a line outside, a centred line or "Wider" the box of the text grows, while the letters keep their size. “Bisel” and “Segmentos” exist for filled letters only.

Layers and name tags

A name tag for a multicolour print is a text in layers: the letters on top, under them the same text a little wider in a second colour, at the bottom a plate without holes in a third. layerling makes it in one click:

  • A new name tag: choose “Etiqueta de nome” in the shape library and place it. It says "Name" in white letters on a red rim and a dark plate.
  • From a text: select the text and click “Criar camadas” at the top of its settings.

All settings of the tag are in the card “Etiqueta de nome”, at the top of the settings:

  • “Texto” and “Fonte”, fonts of your own too. The tag grows with the words.
  • “Tamanho das letras”: how tall the capital letters are, in mm. All layers follow and stay lined up.
  • “Letras de cima para baixo”: stands the tag upright with the letters under one another, all layers along.
  • “Camadas”: one row per layer, from the top down. Each row has the colour (click the coloured square), how much wider the layer is than the letters, its height and “Sem furos”, which fills the holes in letters such as O and A. “Cantos” sets how a wider layer goes round the corners of the letters: “Redondos”, “Chanfrados” or “Vivos”. The top row is the letters themselves. + adds a layer at the bottom, – takes the bottom layer away. A tag has two to six layers.
  • “Furo para chaveiro”: gives the bottom layer a straight tab with a round end and a hole for a key ring; the tab grows with the hole. A 3 mm hole, the default, makes a tab 6.5 mm wide that sticks out 6.75 mm, the hole's edge 2 mm from the edge of the bottom layer. Choose the “Diâmetro do furo” and the “Lado”: “Esquerda”, “Direita” or “Em cima”. “Livre” takes the hole off the tag and puts a “Aba para chaveiro” of its own beside it, in the bottom layer's colour and height: an ordinary shape you move and turn with its handles wherever the tag needs it. Once it is in place, “Fixar na etiqueta” in its properties makes it part of the nearest tag, just where it is: the hole goes through every layer it reaches, the ear joins the bottom layer, and both keep to that corner of the letters when the words or the size change. “Livre” brings the tab out again where it was, to move it once more. The hole goes through every layer it touches, and the tab moves along when you change the words, the letter size or the font. “Posição ao longo do lado” moves the tab up or down along its side (along the top: left or right), up to where it would leave the side; 0 is the middle. Use it when the middle of the side meets a gap, as beside a J, and move the tab to the part of the letter that reaches out.
  • “Borda das letras”: rounds or chamfers the top edge of the letters on the top layer, the way a printed tag is finished: “Nenhuma”, “Arredondada” or “Chanfrada”, with the “Tamanho da borda” (0.4 mm to start with, at most as high as the layer). It works for every font and word. The edge is part of the letters' mesh, so the edge tool takes such a text as a mesh, which for a text this fine is heavy; pick the edge here instead.

Every change shows at once. The tag is a bundle: it moves as one, and each layer stays a body of its own in its own colour, the way a slicer needs them for a multicolour print. To round or bevel the edges of one layer, click “Editar conjunto” and pick the layer, see Breaking edges and hollowing bodies.

Many name tags at once

Type the names into “Lista de nomes”, one per line, up to a hundred. The button below says how many tags it will make, for example "Make 12 name tags". Every tag gets the same layers, letter size and key ring hole and is an object of its own; they are laid out in rows below the first, 5 mm apart. A plain text has the name list too, further down in its settings.

Icon tags

An icon tag is the same tag with an SVG icon instead of letters: a heart, a cloud, a club's logo. The icon on top, under it the same outline a little wider in a second colour, at the bottom a plate without holes.

  • A new icon tag: choose “Etiqueta de ícone” in the shape library. A small window opens: click “Procurar…”, pick an SVG, PNG or JPG file, check the picture, type the “Largura (mm)” of the icon and click “OK”. The tag stands in the middle of the plate, in the same layers as a new name tag.
  • From a sketch body: an imported SVG, or a sketch you drew, has “Criar camadas” at the top of its settings.

The card “Etiqueta de ícone” at the top of the settings holds:

  • “Outro arquivo…”: puts the icon of another file (SVG, PNG or JPG) on the tag; the layers and the width stay as they are.
  • “Largura”: how wide the icon on top is, in mm. All layers follow and stay lined up.
  • “Camadas”: the rows as on a name tag - colour, how much wider, “Cantos”, height and “Sem furos”, + and –, two to six layers. The top row is the icon itself.
  • “Furo para chaveiro”: as on a name tag: a hole for a key ring through every layer, with a tab with a round end on the bottom layer, beyond the icon. “Diâmetro do furo” and “Lado” choose its size and where it sits; “Livre” gives a tab of its own, as on a name tag. The tab is made for the outline of the icon, so on a very ragged icon check where it meets the plate. “Posição ao longo do lado” moves the tab along its side, as on the name tag.
  • “Quantidade”: how many tags you want, 1 to 100. “Quantas couberem” works it out from the plate of the printer chosen in the settings, for small logos a full plate. The button below makes them, 5 mm apart, laid out on the middle of the plate; the first is the tag itself.

The SVG needs closed outlines; a drawing of open lines only cannot become a tag. A sketch body whose fill is a line keeps it: the area of that line is the icon.

A picture (PNG or JPG) is traced into an outline, and the preview shows the outline. Under “Contornado a partir de” you choose whether the “Parte escura” or the “Parte clara” becomes the icon; at first it is the part that is not the background. Transparent pixels never belong to the icon. An SVG that holds nothing but one picture, as Inkscape saves an imported bitmap, is traced the same way. The outline follows the pixels, so a small picture gives a rough edge: pictures of a few hundred pixels or more work best. “Outro arquivo…” takes the part of a picture that is not its background.

QR codes

A QR code turns a text or a web address into a pattern a phone camera reads: a link to your shop on a sign, the Wi-Fi name on a coaster, a phone number on a key tag.

Choose “QR code” in the shape library. A window opens; the cursor is already in the text field:

  • “Texto ou endereço”: what the code says. Enter makes the code, Shift+Enter starts a new line. Below the field you see how much of the room is used; umlauts and other special letters take two bytes. When the text is too long, the field says so.
  • “Correção de erros”: L, M, Q or H. A higher level can still be read when part of the code is dirty or scratched (L about 7 %, M 15 %, Q 25 %, H 30 %), but needs more modules for the same text, so each module gets smaller. M is chosen at first.
  • “Construir como”: “Só o código” makes the code alone, 4 mm high. “Em relevo sobre uma placa” puts it 1 mm high on a white plate 3 mm thick, as a bundle of two colours, so a multicolour print prints the code dark and the plate light. “Gravado” cuts the code 1 mm deep into the plate.
  • “Tamanho por”: type the “Largura” of the whole code (40 mm at first) or the size of one module; the other number is shown below. Modules under 0.8 mm get a warning. That is a rule of thumb for a 0.4 mm nozzle, not a guarantee: printer, material, colours and the phone all play a part.
  • “Zona de silêncio (4 módulos)”: scanners need an empty rim four modules wide round the code. On a plate the rim is part of the plate; switch it off only if the plate sits on a larger light surface. The code alone has no rim of its own: leave the room free round it.
  • Heights: the height of the code, or on a plate the code height or engraving depth, and the plate thickness.

The preview shows the code as it will be built. “OK” puts it in the middle of the plate.

The code is a body like any other: move it, turn it, scale it (keep width and depth the same, or the code is stretched), group it, or make it a hole and group it into a part of your own to engrave it there. Scaling it scales the whole code; each module stays square.

The card “QR code” at the top of its settings holds the text. Change it and click “Criar de novo”: the code is built again where it stands and as wide as it is now. Error correction, quiet zone and build stay as they were chosen; for other choices make a new code from the library.

Scan the code with your phone before you print it, and once more after printing. Dark on light reads best; a light code on a dark plate is not read by every phone.

Text on a circular arc

Should the lettering not run straight but follow the edge of a coin, a lid or a ring? For that there is the setting “Em arco”.

Once you switch it on, the text runs along the circle. All letters stand on the same baseline, as evenly as with normal text. There are five settings:

  • “Raio do arco” (5 to 500 mm): The radius of the circle the letters' baseline runs on. The letters stay where they are; only their bend changes.
  • “Letter width (%)” (25 to 400 %): How wide each letter is drawn, in per cent of its own width. Below 100 the letters get narrower, above it wider; their height stays, and the arc they take grows or shrinks with them. For a tall, narrow lettering on a coin, for example. On straight text “Esticar as letras até a moldura” does this with the frame.
  • “Tamanho das letras”: How tall the letters are. It no longer depends on the width of the shape.
  • “Pela parte de baixo”: Moves the text from the top of the circle to its bottom. The letters then point with their heads to the centre.
  • “De cabeça para baixo”: Turns only the letters over so you can read them from the other side. The text stays in its place on the circle.

The centre of the circle is the centre of the shape. That is why aligning works as usual: if you centre the text with a cylinder or ring, it sits exactly concentric on it. When you pull a handle, radius and letter size grow together, so the lettering is not distorted.

Tip: At the top of the circle the letters stand outside the baseline; with “Pela parte de baixo” they stand inside, heads towards the centre. For the lettering to fit on a disc, the radius plus the letter size should be smaller than the disc's radius.

9. Threads, gears and other parts

Screws, nuts and tapped holes that fit together, plus gear, spring, bent tube, dovetail, teardrop hole, counterbore and countersink.

Este capítulo ainda não foi traduzido para o português. Segue o texto em inglês.

Besides the basic shapes, the library contains some parts that would be tedious to put together yourself. All of them can be changed afterwards in their settings.

Threads

Choose “Rosca” in the shape library. Under “Tipo” you decide what it should be:

  • “Barra roscada”: a cylinder with thread, for example a screw without a head.
  • “Parafuso”: with a head. You choose the “Cabeça”: “Cabeça cilíndrica (Allen)”, “Cabeça escareada” or “Cabeça sextavada”. There are also “Cabeça quadrada”, “Cabeça flangeada” (a hex with a disc under it), “Cabeça borboleta” and “Manípulo estrela”: the last two are turned by hand, start five times as wide as the thread and print lying flat, without supports; their “Diâmetro da cabeça” (“Envergadura” on a wing head) goes from three to eight times the thread. Further down you set the head's “Diâmetro da cabeça” (on a hex head “Chave da cabeça”; a countersunk head's diameter follows its height) and the “Acionamento” in its face: “Sextavado interno”, “Torx”, “Phillips”, “Fenda”, “Robertson (quadrado)” or “Nenhum” for a screw turned by hand or with a spanner. “Tamanho do acionamento” is the socket's width across flats, the Torx star's outer diameter or the span of the cross; “Profundidade do acionamento” is how deep it goes, at most nine tenths of the head, and 0 leaves it out. Until you change them they follow the size; a hex head starts without a drive. The drive is part of the exact body, so it also comes out in the STEP export. With “Fenda”, “Tamanho do acionamento” is the slot's length and its width a fifth of it, so a flat screwdriver or a coin turns the screw; it starts as long as the head allows. “Robertson (quadrado)” is the square drive common in Canada: “Tamanho do acionamento” is the square across flats, and it starts at the bit for the size, #2 (2.84 mm) on M4 and M5. “Altura do colar” puts a round collar between the head and the thread, for example a spacer under a star knob or a shoulder that holds the head off the part; 0 leaves it out. “Diâmetro do colar” starts at twice the thread and stays inside the head, so the collar prints on it without supports; the thread keeps its length. A countersunk head has no collar. A nut has the same two fields: its collar stands on the top face, narrower than the nut, with the thread running through it, and the height counts the body only.
  • “Porca”: the matching nut. The washer to go with it is a “Tubo”: choose the screw size under “Arruela”, and outer and inner diameter and thickness follow ISO 7089. Under “Formato da porca” it can also be “Quadrada”, “Flangeada” (with a disc under the hexagon), “Borboleta” or a “Manípulo estrela” to turn by hand; the wings lie flat, so a wing nut prints without supports.
  • “Furo roscado”: a tapped hole. It is a hole. Drag it into a part, group both, and the part has an internal thread. For a hole a bolt screws into, always use the “Furo roscado”: a “Barra roscada” or “Parafuso” set as a hole has the bolt's full size without play and comes out too tight. If you set one as a hole anyway, layerling points this out, and “Transformar em furo roscado” turns it into a “Furo roscado”.

You pick the size under “Tamanho” from a list: metric from M2 to M24, the inch sizes UNC and UNF from No. 4 to 1 inch, and the pipe threads G1/16 to G4. If you choose “Personalizado”, you set “Diâmetro” and “Passo” yourself. For an inch size or a G size the field asks for “Fios por polegada” instead of the pitch in millimetres.

The list groups the sizes by series, and a line under the field names the series of the size you picked, with examples you know from everyday life:

  • M, metric coarse: the ISO metric coarse thread to ISO 261, as on standard screws and nuts.
  • UNC, US inch coarse: the camera and tripod screw is 1/4"-20 UNC (ISO 1222), larger tripod heads use 3/8"-16 UNC.
  • UNF, US inch fine: the same diameters as UNC with a finer pitch (ASME B1.1).
  • G, pipe thread: a shower hose connects with G1/2, a washing-machine inlet hose with G3/4. A garden tap ends in G3/4, smaller taps in G1/2; that is where the tap connector of a click-on hose system screws on.
  • “NPT – US pipe, tapered”: the American tapered pipe thread to ASME B1.20.1, from 1/16" to 4", found on fittings, valves, pressure gauges and air tools. It seals on the taper, usually with tape or sealant. The size names the pipe: the diameter is its outside diameter, which the thread has at its wide end. Choosing an NPT size switches on “Tapered (1:16, NPT)” and sets the profile to “Personalizada (trapézio)” with 60° flanks; another size chosen afterwards makes the thread straight again.

The G sizes are the parallel Whitworth pipe threads to ISO 228-1, found on fittings for water, gas, hydraulics and pneumatics. The size names the pipe, not the thread: a G1 measures 33.249 mm across the thread. Choosing a G size sets the profile to “Whitworth (55°)”, and choosing a metric or inch size sets it back to “Triangular (ISO)”. A “Trapezoidal” or “Redonda” profile you picked yourself stays. The standard only defines the thread, so the head of a screw and a nut on a G size get the same proportions as on a diameter you set yourself. The tapered pipe threads R, Rc and Rp are not included.

The last series in the list, “PCO – Garrafas”, holds PCO 1881: the 28 mm neck of most water and soda bottles, 27.4 mm across with a pitch of 2.7 mm. Its thread has wide flat crests, so choosing it sets the profile to “Personalizada (trapézio)” with a “Profundidade da rosca” of 1.6 mm and a “Ângulo do flanco” of 30°; another size chosen afterwards brings its own profile back. Make the neck as a “Barra roscada” and the cap as a “Porca”, or subtract a “Furo roscado” from a cylinder. The measures follow the drawing of the standard as the OpenSCAD library BOSL2 has it; print a test piece before a whole cap. The series also holds S60x6 (IBC), the outlet thread of IBC containers (DIN 6063-1, line KS 60): 60 mm across with a pitch of 6 mm, 3 mm deep, set up the same way with a “Ângulo do flanco” of 30°. The standard draws its flanks unequal, one about 10° from the upright and the other 20°; the profile here has two equal flanks, so a printed pair fits with some play. Canisters and washing-up liquid bottles have no common standard, so measure the neck you have and enter its values under “Personalizado”.

More settings:

  • “Sentido”: “Rosca direita” or “Rosca esquerda”.
  • “Entradas”: Threads side by side, as on a lead screw: a T8x8 has 4 starts at 2 mm, each climbing 8 mm a turn. The pitch field then reads “Passo entre filetes”: the distance from one thread to the next, which sets the depth of the profile, and the note under it gives the lead. A size from the list and a tapered thread have one start.
  • “Perfil”: “Triangular (ISO)” is the standard profile of metric and inch threads, “Whitworth (55°)” that of the G pipe threads: 55° with rounded crests and roots. “Trapezoidal” and “Redonda” have flat crests and roots. That usually prints more reliably because no thin tips result.
  • “Tapered (1:16, NPT)”: The thread narrows 1 in 16 on the diameter, as a tapered pipe thread does; the “Diâmetro” is then the one at the wide end. A “Barra roscada” or “Parafuso” narrows towards its tip at the top, a “Porca” or “Furo roscado” widens towards its mouth at the top, so a tapered rod turned upside down screws into it. Any profile can be tapered, and the tapered thread is an exact body as well, for the edge tool and the STEP export.
  • “Personalizada (trapézio)”: A trapezoid you shape yourself, with a flat crest and a flat root of the same width. “Ângulo do flanco” is the angle between the two flanks of a tooth: 60° is the sharp V thread, 30° the trapezoid thread, and at 90° or less no flank is flatter than 45°, so the thread prints without supports. “Profundidade da rosca” and “Diâmetro do núcleo” are one measure said two ways: the core diameter is the diameter minus twice the depth, and changing one changes the other. A new own profile starts with the V thread's depth at 60°. The depth has limits that depend on the angle and the pitch: not shallower than a tenth of the pitch, not deeper than 40 % of the diameter, and not so deep that the two flanks take more than nine tenths of the pitch. If you change the pitch, the depth follows in proportion; if you scale the thread, so does the depth. The play and the chamfers work as with the other profiles. Through the MCP bridge the profile is custom with threadFlankAngle and threadDepth.
  • “Folga (XY)”: For nut and tapped hole, the room that makes sure a printed pair really turns. The coarser your printer works, the more clearance the pair needs. It is the extra room across the whole diameter, and the gap between the flanks of a V thread is only about half of it, so a printed pair needs more than you might expect: new nuts start at 0.4 mm, 0.3 is tight and 0.5 loose. Print a test pair first. Rods and screws have a clearance of their own here, which makes the bolt that much thinner in diameter. It is set to 0. Which side gets the room depends on what you pair:
  • Printed screw and printed nut: leave the screw at 0 and give the nut the room (the 0.4 mm it starts with).
  • Real screw in a printed nut or tapped hole: the printed side takes all of it, so the nut keeps its 0.4 mm. A tighter 0.3 mm is worth a test if the screw wobbles.
  • Printed screw in a real nut: the real nut has no play, so the screw has to be thinner: 0.3 to 0.4 mm here, as much as a printed nut would have.
  • “Folga ao longo do eixo (Z)”: For nut and tapped hole, the play along the axis, on top of the “Folga (XY)”. Every tooth of the nut gets this much thinner, the diameter stays as it is. The reason: the “Folga (XY)” works on the diameter only and opens the flanks of a V thread to about 0.58 of its value. Anyone who wants air between the flanks has to open the diameter wide and gets sideways slop for it. The play along the axis sets the two apart. It is set to 0, so a saved thread does not change, and it goes up to a fifth of the pitch at most, because above that nothing would be left of the nut's teeth. The field exists for nut and tapped hole only; rod and screw keep their own clearance. More below under "Threads for 3D printing".
  • “Chanfro, ponta superior”, “Chanfro, ponta inferior”, “Chanfro da cabeça” and “Chanfro da borda”: Chamfers at the ends so the thread starts cleanly and the head has no sharp edge. Each end of a rod, nut or tapped hole has its own chamfer, so the top can be long and the bottom short or none. A screw has only one at its tip, labelled “Chanfro”. On a nut or tapped hole the chamfer is the room the mouth opens beyond the outer diameter; the cone runs at 45 degrees on down to the thread core, so no ledge is left at the outer diameter.

Switching a thread between “Barra roscada” and “Furo roscado” keeps its length. A nut and a screw start from their standard measures.

  • “Qualidade”: How finely the thread is calculated. Higher is more exact, but slower.

Printed threads are a topic of their own. Make the screw-and-nut pair as a test first before you print a large part, and adjust the clearance to your printer.

Threads for 3D printing

A printed thread needs air in two places, and they act differently:

  • Clearance in the diameter (“Folga (XY)”): makes the nut wider. The screw then has half the value as air on each side, 0.2 mm at 0.4 mm. The thread turns easily, but the screw can wobble sideways.
  • Play along the axis (“Folga ao longo do eixo (Z)”): makes the teeth of the nut thinner. The screw can then move back and forth along the axis by that value when it is not tightened. There is no extra air to the side for it.

Together they make the gap between the flanks: about 0.58 times the clearance in the diameter plus the play along the axis. An example for a 0.3 mm gap: it used to take 0.5 mm in the diameter, that is 0.25 mm of air on each side. Now 0.2 mm in the diameter (0.1 mm on each side) and 0.2 mm along the axis do it, and the gap is 0.32 mm.

Consequences to know

  • The screw has play along the axis. Without load it can move back and forth by that value. For fastenings, lids and housings that does not matter; for a lead screw that has to position exactly it does, so keep it small or at 0 there.
  • The nut's teeth get thinner. With 0.3 mm at a pitch of 1.75 mm every tooth is almost a third thinner at its middle and so clearly less strong. For heavily loaded parts take a coarser thread instead.
  • More to calculate. The tooth shape gets extra points, so the thread has more triangles and takes a little longer to compute.
  • No true arc in the STEP export for the Whitworth profile. A “Whitworth (55°)” thread with play along the axis goes to the edge tool and the STEP export as a tooth shape made of straight pieces, not with the true circular arcs. At 0 everything stays as before.

Tips

  1. A test pair first. A screw and a nut, each only 4 to 6 mm tall, take a few minutes. Print three pairs with different play side by side and take the one that turns easily and does not wobble.
  2. Start with values that often fit. Clearance in the diameter 0.2 to 0.3 mm and play along the axis 0.2 mm. If the screw wobbles sideways, lower the clearance in the diameter; if it jams, raise the play along the axis. If you would rather do without the play along the axis, use 0.4 mm in the diameter as before.
  3. The play along the axis should be at least one layer height. What lies below one layer the printer does not resolve. With a layer height of 0.2 mm, 0.2 mm is a good start; with 0.1 mm, less is enough.
  4. Print screw and nut upright. The axis points up, so every turn lies in whole layers and the flanks come out clean. Lying down, the flanks sag.
  5. Fine pitches are hard. Below about 1 mm of pitch the turns often fuse. A coarser thread, or a “Trapezoidal” profile with flat crests, prints more reliably than a fine V thread.
  6. Avoid thin tips. The V thread has a narrow tip that the printer hardly hits with its nozzle width. The “Trapezoidal” and “Redonda” profiles have flatter teeth.
  7. Deburr and run it in. The first turns are often stiff because small remains of the print stand on the flanks. Turn it back and forth a few times and it runs easier. The chamfer at the start helps threading it in.
  8. Another printer or filament. The play depends on the printer, the material and the nozzle. Print the test pair again when you change either.

The edge tool takes a thread as its exact body. You can chamfer or round the part that carries it with the thread already in place, or the rims of a screw head, see Breaking edges and hollowing bodies. Working out a thread's edges takes a while: a few seconds for an M6, about half a minute for a G1/2 pipe thread. The quickest way to break the edge of a screw head is still the head chamfer in the properties.

Gears

“Engrenagem” comes as “Engrenagem reta”, “Engrenagem helicoidal”, “Engrenagem espinha de peixe” and “Engrenagem cônica”, and as “Coroa interna” and “Cremalheira” (further down). New gears have “Evolvente” under “Forma do dente”: teeth with involute flanks, as gear generators and engineering use them. Such teeth roll cleanly on each other. You set the number of “Dentes” (6 to 500) and the “Módulo (mm)”, and the size follows: the outside diameter is module × (teeth + 2), the pitch circle module × teeth. New gears start at module 2. Two gears mesh when they have the same module and the same “Ângulo de pressão” (usually 20°) and their centres stand (teeth + teeth) × module / 2 apart. Select both gears and the properties panel gives that centre distance and how far apart the centres are now. If the gears should stay where they are, it also names the module at which they would mesh there, and “Ajustar o módulo das duas” gives both gears that module in one step; each keeps its teeth, height and centre hole. With more than two gears that would undo the pair before: the module of the middle gear changes again. So use “Keep {name}, fit the other” instead, once for each of the two gears: that gear stays exactly as it is, and the other gets its module and is moved along the line between the two centres to the distance where they mesh. Fit a chain of gears one pair after the other, each time keeping the gear that is already in place. If a tooth then meets a tooth instead of a gap, turn one of the gears by half a tooth, which is 180° divided by its number of teeth. “Folga entre dentes” takes a little off the teeth so a printed pair does not bind. The value is for the pair, and each gear takes half of it; 0.2 mm is a good start, 0 gives the exact gear. Below the base circle the flank runs straight down to the root and is not undercut as a cutter would do it. That suits printing, but a very small pinion below about 17 teeth may rub slightly at the root.

A helical gear adds the “Ângulo da hélice”. With involute teeth it is the true helix angle on the pitch circle: two helical gears mesh when they have the same module and the same angle, one positive and the other negative. The “Engrenagem espinha de peixe” is two helical halves turning opposite ways: the teeth run one way up to half the height and back after it, like an arrow. That has two advantages for 3D printing: the gear centres itself on its shaft, and it has no axial thrust, because the forces of the two halves cancel. A helical gear, in contrast, pushes sideways along its axis. You set the “Ângulo da hélice” and the “Qualidade da hélice” as for the helical gear; the angle applies to each half. Two herringbone gears mesh when they have the same module and the same angle with opposite signs, one positive and the other negative. There is no groove in the middle, as on milled herringbone gears: the two halves run into each other without a step.

The bevel gear takes the involute teeth and makes them smaller towards its top. That is an approximation, not an exactly worked out bevel pair. Its own “Ângulo da hélice” (0 to start with) turns the teeth while they taper, as on a spiral bevel gear, for instance to remake the tapered helical gear of an old machine. Such a gear stays a triangle mesh: the edge tool and the STEP export leave it out.

“Redondo” are round teeth made of arcs, like Tinkercad's Useful gear: tip and gap run into each other without a corner. Small gears print more forgivingly that way and turn more easily, and on a knob the teeth make a pleasant grip. Round teeth are set by “Dentes”, “Módulo (mm)” and “Folga entre dentes” too; they have no pressure angle. They stand lower than involute teeth, so the outside diameter is module × (teeth + 1.2). Round gears with the same module mesh, at the same centre distance as involute ones; with an involute gear they do not fit.

“Simples” are the straight teeth every gear had so far. There you set “Tamanho do dente” and “Largura do dente” by hand. Older designs keep them until you change the tooth shape. All three tooth shapes have the “Furo central”.

The “Coroa interna” has its teeth pointing in: a ring that a smaller gear runs inside, like the outer wheel of a planetary set. You set it like an involute or round gear by “Dentes”, “Módulo (mm)” and “Folga entre dentes”, plus the “Aro”, the ring outside the teeth. Its outside diameter is module × (teeth + 2.5) plus twice the rim, with round teeth module × (teeth + 1.7). A gear of the same module runs in it when its centre stands (ring teeth − its teeth) × module / 2 from the ring's centre; select both and the properties panel gives that distance. For a planetary set, ring teeth = sun teeth + 2 × planet teeth, for example 30 = 12 + 2 × 9. A ring gear has no centre hole, it is the ring itself. Between 26 and 33 teeth its tips are up to a quarter module shorter, because a tiny edge would otherwise form at the base circle; meshing is not affected.

The “Cremalheira” is the gear of endless radius: a bar with teeth along one side, whose flanks are straight lines at the pressure angle with involute teeth. Its width (along X) is teeth × pitch, the pitch being π × module, so racks of one module line up end to end, each end falling in a gap. Its length (along Y) is the thickness of the bar and free, as long as the teeth and half a millimetre of bar fit in. The teeth point to the front, towards the viewer of the home view; turn the rack as you need it. A gear of the same module rolls on it when its centre stands its teeth × module / 2 in front of the pitch line; the pitch line lies a module behind the tooth tips, 0.6 module with round teeth. Ring gear and rack come with involute and with round teeth, not with simple ones; switching the gear type keeps the module.

The edge tool and the STEP export take every gear as its exact body, involute flanks as smooth curves. A helical gear on an oval footprint stays a triangle mesh, and so does a helical gear with involute teeth from about 31 teeth. The herringbone gear stays a triangle mesh in the same two cases. From about 31 teeth that applies only to the edge tool: the STEP export writes such a gear exactly at any number of teeth, which takes up to about a minute for a very large one. Small teeth limit how far edges can be rounded: on a gear with simple teeth, 30 mm across with 12 teeth the flat between two teeth at the foot is only about 0.65 mm wide, so rounding every edge works up to about 0.5 mm, and on a bevel gear, whose top is smaller, up to about 0.4 mm. The teeth of a helical or herringbone gear lean, which narrows that flat across its slanted edges: the larger the helix angle against the gear's height, the smaller the rounding that fits. The edges of its two flat ends can be rounded, but chamfering just those edges fails in the CAD kernel; round them, or chamfer all edges together at a smaller size, such as 0.2 mm. On a herringbone gear with involute teeth and a helix angle of about 15 degrees or more, as by default, rounding or chamfering all edges at once is refused; round the ends, or the edges where the halves meet, on their own.

“Junta Hirth” is a disc whose top is a ring of V-shaped teeth running out from the centre. A copy of it, turned over, locks into it at any multiple of one tooth: for a hinge you can set at an angle, a tripod head or a knob that clicks into place. Every crest and every root is a straight line through one point on the axis, so the teeth grow from nothing at the centre to their full height at the rim and the two halves centre themselves on each other. You set the number of “Dentes” (6 to 90), the “Altura do dente” at the rim, the “Furo central” (0 for none) and the “Diâmetro”; the crests reach the full height. The tooth height goes up to the joint's whole height: the roots then reach the bottom at the rim, which suits teeth set on top of another body. New joints have right-angled teeth, and changing the number of teeth or the size keeps the angle between the flanks, which the properties panel shows; only the tooth height changes it. “Forma dos dentes” switches from “Simétrica” teeth to “Dentes de serra”: one flank of every tooth then stands at the angle set under “Flanco íngreme” to the face at the rim (45° to 90°, 90° being a straight step) and the other takes the rest of the tooth, so the joint turns over the gentle flanks one way and holds the other way. “Flanco íngreme do outro lado” swaps the two. The properties panel then shows the gentle flank's angle. A copy turned over locks into saw teeth just the same. The joint stays round like a cylinder, as stretched its teeth would no longer interlock all round: every handle on the workplane changes its one diameter. For the partner, duplicate the joint, turn it 180° about X (front to back) and set it on the first, centre over centre and lifted by its height less the tooth height: then every crest sits in a root. Turned about another axis it may not fit, as one tooth would then stand on another. The Hirth joint is an exact body for the edge tool and the STEP export.

“Polia GT2” is a pulley for a GT2 timing belt with 2 mm pitch, the belt of most 3D printers. Its grooves have the GT2 shape made of arcs, so the belt sits in them as in a bought pulley. As the pitch is fixed, the “Dentes” (10 to 200) set the size: the outside diameter is teeth × 2 mm / π less 0.51 mm, 12.22 mm for 20 teeth, and the properties panel shows it with the pitch circle. Any number of teeth works, not just the sizes you can buy. From the bottom up it has a flange, the toothed band as wide as “Largura da correia” (about 7 mm for a 6 mm belt, 11 mm for a 10 mm belt), a second flange and the hub. “Espessura das flanges” is the thickness of each flange (0 for none) and “Altura das flanges” how far they reach past the teeth; “Altura do cubo” (0 for none) and “Diâmetro do cubo” set the hub, “Furo central” the bore. Width and height follow from these measures: a side handle on the workplane changes the number of teeth, the top handle the belt width. For a set screw, put a hole cylinder through the hub. The pulley is an exact body for the edge tool and the STEP export; from about 117 teeth the edge tool takes it as a triangle mesh, while the STEP export stays exact.

Springs

The “Mola” has “Voltas” and a “Arame”. Together with the height they decide how soft the spring is. “Enrolamento” sets which way the wire runs: “Enrolamento à direita” like a usual compression spring, or “Enrolamento à esquerda”.

The edge tool and the STEP export take a spring as its exact body: a round wire along a helix, cut square at both ends. You can round or chamfer those two wire ends, for instance.

Under “Forma” the spring becomes a “Plana” spring: a band that runs in waves across the plate and flexes in its own plane, printed lying down. “Padrão” gives “Ondas redondas”, a “Zigue-zague” or “Quadrado” turns, “Pontas” an “Olhal” with a hole, a “Aba” across the band or “Nenhuma”. “Curvas” and “Largura da fita” set how soft it is; length is the spring's length, width how far the waves reach and height how thick it is printed. A flat spring is an exact body too.

Bent tubes

A “Tubo curvado” consists of up to twelve sections: a straight piece followed by a bend. For each you set the “Comprimento reto”, the “Ângulo da curva”, the “Raio da curva” and the “Ângulo de giro”. The section you are editing is lit up in orange on the tube, so you can follow the order. A roll angle of 0° bends within the plane of the workplane, at 90° the tube bends upward. The profile can be round, square, hexagonal or octagonal, the inside likewise, or fully solid. If the tube runs into itself, layerling warns you.

Loft

The “Transição” joins one outline at the bottom to another at the top, like a loft in Fusion: a hose adapter from one diameter to another, a square fan onto a round duct, a stand that turns round towards the top. For each end you pick “Contorno inferior” and “Contorno superior”: “Círculo / elipse”, “Retângulo” with “Raio dos cantos inferiores”, or “Polígono” with its number of corners, plus the width and length of each end and the height. “Deslocamento do topo na largura” and “Deslocamento do topo no comprimento” move the top end sideways for a slanted transition; the bottom end stays where it is.

“Espessura da parede (0 = maciço)” turns the solid body into a tube open at the top and the bottom. The opening is smaller by the wall at both ends, measured across; where the wall slants it is a little thinner. Drag the frame bigger and both ends grow along, while the corner radius and the wall keep their size.

“Transição suave (%)” makes the transition smooth. At 0 the sides run straight from the bottom to the top, as on a cone. At 100 they leave both ends straight up and change their size in between along an S-curve: a hose adapter that flares smoothly from a narrow to a wide pipe, instead of running like a funnel. In between the slider mixes the two. A smooth transition works together with “Espessura da parede (0 = maciço)”, a twist, a tilt and a sideways offset; a tube with a wall stays open at both ends. It is an exact body like the straight one, so its edges can be chamfered and filleted, but it is built through several sections and takes a little longer to calculate.

“Segmentos por círculo” sets how finely the circles and rounded corners are drawn: how many straight pieces a full circle is made of in the view and in STL, OBJ and 3MF. It starts at 96, which is smooth for most parts; for a large round end you want to see without facets, raise it, up to 360. More pieces mean larger files. A polygon keeps the “Cantos inferiores” you set. The field shows when an end is round or has a rounded corner.

“Torção” turns the section evenly about the vertical on the way up, up to 360° either way; the sides then wind round. “Inclinação do topo, frente/trás” and “Inclinação do topo, esquerda/direita” tilt the top end, up to 45°: a positive value raises its front edge or its right side. The sections in between tilt by their share, so the wall runs smoothly into the slant. The highest point stays at the set height. If the height later becomes so small that the slanted end would reach under the plate, the tilt gives way until it fits. A bend along a path, such as a pipe elbow, is not something the loft does.

“Seções intermediárias” adds up to twelve sections between the bottom and the top, for a body that does more than run from one outline to another: a fuselage, a bottle with a neck, a vase with a waist. Each section has its own outline, width and length, corner radius or number of corners, its height above the bottom and its sideways offset from the middle of the bottom end; “Seção” picks the one the fields below it are about, as with the segments of a bent tube. A new section goes into the largest gap, sized between its neighbours, and is the one shown next. “Passagem pelas seções” sets how the body runs through them: “Suave” lays one curved surface through every section, and between two sections it stays within their sizes instead of bulging past them; “Reta” runs flat walls from section to section. “Espessura da parede (0 = maciço)” works here too. Twist, tilt and “Transição suave (%)” are for a loft with two ends only and are hidden while there are sections between. A loft without them stays exactly as it was.

The loft is an exact body, twisted and tilted too: its edges can be chamfered and filleted, and STEP export keeps it. Add a flange with screw holes as usual and group them.

Gridfinity

The “Gridfinity” shape makes parts for Gridfinity, the open storage system by Zack Freedman: bins on a 42 mm grid that stand in a baseplate and stack on one another. The measures follow the published Gridfinity specification, so a bin from layerling fits a baseplate made with another generator, and the other way round. layerling is not part of the Gridfinity project, which is released under the MIT licence. Under “Tipo” you choose:

  • “Caixa”: a bin with a foot under every grid unit. “Unidades na largura” and “Unidades na profundidade” count grid units of 42 mm (a bin is 0.5 mm smaller, 41.5 mm for one unit); “Unidades na altura” counts height units of 7 mm, up to 20. The “Borda de empilhamento” on top of the wall holds the feet of the next bin and makes the bin 4.4 mm taller: a bin of 3 units with the lip is 25.4 mm tall. With “Furos para ímãs” every foot gets a hole for a 6 × 2 mm magnet in each corner.
  • “Base”: the plate the bins stand in, 5 mm tall, with a socket for every grid unit. It is an open frame with no floor and no magnet holes; with “Swallowtail” it stands on a floor (see below).
  • “Bandeja”: a tray of any size with a flat bottom, for board game inserts and parts that need no grid. “Comprimento”, “Largura” and “Altura” are free in mm, 10 to 252 mm across and deep and 3 to 140 mm high. It has no feet, no stacking lip and no magnet holes, so it does not stand in a baseplate or stack, and its corners are rounded by 3.75 mm, as a bin's are. Everything below about a bin's inside works on a tray too: its floor is 1.2 mm thick until you set it, its dividers and label shelves run up to its top, they and its finger scoops come at any height that leaves them room, and it takes as many compartments as leave each at least 6 mm wide, up to 24 along a side and 40 in all. A bin turned into a tray keeps its size, a baseplate turned into one is 20 mm high, and a tray turned back into a bin or a baseplate is rounded to grid units; with “Bandeja” as the type under “Padrões das formas” in “Configurações da área de trabalho”, a new tray starts 80 mm wide, 40 mm long and 20 mm high.

The size of a bin or baseplate is always whole grid units (or cells of 21 mm on the half-size grid below), up to 6 × 6 (252 mm, which fits a 256 mm print bed), plus a baseplate's padding (see below); a drag on a handle snaps to the nearest unit. For a larger print bed, switch on “Base grande (até 12 unidades)”, and a baseplate can have up to 12 × 12 units (504 mm); with your printer chosen in “Configurações da área de trabalho”, a plate larger than the printer's bed is flagged. Switching it off brings a larger plate back to 6 units and keeps its padding; at 12 × 12, working out its edges or a STEP export takes about half a minute. The wall (0.95 mm), the floor (1.2 mm) and the depth of the magnet holes (2.4 mm) are not in the specification; the depth of the holes is fixed, and the wall and the floor can be set (see below). The sizes in this section are for the 0.95 mm wall. The specification's M3 screw holes are not made. The top of the lip is sharp, as the specification draws it; if your printer leaves it ragged, chamfer it with “Chanfro da borda de empilhamento”, up to 1 mm, which is the edge tool's chamfer of that size built in, or round it with the edge tool. A bin stacked on top rests on the lip's slope right up to the top, so a chamfer takes the top of that away: about a tenth at 0.25 mm and over a third at 1 mm. Bin, baseplate and tray are exact bodies, so fillet, chamfer and the STEP export work on them. To divide a bin, group thin boxes into it as walls: stand them on the floor, 5.95 mm up (1.2 mm in a tray, or on the raised floor), and on a bin with the lip keep their top at least 0.5 mm below 7 mm per height unit, measured from the underside of the bin (20.5 mm for 3 units), because the feet of the next bin reach 0.35 mm down into the bin. Print bins and baseplates without supports, standing as they are on the print bed.

A bin can also be made on a half-size grid: switch on “Grade de meio tamanho (21 mm)”, and then “Unidades na largura” and “Unidades na profundidade” count cells of 21 mm, up to 12 (the same 251.5 mm as 6 units). Every cell has a foot of its own, 20.5 mm across at the top with the specification's steps, and four of them stand in one socket of an ordinary baseplate, so a bin of 1½ or 2½ units fits beside whole ones. When “Grade de meio tamanho (21 mm)” is switched on, the bin keeps its outline (2 units become 4 cells); when it is switched off, an odd number of cells is rounded up to whole units. The lip follows the bin's outline as before. With “Furos para ímãs” each foot gets one hole, 2.5 mm both ways from its middle towards the corner of its cell that lies on the 42 mm grid, counted from the bin's left back corner: the holes line up with those of a baseplate with magnets from another generator when that corner stands on a corner of the grid; a bin of an odd number of cells can also be turned by 180°, so that this corner stands on a corner of the grid at the front right. The baseplate stays on the 42 mm grid. The half-size grid is not part of the specification.

A bin of 3 height units or more can have label shelves along its inner walls: switch on “Apoio de etiqueta atrás”, “Apoio de etiqueta na frente”, “Apoio de etiqueta à esquerda” or “Apoio de etiqueta à direita”, in any combination. Each shelf that is on gets its own “Largura do apoio”, “Comprimento do apoio” and, for a shorter shelf, “Posição do apoio”; the corner settings below them apply to all of them. A shelf is flat on top for a label, with a 1.2 mm strip down at the front and an underside rising at 36 degrees. Its top is 0.85 mm below 7 mm per height unit, measured from the underside of the bin (20.15 mm for 3 units), so the feet of a bin stacked on the lip stay 0.5 mm clear of it. A bin made lower than 3 units shows no shelves; they come back at 3 units. Label shelves are not part of the specification.

“Largura do apoio” is how far a shelf reaches into the bin: 14 mm, at most 17.2 mm in a bin of 3 units (less with a raised floor), and 16.8 mm for two shelves facing each other in a bin 1 unit deep with 2 mm corners. With “Comprimento do apoio” at 0 a shelf runs from wall to wall. A shorter one, at least 10 mm, brings up “Posição do apoio”, which moves it from the middle of its wall: to the right on the back and front walls, as the front view shows them, and towards the front on the side walls. An end that comes within 1 mm of a wall (1.8 mm with the stacking lip, whose support leans in there), or that stops on that wall's shelf, runs on into it, and two shelves that meet in a corner join into one. Where a shelf meets a wall or another shelf and there is room, the corner is rounded or chamfered: choose “Redondos” or “Chanfrados” under “Cantos do apoio”, and the size with “Tamanho do canto” (2 mm; 0 leaves it sharp). With “Redondos”, a shorter shelf's free ends have their front corners rounded too, by the same size but at most half the shelf's width.

A bin can also have a finger scoop along any of its inner walls, so that small parts can be pushed out up the curve instead of being picked out where the floor meets the wall: switch on “Curva para os dedos atrás”, “Curva para os dedos na frente”, “Curva para os dedos à esquerda” or “Curva para os dedos à direita”, in any combination. The floor rises along a quarter circle into the wall, from wall to wall, and two scoops on neighbouring walls meet in their corner. A bin with a scoop also has every floor edge rounded by 2.8 mm, the radius of its inner corners, and the scoop is that rounding made larger on its wall. Once a scoop is on, “Raio da curva” appears below the switches and applies to all of them: until you set it, it is half the height from the floor up to where the lip's support leaves the wall, 1.65 mm below 7 mm per height unit, measured from the underside of the bin, or up to the top of a bin without the lip (6.7 mm in a bin of 3 units with the lip, less with a raised floor). It is at least 3.5 mm and stays at least 0.5 mm less than that height, and across the bin it leaves at least 2 mm of floor, between two scoops facing each other or between a scoop and the wall opposite it. A bin of 1 height unit has no room for a scoop and shows no switches for it; they come back at 2 units. Finger scoops are not part of the specification either.

A bin can also have a raised floor, for a bin blank to cut shapes into: “Altura do fundo” sets the floor's height, measured from the underside of the bin (5.95 mm, the 1.2 mm floor on the feet, until you set it), and the bin is solid up to it. With the lip, another bin still stacks on it as long as the floor goes no higher than where the lip's support leaves the wall, 1.65 mm below 7 mm per height unit (19.35 mm for 3 units), so the lip stays whole and the feet of a bin stacked on it stay 1.3 mm clear. Above that height the lip is filled too, and the bin is a solid block with a flat top at the lip's top, 4.4 mm above 7 mm per height unit (25.4 mm for 3 units): as tall as the bins with the lip beside it, with no lip for a bin on top and none to chamfer, so “Chanfro da borda de empilhamento” goes, and with no inside “Espessura da parede” goes too. Between the two the field takes no height: going up, typed, stepped or dragged, it goes on to the lip's top; going down from a filled bin it stops at the highest floor a bin still stacks on. A height between them kept in a bin from an earlier version, or left there by a thinner wall, is built at that highest floor too. Without the lip it goes up to the top, and the bin is a solid block. Group holes in the shapes of your tools into it, as deep as you need. Finger scoops start on the raised floor, and label shelves reach less far into the bin so that their underside still ends above the floor; once the floor leaves them no room, their switches go (the scoops above 15.35 mm, the shelves above 15.54 mm, in a bin of 3 units with the lip) and come back when you lower it. A bin of 1 height unit with the lip and a wall of 1.6 mm or less has no room for a floor a bin still stacks on: any floor raised in it fills it to the lip's top, 11.4 mm. A raised floor is not part of the specification either.

“Espessura da parede” sets the wall in from the outside, which never changes, so the bin still fits and stacks as any other. It is 0.95 mm until you set it, from 0.8 mm (two lines of a 0.4 mm nozzle) up to where the walls meet. The inner corners are rounded by 3.75 mm less the wall, and square from a wall of 3.75 mm; the rounded floor edges follow them. With the lip, a wall over 1.75 mm stops at a flat ledge 0.85 mm below 7 mm per height unit, so a stacked bin's feet stay 0.5 mm clear, and a floor that still takes a stacked bin goes no higher than that ledge. Where the walls leave less than 1 mm inside, the bin is built solid and “Altura do fundo” is hidden. Finger scoops and label shelves without room are left out, and fewer compartments are built and offered. A bin open in full on all four sides has no wall to set. A bin switched open on all four sides is never built solid; a side whose wall leaves no room for its opening is open in full.

On a bin, “Raio dos cantos” rounds its outer corners less than the specification's 3.75 mm, down to 0 for square ones, so bins side by side in a drawer leave only their 0.5 mm gaps where four of them meet. Only the outer wall takes it, from 0.5 mm over the feet up: the feet, the inside and the slopes of the lip a stacked bin rests on keep their rounding, so the bin fits in a baseplate and stacks as before, and a bin of one unit still sits down on the slopes of its socket. Over a square corner the wall ends flat, level with the top of the lip (the bin's top without one) or with the foot of its chamfer. A corner on an open side is square already.

A bin can also be divided into compartments without grouping walls into it: under “Compartimentos”, just below “Propriedades”, “Colunas” and “Linhas” set how many, up to 4 per grid unit each way (2 per cell of the half-size grid) and 40 in all. The dividers run the full height, from the floor (or the raised floor) up to 0.85 mm below 7 mm per height unit, where the label shelves stop too, so a bin stacked on the lip sits as before. Dividers need a bin of 2 height units or more, with the floor at least 3 mm below their top; with less room the bin is built without them, and they come back once it has room again. “Espessura da divisória” is 1.2 mm until you set it, from 0.8 to 3 mm. The dividers start evenly spaced. To move one, pick it under “Entre colunas” or “Entre linhas”, counted from the left or from the back, and set its “Posição”, measured from the inside of the left or back wall to the middle of the divider; every compartment stays at least 6 mm wide. Once a divider has been moved, the dividers running that way keep their places in millimetres when the bin is resized; a new number of compartments spaces that way's dividers evenly again. Each compartment has the bin's inner corners, rounded by 2.8 mm, and its floor edges are rounded by 2.8 mm too, with or without a finger scoop. Finger scoops are repeated in every compartment: with a scoop on the back wall, each compartment has one on its back side, against the wall or a divider. In a narrow compartment the radius is made smaller so that 2 mm of floor stays flat, and a compartment too narrow even for 3.5 mm loses the scoops that run that way; a note under “Raio da curva” says so. Dividers are not part of the specification either.

A bin with dividers can have a label shelf in each compartment instead of the shelves along its walls: those are for bins without compartments, and their switches come back once the bin is one compartment again. In a bin of 3 height units or more, choose a compartment with “Linha” and “Coluna” (each shown when there is more than one), and under “Apoio de etiqueta” the side its shelf stands against, the bin's wall or a divider; a side is only offered while a shelf there still leaves the compartment open. “Comprimento do apoio (%)” runs from 10 to 100; a shelf that would come out shorter than 4 mm is left out, and a note under it says so. A shorter shelf brings up “Posição do apoio”: “Esquerda”, “Meio” or “Direita” on a back or front side, or “Trás”, “Meio” or “Frente” on a left or right side. “Largura do apoio” is 14 mm until you set it, less in a narrow compartment, and a shelf never reaches so far that it closes its compartment off: at least 6 mm stays open in front of it. The shelves have the profile of those along the walls, and “Cantos do apoio” and “Tamanho do canto” under “Propriedades” apply to them as well.

Every label shelf, along a wall or in a compartment, can carry a text raised 0.4 mm on its top as part of the bin: type it under “Texto” below the shelf's rows, up to 24 characters on one line. Once a shelf has a text, “Fonte” below the corner settings sets one font for all of them, a built-in one or one of your own as for a text: “Usar” in the “Suas próprias fontes” window puts a font on a selected bin too, and a design keeps the outlines of the letters the bin uses, so it opens with the same letters on another computer. The letters are kerned and made as large as the shelf's top lets them. “Tamanho das letras”, below “Fonte”, sets how high the capitals are, the same on every shelf, so labels of different lengths match; a shelf too small for it makes its letters as large as it lets them, and 0 lets each shelf make them as large as it can. The letters keep 1.5 mm from the wall with the stacking lip and the 0.95 mm wall, as the lip's support leans over the shelf there, and 0.3 mm without the lip or against a divider; 0.4 mm from the front, and from a free end 0.4 mm, or the rounding's size where its corners are rounded (2 mm until you set it); and they stay clear of the inner corners' rounding and of a shelf they meet in a corner. The back and front shelves read from the bin's front, the side shelves along their wall as seen from inside the bin, and a mirrored bin keeps its letters the right way round. The letters' top is 0.1 mm under the feet of a bin stacked on the lip. A text whose capitals would come out under 3 mm high is left out, and a note under it says so; a shorter text, or a wider or longer shelf, makes room. A tray has no text, as its shelves run up to its top. The letters are part of the exact body, so the STEP export has them. Inside a mirrored group the letters read the wrong way round, as a text's do; ungrouped, the bin puts them right. The edge tool works exactly on up to 700 pieces of outline at a time, the letters of every bin selected counted together: about 35 letters in Multilanguage, about 15 in Serif or Script; past that, some of the bins go to the edge tool as their meshes. To print the letters in another colour, add a colour change in your slicer at the shelf's top, 20.15 mm in a bin of 3 units; it also colours everything above it: the top 0.85 mm of the walls and the lip, 5.25 mm in all.

“Cor das letras”, below “Fonte”, gives the letters on all the bin's shelves a colour of their own. Until you pick one they have the bin's colour, and a note under the row says so; the arrow beside it gives them the bin's colour again, as does picking the bin's colour. The bin stays one body: the view draws the letters' tops and sides in their colour, and a 3MF gives those faces that colour in the bin's one object and paints them, and every other face in the file, with their colour's filament, as painting in the slicer would, so Bambu Studio, PrusaSlicer 2.9, OrcaSlicer and the slicers built on it, such as Snapmaker Orca and ElegooSlicer, print the letters with a filament of their own, without a colour change. The slicer shows them in its own filaments' colours: the first colour in the file, usually the bin's, is filament 1 and the letters' the next, the same in every body of the file, so set those filaments to the colours you want. Tried in Snapmaker Orca; not yet in Bambu Studio, ElegooSlicer or PrusaSlicer 2.9: feedback is welcome. Cura reads neither the colours nor the painting; for it, the colour change above still does it. An OBJ has colours only on its points, so the border between the two colours is not sharp. An STL and the STEP export have one colour, and so does a bin after the edge tool, “Vazar”, “Dividir” or “Simplificar malha”, which leave a body without the bin's settings, also once it is made exact with “Make exact”. Where a bin overlaps another body of its colour, the export may join the two into one body, and the letters then come out in the bin's colour. In a group or a bundle the letters keep their colour while “Multicor” is on, as the parts keep theirs, also when the group goes into another one. A new group of solids, and a group in which a hole cuts the bin, start with it off, in one colour.

A bin can also be open on any side, so that bins standing side by side make one long run: switch on “Aberta atrás”, “Aberta na frente”, “Aberta à esquerda” or “Aberta à direita”, in any combination; with all four only the floor on its feet is left. An open side has no wall and no stacking lip above the floor. The walls beside it and their lip run straight out to the bin's outline and end square, so two open bins next to each other are 0.5 mm apart like any two bins, and the floor runs flat out to the edge and ends square there. A label shelf or finger scoop on an open side is not built and its switch goes, and so do that side's scoops against the dividers; the setting is kept for when you close the side again. Shelves and scoops on the walls beside it, and dividers that meet it, run out to the edge, and a compartment offers no label shelf on an open side; one already chosen there is left out, and a note under “Apoio de etiqueta” says so. The feet and the magnet holes stay as they are. A bin stacked on an open bin is held by the lip on the closed sides only. A bin whose floor is raised to the top (with the lip, to the lip's top) is a solid block and shows no switches for open sides. Open sides are not part of the specification either.

A side switched open can also be opened only partly, for a slot to reach into or a lower wall at the front. Under the switches, each open side has its own rows, named here for the front: “Profundidade na frente” is the opening's depth, measured down from the top of the lip (from the bin's top without the lip), at least 2 mm; “Largura na frente” its width along the side, at least 5 mm; “Posição na frente” its position, “Esquerda”, “Meio” or “Direita”; and, at an end, “Distância na frente” its distance from that end. To begin with the opening is the whole side down to the floor, which is the open side described above. A depth within 0.5 mm of the floor goes down to the floor, and a width within 0.5 mm of the whole side is the whole side. Anything less keeps the side's wall, its rounded corners and the lip, and cuts a notch with a flat bottom and square ends out of them: down to the floor a slot, across the whole side a lower wall. The opening stays on the straight part of the wall between the corners, or runs out to the edge beside a side that is open in full, where the wall has no rounded corner; a side whose straight part is shorter than 5 mm is open in full. The floor, the dividers and the lip on either side of the notch stay, so a bin stacked on it still sits on the lip, and the side's label shelf, finger scoop and compartment label shelves stay off as on any open side. On a bin built solid by its wall, a side switched open is open in full. A side opened partly still has a wall, so “Espessura da parede” stays even with all four sides switched open. Once a side is opened partly, “Cantos da abertura” (“Redondos” or “Chanfrados”) and “Tamanho dos cantos da abertura” (0, square, until you set it; up to 10 mm, the row offering as much as the largest corner takes) appear below the open sides' rows and round or chamfer the notches' corners seen from outside the wall, the two at the top and the two at the bottom, alike on every side opened partly. The top corners take the size first and the bottom ones what the depth leaves, so a size over half the depth leaves the bottom corners less, and they stay square once the top ones take all of it. Each corner takes as much of the size as the notch and the wall beside it leave room for, so on an opening placed at an end, the top corner there is no larger than the opening's distance from that end; where a corner would end just beside an edge of the wall, it is made up to 0.5 mm smaller to keep clear of it, and under 0.5 mm it stays square. An opening across the whole side has no top corners, and one run out to the edge beside a side open in full has none at that end. With the lip, a top corner is rounded or chamfered in full on the outer wall only, a little less under a chamfered lip; further in, where the lip slopes down, less.

A baseplate can have padding, for a drawer that is not a whole number of grid units: “Faixa atrás”, “Faixa na frente”, “Faixa à esquerda” and “Faixa à direita” add a solid border at the plate's 5 mm height (7.4 mm with “Swallowtail”) outside the grid, from 0 to 41 mm on each side. The grid stays whole units of 42 mm and moves away from the padded sides, and the outer corners keep their rounding unless “Raio dos cantos” changes it. The plate's size is the whole plate with its padding; a change of padding keeps the units, and dragging a side changes the units and keeps the padding. To fill a drawer, type its inside size into “Largura da gaveta” and “Profundidade da gaveta”: for each, the plate takes as many units as fit, up to 6 (12 with “Base grande (até 12 unidades)”), and splits what is left, less 0.5 mm so the plate drops in, evenly between the padding on the two sides of that direction; the two rows show the drawer the plate fills. A drawer 230 mm wide gives 5 units, 210 mm, and 19.5 mm of padding, 229.5 mm in all; check that the plate fits your print bed. A drawer that one plate on your bed cannot fill takes several baseplates side by side, each padded only on the sides that face the drawer's walls; set their padding with the padding rows. A bin keeps the padding settings and is built without them; they come back when it is made a baseplate again. Padding is not part of the specification either. Below the padding rows, “Raio dos cantos” sets the radius of the plate's four outer corners, 4 mm as the specification draws them, down to 0 for square corners that sit in a drawer's corners; a drawer whose inside corners are rounded takes a radius at least as large as theirs, up to 4 mm. The sockets keep their rounding, so bins fit as before.

A drawer that is not a rectangle - with a corner cut away, a rounded back or an L shape - takes a baseplate fitted into its outline. Draw the drawer's inside as a sketch, or use any shape standing on the workplane, select it together with a baseplate and click “Ajustar base ao contorno” in the properties panel. The plate fills what the shape stands on, set in by 0.25 mm as a drawer fit is: whole 42 mm cells on one grid, placed where it holds the most, at most 6 across and 6 deep (12 with “Base grande (até 12 unidades)”), and solid everywhere else, so every socket still takes an ordinary bin. The plate moves there; the shape stays where it is. The plate's size is then in mm, and “Comprimento” and “Largura” stretch its outline; the hint under “Largura” says how many cells it holds. Switching off “Ajustada a um contorno” turns it back into a plate of whole units with padding. An outline can be as large as one plate takes, 334 mm a side, or 586 mm with “Base grande (até 12 unidades)”, which then stays on while the outline needs it; for a drawer at an angle, turn the plate along it before fitting. It also has to be at least 10 mm a side, with no more than 1000 points. A photo of the drawer can give the outline too: use “Calibrar” on two points whose distance you have measured, then “Traçar”. A photo taken at a slant is not true to size, so treat the trace as a starting outline and check its measurements.

Baseplates printed in several pieces can be joined with “Swallowtail”, named after the swallowtail cramps that held the stone blocks of Egyptian temples together. Switched on, the plate stands on a 2.4 mm floor, 7.4 mm tall instead of 5: its sockets end on the floor, so bins stand 2.4 mm higher.
