Under each side without padding it has half a bow-tie pocket at the middle of each cell, 2 mm deep, so two plates side by side, their cells in line, make whole pockets across the seam. “Adicionar conectores” lays the keys out in front of the plate, flat and ready to print: one for each pocket at its back and right, so that every pocket across a seam with the next plate gets one. Clicked again, it lays them out anew, and the keys it laid out for the plate before give way. Press a key into each pocket across a seam from below: its slotted ends squeeze past a lip at the bottom of the pocket and spring out behind it, so it clicks in and holds the plates together. The lip is only where the key's ends are slotted, so the key's middle passes the seam freely. “Folga dos conectores” sets how much smaller than its pocket each key is, 0.05 mm on every side unless you change it: raise it if the keys jam or break on your printer, lower it if they sit loose, and click “Adicionar conectores” again; the plate stays as it is. A padded side faces a wall of the drawer and has no pockets, and a plate fitted to an outline is one piece for its drawer and has no “Swallowtail” switch. Swallowtail is not part of the specification either.

Hinge

The “Dobradiça” prints in one piece and moves afterwards (print-in-place): two leaves lying open flat on the plate, with alternating knuckles on one axis between them. The pin belongs to the back leaf and runs with play through the knuckles of the front one. You set the “Comprimento (eixo)”, the “Largura aberta” and the “Diâmetro do nó”, plus the number of “Nós” (odd, so the pin is held at both ends), the “Diâmetro do pino” and the “Espessura da aba”.

“Folga” is the gap between the moving parts: around the pin, between the knuckles and in front of the leaves. With 0.4 mm a well-tuned printer usually breaks free with a small twist; if the parts fuse, raise it, if it wobbles too much, lower it. Print the hinge lying down as it appears on the plate, without supports (a raised leaf, below, needs them under it). If you would rather use a pin of your own, such as a piece of filament or wire, which is smoother than a printed pin on a small hinge, choose “Sem pino (use o seu)” under “Tipo”: the printed pin is left out and the bore, the pin diameter plus the clearance, runs through every knuckle, the ends included. With “Ângulo de abertura” you fold the second leaf up about the pin to place the hinge as it stands in your design: 0° lies flat as it prints, 180° is closed, and below 0° it folds down past lying flat, as far as -180°. The angle does not stop where the leaves meet; “Verificar folga” with “Verificar as peças separadas de um objeto (impressas no lugar)” shows whether they touch. The knuckles stay where they are and the hinge remains one piece; remember to set it back to 0° before printing in place. You can add holes to the leaves or group them into a larger part, such as a lid.

A hinge can also be made “Com cones” (under “Tipo”): every other knuckle then ends in cones that nest into conical recesses of the knuckles beside it. There is no pin and no long bridge that could sag, so it prints lying flat; the cones stand at 45°. Like the other styles it is an exact body, so chamfers and fillets work on it and the STEP export holds its true cones, and it makes fewer knuckles where they would be too short for a cone. Instead of the number of knuckles you can give the “Largura do nó (máx.)”: the knuckles are then at most that wide and their number follows from the length; typing a number of knuckles takes the width away again.

“Tipo” has four choices: “Com pino”, “Sem pino (use o seu)” (the bore for a pin of your own), “Com cones” and “Removível”. With cones, “Diâmetro do cone” sets how big the cones are where they grow from their knuckle; bigger cones hold better, and by default they are as large as fits. The cone hinge has no pin and no bore, so its leaf may be as thick as the whole knuckle: set “Espessura da aba” to the knuckle diameter and the leaves lie flush with the knuckles; such a hinge opens about 90° and no further, because the thick leaves meet.

For screwing the hinge on, set the “Furos de parafuso por aba”: up to six holes along the axis, at the “Diâmetro do furo” you choose. Under “Furos” they are “Escareados” by default, at 90° for countersunk screws, on the side that faces the other leaf when the hinge is closed, so the heads lie flush; “Retos” leaves them plain. Without further values the holes share the length evenly and sit in the middle of each leaf; “Espaçamento dos furos (ao longo do eixo)” and “Espaçamento dos furos (entre as abas)” set them centre to centre, for instance to match a bought hinge you replace. Every hole keeps half a millimetre of leaf to the edges, the knuckles and the next hole; where fewer fit, there are fewer, and the field says so. “Raio dos cantos” rounds the four outer corners of the leaves. With a pin or without, holes and corners stay exact in the STEP export and for the edge tool.

Under “Formato da aba”, “Dedos” gives each knuckle its own finger, as wide as the knuckle, instead of a leaf on each side; the fingers of the two sides alternate like two combs. As no finger lies under a knuckle of the other side, the hinge folds all the way round, and with the style “Com cones” and fingers as thick as the knuckle (“Espessura da aba” up to the “Diâmetro do nó”) it closes flat, the fingers of one side between those of the other. No leaf joins the fingers of a side: with the printed pin they hang on it, with cones, or without the pin until your own goes in, they are loose pieces. Join each side to your model, for instance one comb to a box and the other to its lid, or group them with it. “Raio dos cantos” then rounds the tips of the fingers; fingers take no screw holes.

“Aba elevada” lifts the front leaf so that, closed, it lies flat on the back leaf with the “Folga” between: it stands higher by the “Diâmetro do nó” less the clearance and twice the “Espessura da aba”, and starts a little further from the axis to keep the clearance to the other knuckles. Such a hinge opens far past lying flat before the leaves meet: with a 6 mm knuckle and 1.1 mm leaves about 125° below 0°, some 305° from closed, where a hinge with plate leaves stops near 84° below 0°. The raised leaf prints over air, so give it supports from the plate. Screw holes, countersinks and nut pockets go with it and still face the other leaf when closed. With the style “Com cones” both leaves and the clearance between them have to fit within the knuckle diameter, so a thicker leaf is made thinner.

“Removível” makes a lift-off hinge, as on many doors: two knuckles, the lower one carrying the pin to the end, the upper one a sleeve that lifts off it, so a lid or a door comes off and goes back on. Its knuckle count is always two. It prints in place lying flat like the others; to print it standing, the pin upright, take it apart with “Separar peças” and stand the pin's piece on its knuckle and the other piece on its sleeve: then neither needs supports. Mirror it for the other hand. Under “Furos”, on every style, “Alojamento de porca” cuts a hexagonal pocket for a nut over each hole, on the side that faces the other leaf when closed, so a bolt from below holds; “Escareado + alojamento de porca” countersinks the back leaf (the one with the pin) and gives the front one the pockets. “Largura da porca (entre faces)” is the nut's width across the flats; at 0 it follows the hole (M3 5.8 mm, M4 7.3 mm, with play). The pocket is as deep as a nut is high but leaves 0.6 mm of leaf below it, so a thicker leaf takes the nut deeper.

Flexi joints

“Articulações flexi” turns a flat body into a figure that moves, such as a fish, a snake or a dragon, printed in one piece (print in place). You draw or build the body yourself, for instance from a sketch or an SVG you extrude. The tool cuts it across its length into links and puts a joint at every cut: one link carries an upright knuckle that is thicker in the middle than at its ends, the next one wraps round it with clearance. So the joint holds without fusing, and every slope is at 45°, so it prints without support. Between the links a wedge stays open, as wide as the links should swing to the side.

Select the body (several parts are joined, holes among them cut away) and click “Articulações flexi”. In the window you set along which side it is cut (“Lado mais longo” takes the longer one), how many “Articulações” there are, the “Folga” (0.4 mm suits most printers) and the angle for “Giro para cada lado”. The joints are sized to the body; without “Ajustar o tamanho das articulações ao sólido” you give the “Diâmetro da articulação” yourself. Without “Todos os elos com o mesmo comprimento” you set how far the first joint lies from the start and the last from the end, so that a head, say, stays one large piece. Where a joint goes, the body should be about 6 mm high and 12 mm wide at least; if one does not fit, the window says which.

With “Os elos se movem” set to “Para cima e para baixo”, the links fold up and down instead, like the bands of a flexi keychain, an egg or a bracelet. Every cut then becomes a hinge lying flat across the body at half its height: three or five knuckles side by side that belong to the two links in turn, with a cone at 45° on each knuckle of the one link reaching into the next knuckle of the other. Beside the knuckles the cut is a V seen from the side, open as far as “Dobra para cima e para baixo”. The hinge takes its size from the body's height, so there is no joint size to set; the body should be 3.5 mm high at least where the hinges go (5 mm or more holds better) and about 15–20 mm wide.

The result is a bundle of links (meshes) that you print as it lies. If you do not like the cut, undo it and try other values. A first test print with two or three joints shows whether the clearance suits your printer.

Knurling

The “Serrilhado” is a round grip with grooves all around, for knobs, thumb wheels and tool handles. Under “Padrão” you pick “Reto”, grooves along the axis as on a control knob, “Cruzado”: two slanted rows of grooves cross into small diamonds, or “Redondo”: grooves and ridges along the axis as a soft wave of arcs, a pleasant grip without sharp ridges. Round grooves stay shallower than half a pitch, or the ridges would bulge at their foot; a depth too great gives way. You set the “Diâmetro” and the “Altura”, the number of “Ranhuras” and the “Profundidade da ranhura”; for crossed knurling also the “Ângulo da ranhura” to the axis. The “Chanfro nas pontas” breaks both ends at 45 degrees, as on a turned knob; 0 leaves them sharp.

Straight and round knurling are exact bodies, so their edges can be broken and rounded. Crossed knurling stays a mesh, because as an exact body it would take almost a minute to compute with 30 grooves. For a knob on a shaft, group the knurl with a hole, such as a “Rosca” set as a tapped hole. Grooves shallower than 0.4 mm hardly any printer prints cleanly, and layerling does not set them closer than 0.8 mm around the grip: a thin grip gets fewer of them.

Dovetail

The “Rabo de andorinha” is the joint in which two parts lock into each other and can only be slid together sideways. You set the width at the wide end, the “Largura do pescoço” and the length of the tail. Copy the tail for the other side and make the copy a hole: “Folga como buraco” then gives a little play so the joint does not jam after printing.

Tip: A tapped hole cuts into the part it overlaps when grouped. So put it a bit into the material rather than just touching the surface.

Teardrop hole

A hole lying on its side gets a bridge across its top when printed, and the bridge sags. The “Furo em gota” therefore has a point on top: every layer rests on the one below, and the hole comes out round enough without supports. Set the “Diâmetro (parte redonda)” to the size of the hole, about 3.4 mm for an M3 screw, and the “Comprimento do furo” long enough to reach through the part. The “Ângulo da ponta” is 90°, so the flanks meet at 45°. Most printers handle that cleanly; a flatter point needs more height, a steeper one saves it.

Make the teardrop a hole and group it with the part. Its length runs along the depth and the point faces up. For a hole in the other direction, turn it by 90° around the vertical axis.

A tapped hole on its side sags at the top in the same way. Give it a teardrop of its own: add a “Furo em gota” hole whose “Diâmetro (parte redonda)” is the core of the thread, the diameter its teeth leave free (about 8.4 mm for M10), the same length as the tapped hole, and select both. Click “Alinhar” and bring them into line in the middle - the middle of the teardrop is the middle of its round part, not of its box with the tip, so the two circles lie on each other - and group both with the part. The thread is cut as usual and the tip opens the top of the hole, so it prints without supports.

Port openings

A box for electronics needs an opening for the cable. The “Abertura de conector” is that opening: a hole lying on its side, with rounded corners. Pick the socket under “Conector” - “USB-C”, “Micro-USB” or “USB-A” - and it gets the socket's size plus about 0.25 mm of room on every side. “USB-C com espaço para o plugue” is for a socket that sits behind the wall, where the plug's housing has to reach in. The width, the height and the “Raio dos cantos” can be changed by hand; the list then shows “Medidas próprias”. “HDMI”, “Mini-HDMI”, “Micro-HDMI”, “DisplayPort” and “Mini DisplayPort” have their lower corners cut off at a slant like the socket, DisplayPort only the left one, and “RJ45 (rede)” fits a network jack; these sizes come from the makers' recommended panel cut-outs and the VESA drawings. “Folga extra” adds more room on every side on top of that, and the list still shows the socket: for a printed box 0.2 to 0.5 mm, so the board slides in.

For model batteries and motors the list has “XT30”, “XT60”, “MT60 (3 pinos)” and “MPX (Multiplex)”, lying and about 0.25 mm wider than the plug all round, so the plug goes through - the sizes from the Amass drawings and Multiplex. “D-Sub 9 (porta serial, RS-232/RS-485)” is the panel cut-out for the serial port's plug (RS-232 or RS-485), its sides slanting like the plug. Its two 3.18 mm screw holes come with it, 24.99 mm apart at the opening's middle height: the opening and the holes are one group, so they move and turn together, and grouped with a wall all three are cut.

For Anderson Powerpole (PP15, PP30 and PP45) the list has “Powerpole, 1 polo” to “Powerpole, 4 polos”: the housings stacked side by side, 7.9 mm per pole, with room for their dovetail tongues and about 0.25 mm all round - the sizes from the Anderson drawing.

It comes as a hole, facing front. Set the “Profundidade” a little more than the wall is thick, move it to where the socket sits on the board and group it with the box. For a side wall, turn it by 90° around the vertical axis.

SBC boards

The “Placa SBC” is a single-board computer true to size, to build a case around: the board with its four mounting holes, and its parts, each in its own colour: the sockets in their own outline - USB-C with round ends, the HDMI sockets with their lower corners cut - the USB and network housings with their openings, the audio jack with its round collar, the pin headers with a dot for every pin, the larger chips as blocks. Choose it under “Placa”: Raspberry Pi 5, 4 Model B, 3 Model B+ or Zero 2 W, BIGTREETECH Pi V1.2, or one of the small ESP32 boards: Seeed Studio XIAO ESP32-C6, ESP32-C3 Super Mini or ESP32-C6 Super Mini - these have no mounting holes, their USB-C is at the right end, and their castellated pins show as dots. The two Super Minis have no maker's drawing; their sizes come from published community models and are all estimated. Or one of the microcontroller boards: Adafruit ESP32-S3 Feather, Arduino UNO R3, Arduino MEGA 2560 Rev3, Arduino Nano or LOLIN (WEMOS) D1 mini V4.0.0 - their USB socket is at the left end, as in the makers' own PCB files, and the UNO and the MEGA keep their stepped outline. The Feather's heights come from Adafruit's 3D model; Arduino's files give none, so on the UNO, the MEGA and the Nano they are estimated. The D1 mini follows Wemos's dimension drawing, without its two mounting holes; its parts' sizes and heights are estimated. The Raspberry Pi Pico, Pico W, Pico 2 and Pico 2 W come from Raspberry Pi's own 3D models, with micro-USB at the left end; the Pico 2 W has no model of its own and takes the Pico W's parts, estimated. Two camera boards follow: the ESP32-CAM (AI-Thinker) with its ESP32-CAM-MB USB programmer board under it, and the nulllab ESP32-S3-CAM with USB-C; neither maker gives the parts' places and heights, so they are estimated, and the microSD card slot is a connector at the edge on the ESP32-CAM. On both, Camera lens up through the lid makes the lens reach up through a lid by Reach up. Last come the ESP32 boards with the WROOM module: Espressif's ESP32-DevKitC V4 (38 pins) from Espressif's own dimension drawing, and the 30-pin ESP32 DevKit V1, sold unbranded, from a published true-size drawing and so all estimated. On every board with buttons, Button reach (0 at first, up to 100 mm) makes RESET, BOOT and power reach the way they are pressed: up through a lid, or out through the wall for the Pi 5's power button and the D1 mini's RESET, which are pressed from the side. Its front edge, with USB-C and HDMI, faces you. The outline and the holes come from the makers' drawings and models; a height no drawing gives is estimated.

The board shows where the posts for its screws go and how tall the case must be. For the openings, give the connectors room under “Folga dos conectores” - 0.2 to 0.5 mm for a printed case - make a copy of the board a hole, put it where the board sits in the case and group it with the case: every connector at the edge cuts its opening through the wall. The real connectors stand out of the board only 1 to 3 mm, less than many walls are thick: “Atravessar a parede” makes each connector at the edge reach that much further out on its side, so it cuts right through - a little more than the wall is thick. Another board or setting makes it again where it stands. Every board takes both settings the same way.

The microSD card slot is a connector at the left edge too, under the board (on the Zero 2 W on top), so the reach cuts the card's way through the wall; the board then stands on the slot, 1.4 mm under its underside. The ribbon cables can come out as well: “Cabos flat para cima pela tampa” opens the camera, display and PCIe connectors up through a lid, “Cabos flat para o lado pela parede” lays an opening from each across its long side - the way the cable leaves it - to the nearer edge and on by the reach; on the Raspberry Pi 5 the camera and display cables come out at the PCIe end, the three openings one above the other, on the Pi 4 and 3 B+ the camera's above the display's. “Conector GPIO para cima pela tampa” takes the pin header up through the lid, for a HAT or jumper wires. What goes up reaches “Alcance para cima” over its top, at least 20 mm, and gets the clearance round it.

Counterbore and countersink

A screw head often should not stand proud. The “Rebaixo” cuts a round pocket for a socket-head screw (DIN 912), the “Escareado” a cone for a countersunk screw (DIN 7991). Both stand with the head end up: the “Diâmetro da cabeça” is the diameter of the pocket or the cone, the “Diâmetro do corpo” the bore below it, the “Comprimento total” the whole length. On the counterbore you set the “Profundidade da cabeça”, on the countersink the “Ângulo do cone” (90° suits countersunk screws). The defaults fit an M3 screw.

The “Escareado duplo” is a hole chamfered on both faces, for a plate that is to look neat on its front and its back. It has no entry of its own in the shape library: take the “Escareado” and switch on “Dos dois lados” in its properties (bodies that are a double countersink already show the switch on): a cone at each end opens to the “Diâmetro da cabeça”, with the “Diâmetro do corpo” between them. You set the “Ângulo do cone” and the “Comprimento total” as before. If the hole is too short for two full cones, they meet in the middle at that angle and the shaft stays wider than you set: a head of 10 mm, a shaft of 6 mm, 90° and a length of 2 mm make two cones from 10 down to 8 mm. As a hole it is pushed through a part like the others.

Make the shape a hole and group it with the part. Let its top end a little above the surface the head should sit on, so the pocket opens cleanly. For the pocket of a hex nut, use a “Polígono” with six sides as a hole. Under “Tamanho do parafuso” you pick M2 to M30 (the countersink up to M20), and the shaft (clearance hole to ISO 273, medium), head diameter and depth or angle follow the standard (DIN 974-1, ISO 15065); the length stays. On the hexagon, “Alojamento de porca” sets the width across flats and the height of an ISO 4032 nut, with 0.4 mm of room for printing.

A drilled blind hole does not end flat but in the cone of the drill's tip (Discussion #621). The “Rebaixo”, the “Escareado” and a “Cilindro” set as a hole can end that way: under “Bottom”, pick a drill point of 90°, 118° (a common twist drill) or 135°, or “Drill point, other angle” and type the angle under “Point angle”, from 60° to 150°. As in a drawing, the depth – the cylinder's “Altura”, the screw hole's “Comprimento total” – counts to the shoulder where the cone begins; the tip lies beyond it, about 0.3 times the diameter at 118°, and the line under the angle says how far. The cone is as wide as the hole, on a screw hole as wide as its shaft. “Flat” leaves the bottom as it always was. A solid cylinder keeps its flat end, and so does the double countersink, which goes through.

A slotted hole leaves a part room to be moved a little before the screw is tightened, to line it up (Discussion #1531). Switch on “Oblongo” on the “Rebaixo”, the “Escareado” or the “Escareado duplo”: the pocket or the cone and the shaft then run round the two ends of a slot and straight along its sides. “Comprimento do rasgo” sets how far; it starts as long as the head is wide and runs along the width, so turn the hole to point it another way. The “Diâmetro da cabeça” and the “Tamanho do parafuso” change the head and keep the slot. A slotted hole has no drill point, and like the round one it is an exact body.

The “Arruela de acabamento” (a rosette, Discussion #1131) is the domed washer that goes under a countersunk or raised countersunk screw, for a tidy look on wood or a cover. It is a solid part, flat underneath; from a low rim a dome rises to the seat, a cone for the screw head, with the bore below it. Under “Tamanho do parafuso” you pick M2 to M20: the bore is the clearance hole and the seat the countersink of that size, the “Diâmetro” and “Altura” follow from them (M3: 10.3 by 2.95 mm, M6: 16.6 by 4.5 mm). You can also set the “Diâmetro”, “Altura”, “Furo central”, the “Diâmetro da cabeça” at the top of the seat and its “Ângulo do cone” yourself. It stays round, and it is an exact body, so the edge tool and STEP work on it.

Screw boss

The “Screw boss” is the post a lid or a board is screwed to in an enclosure: a round post with a hole from the top. Under “Fastener” you choose what goes into it. A “Heat-set insert” is a brass insert pressed in with a soldering iron: “Size” offers M2 to M5 and #2-56 to 1/4-20, the hole as the common inserts want it (M3: 4.0 mm for an insert 5.7 mm long), a millimetre deeper than the insert so the plastic it pushes aside has room, and the post about twice the hole. A “Self-tapping screw for plastics” cuts its own thread: ST2.2 to ST4.2 (DIN 7981), plastics screws of 2.5 to 5 mm (K25–K50) or #2 to #10, with a pilot hole of about 0.8 times the screw, the post 2.5 times it and the hole 2.5 screws deep. “Hole of my own” takes the diameter and depth you type in.

“Hole diameter”, “Hole depth” and “Outer diameter” can be changed by hand; below the diameter the panel says how thick the wall round the hole is, and warns when it is thinner than the fastener wants. A hole as deep as the post goes through. The hole's mouth has a small chamfer, so the insert or the screw finds its way in. “Gussets” adds two to six thin ribs from the post down to the floor; “Width with gussets”, “Gusset height” and “Gusset thickness” set how far out, how high and how thick they are.

Stand the boss on the floor of a hollowed box and group it with the box; in the lid, a “Rebaixo” as a hole over it takes the screw head. Set as a hole and grouped with a solid part, the boss cuts only its hole – the pocket for the insert or the screw, with its chamfer – so a block or a post of your own gets a blind hole for an insert; the hole opens where the boss's top is. Printed holes come out a little smaller than drawn: print one boss first and adjust “Hole diameter” by a tenth or two.

Snap-fit

A lid that clicks shut needs no screws. The “Snap-fit” is a hook on a foot with its counterpart, the catch. With “Part” set to “Hook and catch” the two stand where they sit when snapped in, so you place them on lid and box together; “Hook only” or “Catch only” makes one of them. The barb has a slope below it that lets it slide in, the “Entry angle” (30° goes in easily), and above it the face that holds: at a “Holding angle” of 90° it holds for good, at 45° it can be pulled apart again. The “Undercut” is how far the barb reaches under the catch, “Clearance” the play between the two.

The arm bends by the undercut as it goes in. Below “Arm thickness” the panel says how much it stretches at its root: PLA starts to break above about 2 %, PETG and ABS take about 4 %. A longer or thinner arm, or a smaller undercut, stretches less. The pair stands as it sits in a box printed upright, the lid on top: the hook hangs from its foot, the catch's top slopes at 45°, and only its holding face, as wide as the undercut, reaches out flat, so it prints on the wall without support.

Put the pair where the lid meets the box wall: the hook's foot under the lid, the catch's back against the inside of the wall. “Separar peças” then splits them into two bodies; group the hook with the lid and the catch with the box. If you can, print the lid so the arm lies flat: an arm standing up bends across its layers and breaks more easily.

Ribs

The “Rib” stiffens a floor or a wall. As a “Straight rib” it is as long, high and thick as you set, its “Top” flat, round or chamfered. As a “Gusset” it is a triangle that braces a wall against the floor: “Along the floor” along the floor, “Up the wall” up the wall, both ends cut off short so they print cleanly.

With “Foot” switched on, the rib stands on a thin plate along its whole length, centred under it and wider than it (a gusset's lies under its side along the floor), which holds it on the bed or the floor, so a thinner rib still stands. The foot starts three times as wide as the rib and 0.8 mm thick; “Foot width” is measured all the way across, so the shape is as wide as the foot, and “Foot thickness” from the bottom up.

Under “Foot shape” the foot is “Square” or “Oval”. The oval foot is an ellipse seen from above, without corners that could lift off the bed as the plastic shrinks while it cools. It is as wide as the foot and just long enough that at the rib's two ends it is still twice as wide as the rib, so the ends stand on it as well (under a gusset it is half an ellipse, from the wall to past the tip). On a foot narrower than about 2.7 times the rib the ellipse would get long: it stops at one and a half times the rib's length, but never so short that the ends stand on nothing. The shape grows by what reaches past the ends; the rib keeps its length.

A rib about as thick as the wall or a little thinner, a multiple of the line width (0.8 or 1.6 mm with a 0.4 mm nozzle), and a few times as high as it is thick stiffens without pulling the wall out of shape. Several in a row come from “Padrão”; group them with the box.

10. Measuring and notes

Tape measure, ruler and framing square, distances to the origin, notes that stay attached to a part, and reference points that things snap to.

Este capítulo ainda não foi traduzido para o português. Segue o texto em inglês.

To build a part exactly, you need to measure. layerling has several tools for that. None of them ends up in an export. Wall thickness and gaps inside a part are best measured in the section view with “Medir”.

The tape measure

The tape measure sits at the lower end of the view bar on the left edge (“Trena”). It measures distances between corners, edges and faces. A click on it opens five buttons. If they cover what you want to measure, drag them by the grip on the left anywhere on the workplane; a double-click on the grip puts them back:

  1. “Adicionar medida”: Click one point, drag to the next and click it. The distance is labelled, with the axes it runs along in front: X, Y or Z for a straight one, XY, XZ or YZ across a plane, 3D for all three. Hover over the label to see how far it reaches along each axis, over a point to see its coordinates. While you place the second point, the axes, the distance and the reach along each axis show beside the pointer. A measurement that lies mostly behind another body fades; hovering its line or label brings it back. On an opposing edge or face, the second point snaps in at a right angle to the first when the pointer comes near - or anywhere on that edge or face while you hold Shift. Along the same face or on the workplane, Shift keeps the measurement straight along the main axis. Besides corners and edges, a point snaps to the middle of the flat face under the pointer and to the centre of a round edge, such as the rim of a hole or of a cylinder: a small cross in a circle marks the centre on offer, and when the pointer comes near, the point snaps in and a hint says what it is the centre of (“Centre of face”, “Centre of hole” or “Centre of circle”).
  2. “Mover pontos da medida”: Grab the points and move them, the number follows.
  3. “Excluir parte da medida”: Afterwards click a measurement to remove it. While “Adicionar medida” is active, holding Shift or Ctrl (Cmd on a Mac) and clicking a measurement point or line deletes it right away without switching modes.
  4. “Medir arestas inteiras”: A click on an edge measures all of it. A round edge says its diameter (Ø), the rim of a hole or of a cylinder for example, and an arc its radius (R); point at the number to see the length along the edge. With this switched off, a click puts a point on the edge instead, and the second point goes anywhere, so you can measure the diameter or any other distance. Alt turns the switch round for one click. On a circle, the point across from the first one snaps in when the pointer comes near, and the points sit on the true circle, so the diameter comes out exact.
  5. “Excluir todas as medidas”: Removes every measurement at once. Because this cannot be undone, layerling asks first; with no measurements there is nothing to do.
  6. “Marcar o meio como ponto de referência”: In the middle of every measurement sits a small round mark, its lower half filled. It puts a reference point in the middle of the measurement: after a click on a round edge, such as the rim of a hole, in the centre of that circle - on an imported mesh too, where nothing else marks the middle of a hole - and for a diameter or any straight measurement halfway along it. A shape you drag then snaps to the point with its centre. A point that is there already is not made twice. The tape measure snaps to a reference point like to a corner, so you can measure from the centre of a circle or from the middle of a line: mark it, then click the point.
  7. “Digite um comprimento: o sólido no segundo ponto se move ao longo da linha; um comprimento negativo o leva além do primeiro ponto”: When at least one end of a straight measurement sits on a body, its number can be clicked. Type a new length and press Enter: the body at the second point moves along the measured line until the distance is exactly that, as with the ruler in Tinkercad. If only the body at the first point is selected, that one moves instead. The measuring points stay on the body, so the measurement follows. Measure from a corner, an edge or the centre of a face or a hole to place parts at an exact distance: from the centre of a hole to the middle of a cylinder's top, the cylinder moves centre to centre. A negative length takes it that far past the first point, say 5 mm inside the edge of a box. A reference point belongs to no body, so between two of them nothing moves. When the measurement runs along two or three axes, the field also has a box under the length for each of them (ΔX, ΔY, ΔZ, the reach shown when you point at the number): type there instead, and the body moves along that axis only. Tab goes from box to box, Esc closes the field without moving anything. Pointing at the number tells which body will move, or why none can: it is locked, both points lie on the same body, or neither lies on a body. The message afterwards says what moved and how far; one undo takes it back.

Esc leaves measuring mode.

The ruler

You fetch the “Régua” from the shape library. It is purely a measuring tool: it appears in no export and can neither be grouped nor cut. For every body that touches or overlaps the ruler, it shows the extent as a floating number right in the view. You can change that number right there, and the body follows. Stand the ruler up or tip it, and it measures along its own direction: upright beside a body it shows the body's height. The floating plus symbol creates a copy of the measured shape; it is there while the ruler lies flat. Its printed scale is in millimetres along one long edge, with the tens numbered, and in inches along the other, with a line every sixteenth of an inch and the whole inches numbered. The scale of the unit you work in (the switch at the bottom right) runs along the top edge; a ruler narrower than 15 mm carries only that one.

The framing square

Sometimes you measure better at a right angle. Click “Posicionar esquadro” in the view bar and then the workplane. A framing square with two arms at a right angle, with tick marks like a try square, is placed there. It has no body of its own either. Click close to the corner of a body, and its corner snaps exactly there. The design keeps the square where you set it, also in a saved .lyl file: when you open the design again, it is in the same place, turned the same way and measuring from the same points, until you remove it. If you need it in almost every design, switch on “Começar novos projetos com um esquadro na origem” under “Medidas” in the settings: every new design then starts with a framing square at the origin.

The framing square lies on the workplane. If that sits on the side of a body, the square lies on that side too, see View and workplane. That is how you dimension on a vertical wall: put the workplane on the wall, place the square at its top left corner and click the handle until the arms point right and down.

  • Dragging the handle moves it.
  • A short click on the handle turns it by 90°.
  • The × beside it removes it.
  • Dragging the small circle at the end of an arm makes that arm longer or shorter, in whole millimetres. The lowest button under the handle, “Braços do tamanho da mesa de impressão (arraste a ponta de um braço para mudar seu comprimento)”, makes both arms as long as the build plate is wide and deep, for the printer set in the settings. The square keeps its arms' lengths with the design, and a square set again takes them over.
  • The small button left of the handle switches what is measured from: the outside of a body (endpoint, an icon with lines) or its middle (midpoint, a crosshair). A small switch of the same kind sits beside each green number and sets that number alone: for a standing cylinder the middle in the two arms and the bottom in height, for a lying one the middle across and an end along. When all three agree again, the button at the handle shows the common mode.

If bodies stand at one of the arms, the framing square shows their dimensions automatically, selected or not: bodies inside the square, beside an arm or across it. A body outside it, behind the corner or beside an arm from the outside, gets none. That works on the base plate only, not on the side of a body. The button with the arrow under the square's handle switches that off, so that only the selected bodies show their dimensions; it is kept with the design.

When you select a body, the framing square shows in green how far it is from the corner, along both arms and in height. Click a green number to type a distance, and the body moves exactly there. With several bodies selected, they count as one: the ruler measures their shared outline, and a typed value moves them all together without changing their positions relative to each other.

The guide lines of the green numbers run along the floor, the plane the framing square lies in, to the point below or beside the body; the height has its own arrow. The switch of each number sits in the frame of the number. The arms and the ticks are lines in the room: a body in front of them hides them, as a real square would be hidden. The small eye below the handle switches that: with the eye struck through, bodies hide the square (the start); with the eye open, the square stays in view over everything. The numbers on the arms fade where a body stands in front of them.

With the midpoint, the green numbers count to the middle of the body, in height as well. That way you place a sphere with its centre exactly 15 mm from an edge, without subtracting the radius. On a wall you place a hole 40 mm from the left and 190 mm from the top like this: select the hole, switch to midpoint, type 40 and 190. The height there counts outward from the wall.

Both the tape measure and the framing square stay where they are while you sketch and come back to the 3D view. Neither is in the history. The framing square is kept with the design, and so are the measurements of the tape measure, in the browser and in the .lyl file: they are there again when you open the design. The eye button among the tape measure's buttons hides all measurements and shows them again; whether they are hidden is kept as well, and adding, moving or deleting a measurement shows them first.

The protractor

Click “Protractor” in the view bar to measure an angle. A row of buttons opens beside it, and until you click the button again or press Esc, a click in the view measures with the protractor. Like the tape measure, it snaps to the corners and edges of bodies; beside the bodies it sets a point on the plate.

  • “Angle from three points”: click the corner of the angle first, then a point on each side. While you place the last point, the angle shows already; after the third click it stays, with an arc between the sides. It is the angle at the corner, from 0° to 180°.
  • “Angle between two faces”: click two flat faces. A short blue line on each shows which way it faces, and the label gives both angles the faces make, the smaller first: a 45° chamfer against the top reads 45° · 135°, two sides of a box just 90°. A curved face has no single direction, so the protractor asks for a flat one.

The next click after a finished angle starts a new one, and “Remove the angle” removes it. The angle follows the bodies when they move or turn. Nothing of it is saved or goes into the history: it is gone when you put the protractor away.

Distances to the origin and while moving

In the settings under “Aparência” there are two switches for live dimensions:

  • “Mostrar dimensões do deslocamento” shows by how much you move while dragging. That includes lifting with the black arrow above a body; the way up or down shows at its front corner. The arrow keys show their way as well: the presses add up until you select something else or drag, and Ctrl+↑ and Ctrl+↓ show the way up or down. Once you let go, click such a number and type the exact distance; a minus goes down.
  • “Mostrar distâncias até a origem” shows the distances of the selection to the origin of the plate, also with several selected bodies.

With “Dimensões sempre visíveis” the dimensions stay visible permanently. A body that does not stand on the workplane also shows its height above it; click the number to type a new one. With “Dimension boxes in axis colours” each box takes the colour of its axis, as the handles do: red for X, green for Y and blue for Z. So on a small part you see at a glance which number is which.

For a moment without them, press Q: the sizes and distances around the selection disappear, so a part you move is easy to see. Q again brings them back. A handle you point at still shows its size.

Checking clearance

Parts that should move after printing - a flexi dragon, a hinge printed in place, a box and its lid, an axle in its bore - need a gap between them. Too little, and they stick together; overlapping, they print as one piece. “Verificar folga”, next to “Transição entre esboços”, checks that before you print. It takes the selected objects, or every visible object when nothing is selected (the same ones an export takes), and checks each pair:

  • “Sobreposição” (red): the two share a volume. It shows red inside the bodies, which turn see-through, and the list says how large it is.
  • “Contato” (red): they touch and fuse when printed.
  • “Folga insuficiente” (orange): the narrowest gap is smaller than “Folga mínima”.
  • “Folga suficiente” (green): the narrowest gap is at least that wide.

Each row names the two parts and, for a gap, its width and where it lies: “lado a lado” (within one layer) or “entre camadas” (above or below: there the slicer can only leave whole layers free, so a gap thinner than one layer closes). Click a row: the camera goes there, both parts are outlined, and a line with the number marks the narrowest place. Pairs further apart than 5 mm are not listed. Nothing in the design changes: the check saves nothing and leaves nothing to undo.

“Folga mínima” starts at 0.3 mm; 0.3 is tight, 0.4 usual for a print in place. Changing it sorts the list again at once, without a new check, and the browser keeps the value. “Verificar as peças separadas de um objeto (impressas no lugar)” (on to start) checks the separate parts of one object against each other too: a flexi dragon or a hinge imported as one STL is one object, but its links are separate parts. They are listed as "Name · Part 2". A part inside a cavity of another, a ball in a cage, is a part of its own.

If you change the design while the panel is open, it shows “Algo mudou – verifique de novo”; click that or “Verificar de novo”. Esc or “Fechar” closes the panel. Scaling changes the gaps too: a flexi model scaled to 70 % keeps 70 % of its gaps, so check again after scaling.

The check measures the triangle mesh the slicer gets. A round axle and its bore are polygons with their corners on the circle, so a gap can come out a few hundredths smaller than the round numbers. A pair with too many triangles is listed as “Não verificado”. An AI runs the same check with layerling_check_clearance.

Notes

A note records what the geometry does not say: "This screw is 0.3 mm too tight", "print the lid yet", "dimension from Peter". Place one with “Anotação” or the N key.

  • If you place the note on a body, it travels with it.
  • If you place it beside, it stays on the workplane (“No plano de trabalho”).
  • “Soltar do objeto” releases an attached note from the body.
  • “For the AI” turns a note into a request for an AI agent on the MCP bridge (see "AI with MCP"): the agent reads it with layerling_list_notes, does the work and answers in the same note, under your text. It can also put notes of its own on the model, to ask or report something at a spot. Ask the agent to watch your notes, and it waits for them with layerling_wait_for_notes: you then only work on the model, and every new request is picked up as soon as you tick the box, without going back to the agent's window.
  • “Grupo de união” takes an attached note into the group; “Desagrupar” hands it to the visible part under it, a group inside included. While a group is open with “Editar grupo”, its notes move with the part under them and go back to the group with “Concluído”; cancelling puts them back as they were.
  • If its body is deleted, or no visible body is under it any more, the note stays where it stood, on the workplane.
  • Dragging the pin moves the note. A click on the pin folds the card away, only the small number stays; another click opens it again. A click into the text edits it.
  • While you write, Enter keeps the text and Esc puts it back to how it was before you started; Shift+Enter starts a new line.
  • In a sketch, “Anotação” or N places a note too, anywhere on the sketch. All of a sketch's notes belong to its body: in the 3D view they sit on it, on the top of an extruded or swept body and on the drawn profile of a revolved one, and move with it. When you open the sketch again it shows the body's notes, including those placed in 3D. In the sketch, Undo takes back a note like a line, and “Cancelar” discards what you changed in the notes. Shift+N shows or hides the notes here too.

Notes are saved in the design, appear in no export and can be shown or hidden with “Mostrar anotações e pontos” (in “Opções de visibilidade”, the arrow beside the eye icon) or with Shift+N.

Reference points

A reference point is a bare mark in space, like a pencil mark or a layout point in a workshop: it belongs to no body, is never printed, and other things snap to it. Right-click a body and choose “Marcar o centro”, “Marcar os cantos” or “Marcar os meios das arestas”: the points appear on the top face of the body (of the whole selection, if you selected several). “Marcar o centro desta face” puts one in the middle of the flat face you right-clicked instead, on a side or an end, say. With a pivot set, “Marcar o pivô” puts one exactly on it, so another part's centre snaps to the point the selection turns about.

  • Drag a point to move it: it snaps to the corners, the middles of the edges and faces of bodies, to their real corners and to other points; hold Alt to let it go free. Or click it to see its coordinates and type new ones; they use the unit you set. Each card can be dragged away by its title if it covers something, on its own: the others stay where they are, and a double-click on the title puts it back. The card you touched last stands in front of the others. Delete all in a card, or Delete all reference points in the right-click menu (of a body, or of an empty spot of the 3D view), deletes every point at once. “Excluir” removes it.
  • The tape measure can mark a point too: “Marcar o meio como ponto de referência”, the half-filled mark in the middle of a measurement, puts one in its middle, in the centre of a round hole for example. And it measures from a point: the tape snaps to reference points like to corners.
  • When you drag a shape, its edges and its centre snap to a point, like they snap to other shapes (“Encaixar em outras formas ao mover”). The framing square snaps to points too.
  • Points are saved in the design, appear in no export, and are shown or hidden together with the notes by “Mostrar anotações e pontos” (Shift+N).
  • An AI can mark, list and remove them with layerling_add_reference_points, layerling_list_reference_points and layerling_remove_reference_points.

Reference images

A reference image is a picture to line parts up on: lay a photo of a circuit board on the floor of its case, and place the standoffs, holes and connector cut-outs right on it. It is a guide, not a body: it is never printed, never exported (STL, 3MF, OBJ, STEP, SVG), never part of a group, a bundle or a cut, and the print estimate leaves it out.

  • Open “Importar” and choose “Imagem de referência”, then a PNG, JPG, WebP, GIF or BMP picture. It lands on the workplane - on the plate, or on the face you set the workplane on - with its longer side 100 mm, half see-through.
  • Move, turn and resize it with its handles like any shape. A body in front of it is picked first, so working on top of it does not grab the picture.
  • “Transparência (%)” in its settings fades it from solid to barely there.
  • “Calibrar” gives it its true size, as in the sketch: click two points on the picture whose real distance you know - two mounting holes of the board, say - and type that distance in “Distância real (mm)”. The picture keeps its proportions and its middle.
  • Lock it with the lock in the header of its settings, and it stays put: clicks then go through it to the plate. Pick it in the object list to unlock it.
  • The picture is saved once in the design file, however often it is copied or undone. A large picture makes the file larger by as much; the message when you add it says how large it is.
  • An AI adds, moves, calibrates, fades and locks one with layerling_reference_image. With trace it traces the picture into a sketch body standing on it, as the sketch's “Traçar” does.

11. Preparação para a impressão 3D

Como escolher a sua impressora, ser avisado quando algo não cabe e deitar a peça do jeito certo.

Escolhendo a sua impressora

Abra as configurações (a engrenagem na linha do título, “Configurações da área de trabalho”) e vá para a área “Plano de trabalho”. Em “Impressora” você escolhe a sua impressora numa lista de mais de 230 modelos comuns, entre eles Bambu Lab, Prusa, Creality, Anycubic, Elegoo e muitos outros.

Três coisas acontecem:

  • O plano de trabalho assume o tamanho da mesa de impressão.
  • No canto do plano de trabalho aparecem o nome da impressora e o volume de impressão dela. Se o texto atrapalhar, desligue-o com “Textos na mesa” em “Plano de trabalho”; isso vale também para o nome do projeto, na frente à esquerda.
  • layerling avisa quando algo não cabe.

Os perfis de impressora vêm do OrcaSlicer, então são os mesmos que o seu fatiador conhece. Se preferir trabalhar sem impressora, escolha “Sem impressora - tamanho livre”. Você também pode definir o tamanho do plano de trabalho à mão.

Impressoras delta, como as da FLSun ou da SeeMeCNC ou a Anycubic Predator, imprimem sobre uma mesa redonda. Com uma delas, o plano de trabalho também fica redondo e tão largo quanto a mesa, e um sólido é grande demais assim que passa da borda. Um sólido redondo é medido pelo próprio contorno, não pela caixa em volta dele, então cabe até um cilindro quase tão largo quanto a mesa.

Quando algo não cabe

Um sólido que passa da borda da mesa de impressão fica marcado. Uma mensagem diz quais lados passam e quanto. O mesmo vale se a peça for alta demais: a altura conta a partir do sólido mais baixo, do mesmo jeito que o fatiador apoia o modelo na mesa.

O aviso não impede você de continuar trabalhando. É uma dica, para você não descobrir só no fatiador que a peça é grande demais. Uma peça grande demais muitas vezes pode ser dividida: corte-a em duas com “Dividir” e imprima as duas metades separadamente.

Se você deixa peças ao lado da mesa de propósito, clique no pequeno X da mensagem. O aviso então some só para esses sólidos. Se um deles voltar a caber e depois você o tirar da mesa de novo, ou se outro sólido passar da borda, a mensagem volta. Sólidos ocultos nunca contam, então ocultar as peças deixadas ao lado também funciona.

Deitando a peça do jeito certo

O jeito como a peça fica na mesa decide a resistência e a aparência dela. Duas ferramentas na área “Organizar” ajudam:

  • “Deitar sobre a face”: clique numa face e a peça fica com esse lado para baixo. A melhor direção de impressão em um clique.
  • “Baixar até o plano de trabalho” (D): apoia a peça no plano de trabalho quando ela está flutuando em algum lugar no ar.

Algumas regras práticas para a direção de impressão:

  • Faces grandes e planas para baixo. Elas aderem melhor.
  • Deite peças compridas que sofrem esforço de modo que as camadas não fiquem perpendiculares à carga. É entre as camadas que a peça é mais fraca.
  • Evite saliências mais inclinadas que 45°, ou adicione suportes a elas no fatiador.

Encontrando saliências

No menu ao lado do olho (“Visibilidade”), Mostrar saliências liga a exibição das saliências. Toda face que aponta para baixo com inclinação maior que 45° fica então hachurada em vermelho e branco: é ali que a impressora precisaria de suportes. O que está apoiado na mesa fica sem marcação. Assim você vê, enquanto modela, se uma esfera, um arco ou um furo horizontal imprime sem suportes; o furo em gota foi feito exatamente para isso. Gire a peça ou deite-a sobre outra face com “Deitar sobre a face”, e a hachura acompanha na hora.

A inclinação que a sua impressora aguenta é definida nas configurações, em “Aparência”: de 30° (cuidadoso) a 70° (para impressoras com boa refrigeração da peça). Uma face apoiada em outro sólido continua marcada: layerling só olha para a própria face.

Nervuras de suporte para uma peça inclinada

Uma peça impressa inclinada sobre uma aresta, a 45° por exemplo, muitas vezes não precisa de suportes: as faces são íngremes o bastante. Mas ela se apoia numa aresta fina e pode tombar. A “Nervura de suporte” a segura: uma nervura fina fica sob a face inferior a uma pequena distância, sobre um pé oval, e pontes minúsculas prendem a peça. Gire primeiro a peça sobre a aresta e deixe-a apoiada na mesa.

  1. Selecione a peça e clique em “Nervura de suporte” no grupo “Modificar” da faixa, clique com o botão direito na peça ou encontre-a com Ctrl+K.
  2. Clique na face inferior onde a nervura deve ficar. A face precisa estar voltada para baixo, inclinada entre 15° e 75° e chegar até a mesa; a nervura desce reta pela face a partir do seu clique. Se a aresta de baixo da peça for arredondada ou chanfrada, a face pode terminar até 3 mm acima da mesa: clique na face plana acima do arredondamento.
  3. Ajuste “Bico”, “Altura da camada” e “Primeira camada” como no seu fatiador. A nervura tem duas linhas de bico de espessura e a folga até a peça meia linha; cada ponte tem uma linha de largura e exatamente uma camada de altura e fica sobre uma camada da impressão, para que o fatiador a imprima como uma única linha fina que se quebra de forma limpa. “Altura da nervura” diz até onde a nervura sobe pela face (até a metade no início) e “Pontes a cada” a distância entre as pontes, em camadas inteiras.
  4. Em “Mais ajustes” dá para ajustar à mão a espessura, a folga, a largura das pontes e a espessura do pé (até lá eles seguem o bico e as camadas), além da largura do pé e dos arredondamentos no pé e em cima.
  5. “Criar” adiciona a nervura. Com “Agrupar com a peça” (ligado no início) nervura e peça ficam agrupadas: movem-se juntas e vão para o fatiador como dois sólidos lado a lado, unidos pelas pontes na impressão.

A nervura é um sólido de malha: para mudá-la, apague-a e faça de novo. Cada clique faz uma nervura; para mais, clique em “Outra face” ou repita-a com “Padrão”. A nervura não pode entrar na peça em lugar nenhum, e a peça precisa estar sobre a mesa - senão a janela diz por quê. Seus ajustes ficam guardados neste navegador para a próxima nervura.

“Verificar folga” e “Print check” conhecem a nervura: que suas pontes entrem na peça e que a nervura e as pontes sejam finas e fiquem a uma camada de altura sobre a folga é proposital e não é avisado. Uma nervura feita no layerling 1.148.0 ainda não tem essa marca; faça-a de novo e as verificações a deixam de fora.

Espessura de parede, folga e chanfros

  • As paredes devem ter pelo menos a largura de duas linhas de extrusão, ou seja, 0,8 mm com um bico de 0,4 mm. Peças resistentes precisam de 1,2 a 2 mm.
  • Onde duas peças se encaixam uma na outra, é preciso folga: normalmente de 0,2 a 0,4 mm, dependendo da impressora. Faça um pequeno par de teste antes de imprimir a peça grande.
  • Muita gente faz um chanfro leve na aresta de baixo, a que fica sobre a mesa. Isso evita que a primeira camada se espalhe ("pé de elefante").

A folga da sua impressora: o teste de encaixe

Toda impressora imprime furos um pouco menores e pinos um pouco mais grossos do que foram desenhados, cada uma na sua medida, então a folga de que duas peças impressas precisam é, no início, um palpite. Meça-a uma vez. Nas configurações, em “Plano de trabalho”, “Make fit test” coloca um teste de encaixe na mesa: uma placa de 60 × 20 × 4 mm com sete furos para um único pino de 5 mm, cada um desenhado com 5 mm mais duas vezes 0,05, 0,10, 0,15, 0,20, 0,25, 0,30 ou 0,40 mm, com o valor em relevo ao lado, e o próprio pino de 5 mm, em pé ao lado da placa, com um pequeno chanfro em cima. É feito de formas comuns, então imprime junto com o resto da mesa, sem suportes.

Numa impressora cuja mesa se move para frente e para trás, o pino alto e fino pode balançar, soltar-se ou sair ondulado na base, com ou sem brim. Marque “Test pin on a breakaway base” antes de criar o teste de encaixe: o pino fica então sobre uma pequena placa de 10 mm que adere à mesa. Ele não toca a parede do encaixe, apoia-se num pequeno ressalto no fundo; depois de impresso, balance o pino e ele se solta.

Imprima-o como está e depois empurre o pino, com a ponta chanfrada primeiro, nos furos, começando pelo mais apertado. O furo mais justo em que o pino ainda gira dá a folga da sua impressora. Digite o número dele em “Printer play” ou clique nele entre os valores abaixo do campo. A folga é por lado, em milímetros, e o navegador a guarda para todos os projetos; um campo vazio significa que ainda não foi medida. Com várias impressoras, escolha primeiro em “Impressora” aquela em que você imprime: cada impressora guarda sua própria folga, e os novos usos partem da folga da impressora definida para o projeto. Uma impressora sem folga própria usa a folga definida quando nenhuma impressora estava escolhida.

A partir daí, os novos usos partem da folga em vez do valor embutido: “Gap per side” e “Pin play (per side)” na ferramenta “Lid”, a folga de um novo “Rabo de andorinha” e “Snap-fit”, “Folga (XY)” de uma nova porca ou furo roscado - o dobro da folga, porque essa é a folga em todo o diâmetro - e “Folga mínima” em “Verificar folga”. O mesmo vale para “Clearance per side” dos pinos soltos e fixos e dos rabos de andorinha em “Dividir”. Enquanto um desses campos ainda tiver esse valor, "“From your fit test”" ao lado dele diz de onde vem o número. Uma dobradiça impressa no lugar e as articulações da ferramenta “Articulações flexi” mantêm os seus 0,4 mm: impressas numa peça só, as suas folgas também precisam ficar abertas entre as camadas, o que um pino impresso à parte não mede. A folga para encaixar um ímã ou uma chave Gridfinity, e a folga para um soquete ou uma placa comprados, também mantêm os seus próprios valores. Os sólidos que já estão num projeto nunca mudam, nem um projeto que você abre.

Verificar a impressão

“Print check”, ao lado de “Verificar folga” em “Combinar”, examina os objetos selecionados, ou todos os visíveis quando nada está selecionado, e diz numa janela o que daria errado na impressão. Cada uma das cinco linhas fica verde quando não encontrou nada, e laranja com o quê e onde quando encontrou:

  • “Thin walls”: lugares mais finos que duas linhas do bico - 0,8 mm com um bico de 0,4 mm. O fatiador omite uma parede assim ou a imprime como uma única linha fraca. No alto da janela você escolhe o seu bico em “Nozzle” (de 0,2 a 0,8 com um clique, qualquer outro no campo). Os lugares finos são pintados de vermelho com uma grade clara sobre os corpos, e a linha diz o lugar mais fino e quanta superfície está fina demais. Lugares com menos de 1 mm² e arestas vivas, como a de uma cunha, ficam de fora.
  • “Floating parts”: um corpo, ou uma parte separada de um corpo, que não toca nem a mesa nem outra peça (com margem de 0,05 mm). Ele seria impresso no ar. Uma peça apoiada numa peça que está de pé não é problema.
  • “Small contact with the plate”: uma peça na mesa cuja primeira camada é muito pequena para a sua altura, como uma esfera ou um cone sobre a ponta. Ela pode se soltar durante a impressão. O aviso aparece abaixo de 0,5 mm² de apoio, medido 0,1 mm acima da mesa, por milímetro de altura: uma esfera sempre fica abaixo disso, um cubo de 10 mm tem 10.
  • “Overhangs”: os mesmos números de Mostrar saliências, com o ângulo ajustado lá.
  • “Open mesh”: uma malha importada com arestas abertas, ou arestas compartilhadas por três faces ou mais. O fatiador precisa então adivinhar onde fica o interior.

“Show” numa linha leva a câmera até lá; seleciona as peças flutuantes, as que se apoiam em pouco e as malhas abertas, e nas saliências liga Mostrar saliências. Corpos que se sobrepõem são verificados unidos, como o fatiador os une. Se você mudar o desenho com a janela aberta, aparece “Changed – check again”; clique ali ou em “Check again”. Esc fecha a janela. Nada no desenho muda. Uma IA faz a mesma verificação com layerling_check_print.

Quando estiver pronto

Escolha “Exportar” e depois STL ou 3MF. STL é o formato mais simples. 3MF guarda os nomes e as cores de cada sólido e por isso é prático quando você imprime em várias cores. A janela de exportação também mostra quantos gramas e metros de filamento a peça gastaria impressa maciça. Mais em Arquivos e salvamento.

12. Files, saving and sharing

Where your designs live, how to back them up, which formats layerling imports and exports, and what is possible on a shared server.

Este capítulo ainda não foi traduzido para o português. Segue o texto em inglês.

Where your designs live

layerling saves everything in the browser on your computer. There is no account and nothing is uploaded. (With a copy you host yourself, designs can live in a shared folder on the server instead; see the section on the shared folder further down.) Every change saves itself. The preview picture on the start page shows the view you last had in front of you when you went back with “Página inicial”. If you open layerling in the same browser days later, everything is there.

If you go back to the start page from a design with nothing in it, layerling asks whether to keep it. “Sim” or Enter keeps it, “Não” removes it, so empty designs do not pile up. For a design in a shared folder on a server, “Não” deletes the file from the server, for everyone who uses it.

That has a downside: whoever clears the browser storage or switches to another computer loses the designs. So back up important work into a file.

Folders for your designs

With dozens of designs a single list is not enough. On the start page, “Nova pasta” makes a folder for the designs of this browser; a click on the folder opens it. Folders can hold folders.

  • Into a folder: drag a design onto the folder, or choose “Mover para …” in the design's menu, which lists every folder. A new design, and a file you open or import, made while a folder is open lands in that folder.
  • Out again: the first tile in a folder, .., and the line under the tabs lead back; you can drop a design on them too. A folder dragged onto another folder goes inside it.
  • Rename and delete are in the folder's menu. Deleting a folder deletes no design: what was in it moves one level up.
  • Search looks through every folder; a design that is found shows its folder, and a click on it opens the folder.

“Fazer backup de tudo” keeps the folders: the designs sit in the backup file in their folders, and restoring the backup puts them back there. The folders of this browser are separate from the folders on a server. The card pictures go into the file too, so they are back as soon as you restore.

Backing up and passing on

On the start page every design has a menu with the options to rename, duplicate and delete. The row beside the tabs has the same buttons on every tab. To delete several designs at once, click “Selecionar”: a click on a card chooses it (a tick shows what is chosen), “Selecionar todos” chooses every design in the list, and “Excluir” asks once for all of them. “Concluído” or Esc leaves the selection. With “Fazer backup de tudo” you pack all designs of the open tab into one single ZIP file. “Restaurar backup”, beside it (it is there on a new computer with no designs, too), brings them back, also in another browser or on another computer; “Abrir um projeto ou importar geometria” takes the same file. The “Formas personalizadas” travel in the same file, in the folder Custom shapes, see Shapes. If you restore a backup into a browser that already has some of these designs, those are not added a second time; the notice says how many were already there. A design that cannot be read is left out, and the notice names it. If the page reloads in the middle of a backup, usually because a very large design took all the memory the browser allows, the start page says afterwards at which design it stopped: save that one on its own as a file (see below) or simplify its largest meshes, then back up again. Above the designs of this browser, a short line reminds you that they are kept nowhere else.

Only some designs: after “Selecionar”, “Fazer backup” packs just the chosen designs, in their folders, into one ZIP file, and “Fazer backup” in a folder's menu packs that folder with every design and folder in it. Neither takes the custom shapes along, and “Restaurar backup” brings both back like a full backup. This is for the designs of this browser.

Where a backup goes: in Chrome and Edge a save dialog asks for the folder and the name, and it remembers the folder for the next backup. That way your backups go straight into a folder of your own, on a cloud drive for example. The same goes for “Fazer backup das formas personalizadas”. Other browsers put the file into their download folder; which folder that is, you set in the browser's settings.

If a design opens very slowly or not at all, usually because its history of undo steps has grown very large, choose “Open without history” in its menu on the start page. layerling then reads only the current state, deletes every earlier step for good and opens the design; after a question, because this cannot be undone. To keep the steps, back the design up with “Fazer backup” first.

You back up a single design in the editor: “Exportar”, choose the format LYL and click “Salvar projeto do layerling”. The LYL file is layerling's own design format and contains everything: shapes, groups, sketches, CAD data, imported sources and the history, meaning the undo steps. Under “Histórico de ações salvo” you choose how many of the last steps travel along; it starts at what the settings (the cogwheel in the ribbon) keep under “Histórico”. The last stop, “Nenhum”, saves the design with its current state only - the way to share a file without its undo steps. The export is a copy under the “Nome do arquivo” you give it; the design in your browser keeps its history. Older .skf files from earlier versions can still be opened; they are then saved as .lyl.

Saving into your own folder (Chrome and Edge). There the button opens your system's save dialog, so you pick the folder and the name yourself, and an existing file can be replaced. Afterwards Ctrl+S saves the design into that same file again, without a dialog. A design opened from a .lyl file with “Abrir um projeto ou importar geometria” or the open button of the export window saves back into that file, too. The browser may ask once for permission to change the file. After the page is reloaded the design forgets its file, and the next Ctrl+S asks for it again; the dialog starts in the folder you used last. Firefox and Safari do not allow a page to write into files like this. There the file is downloaded to the Downloads folder as before, and Ctrl+S downloads it again; Firefox can be set to ask for the folder each time under Settings, General, Downloads. If you give the file a different name there, the design keeps its own name, since a version or a date in the file name is often meant that way; the message after saving then offers “Dar este nome também ao projeto”.

When the save dialog saves nothing. If the dialog closes without a file, the message at the top says so and offers “Download instead”: the design then goes to the Downloads folder like in Firefox. The browser reports a dialog closed with Cancel the same way as one it could not use, so on a PC where the save dialog fails for every folder this is the way to keep saving.

Attachments

Instructions, a parts list, notes, a photo or a datasheet can stay with the design as files. “Anexos” in the “Arquivo” group of the ribbon, the paperclip, opens the list; a small dot on the paperclip shows that the design has some.

  • “Enviar anexo”: Choose one or more files: .md (Markdown) or .txt as plain text (UTF-8), .png, .jpg, .jpeg or .webp pictures, or .pdf documents. A file is checked by its content, so a file that is not what its name says is refused, and other types, .svg among them, cannot be attached. A text file can be at most 2 MB, a picture 16 MB and a PDF 32 MB; a design holds up to 32 files and 64 MB together.
  • The list: The arrow downloads a file as it was uploaded. The bin removes it; the row asks once more first, and a removed file cannot be brought back with undo, because attachments are not part of the undo history.
  • Reading a file: The eye on the row of a .md or .txt file opens it in a window to read, without downloading it. Markdown is shown formatted, with headings, lists, tick boxes, tables and code; a text file is shown exactly as it is written. Only links to web pages and e-mail addresses work, and they open in a new tab. Pictures named in the file are not loaded: their description stands in their place. Escape, the cross or a click beside the window closes it. Reading works in the History view too.
  • Looking at a picture: The eye on the row of a picture opens it in the same window, shrunk to fit when it is large. A PDF has no eye: download it and open it in the program you read PDF files with.
  • A name that is already there: layerling asks what to do. “Substituir” puts the new content into the file of that name, which keeps its place in the list. “Renomear” adds the new file under another name and suggests the first free one, such as notes 2.md. The cross leaves the new file out. Upper and lower case count the same, and the same file uploaded again changes nothing.

Attachments are saved with the design like everything else: in the browser, in a LYL file, in a backup and in a design on a server, which they reach as soon as one is added or removed. They do not come along with “Inserir neste projeto” or with a custom shape, and a bug report does not contain them. A design with attachments is saved as a newer kind of LYL file: an older layerling says that it cannot open it instead of dropping the files. A design without attachments is saved exactly as before.

Exporting

Click “Exportar” or press Ctrl+E.

If the window covers something, drag it by its title bar to another spot; the Import and Attachments windows move the same way. A double click on the title bar puts it back.

At the top is the file name, below it you choose the format. With something selected, only the selection is exported, otherwise the whole design. If the selection leaves out visible parts, a note in the window says so plainly, and “Selecionar tudo” selects everything visible in one click. Once the file is written, the window closes by itself; if the export fails, it stays open with the message.

FormatForWhat to know
STLslicer and 3D printingA triangle mesh. The simplest and most widespread format. An STL has no parts: bodies that overlap are joined into one mesh. To keep them as separate parts, export 3MF. In Chrome and Edge the first STL export asks where to save, and later STL exports of the design write into that file, until you type another name in the file name field or press “Salvar como…”.
3MFslicer with coloursEvery body stays a part of its own with name and colour. Overlapping bodies are only joined when they share a colour; where a shape sits inside one of another colour, say a logo in a plate, the one built first leaves room for the later one. Suited to PrusaSlicer, Bambu Studio, OrcaSlicer and Cura. Bambu Studio and OrcaSlicer ask on opening how to map the colours onto your filaments, and call the file "not from Bambu" - the message is harmless. OrcaSlicer and the slicers built on it do not read a colour per face, though. A file with a body of several colours, such as a Gridfinity bin with letters in a colour of their own or a group with “Multicor” on, therefore also has every face painted with its colour's filament, as painting in the slicer would: OrcaSlicer and PrusaSlicer 2.9 then print each colour with its filament, PrusaSlicer up to 15 colours, and Bambu Studio 2.9 takes the filaments from the painting instead of asking.
OBJmodelling and exchangeA widely supported mesh format. Colours are stored as vertex colours in the same file, with no extra .mtl. Bambu Studio and OrcaSlicer read them and ask, as with 3MF, how to map them onto your filaments; other programs see only the shape. As with 3MF, overlapping bodies are only joined when they share a colour.
STEPa full CAD programKeeps boxes, cylinders, spheres and cones as exact geometry, and so shapes made from an outline (star, heart, ellipse, tube, half sphere, round roof, rounded box, dovetail, the bores and more), the bent tube, the wedge, the pyramid, the paraboloid, the curved cone, threads, springs and gears, plus fillets and chamfers. The first STEP export in a session loads the CAD kernel (about 22 MB) once.
SVGlaser cutter and plotterA clean top view in millimetres, including holes and curved outlines. Under “Vista”, “Pegada no plano de trabalho” writes only the outlines where the objects stand on the workplane. “Arestas visíveis de cima” writes the edges you see from above as lines, each body in its colour; see below.
DXFlaser cutting shopThe same top view (“Silhueta vista de cima” or “Pegada no plano de trabalho”) as one outline of lines, true arcs and circles - no polylines, splines or curves made of short straight pieces - on layer 0 in white, DXF 2000 in millimetres, not mirrored. Bodies that touch become one outline, so no line is cut twice. Shops ask for one part per file: select the part before exporting. Not yet tried on a laser cutter: feedback is welcome.
PNGforum posts, print sites, questionsA picture of the view as it is, at twice the resolution and without handles, selection frames and dimensions. “Mostrar a mesa de impressão” and “Fundo transparente” are chosen in the window. Turn and zoom first until the picture is right; the selection does not matter here.
LYLlayerling itselfThe editable design with everything that belongs to it.
2Dworkshop, lathe and mill, documentationA drawing at 1:1 as PDF or SVG: front, top and right-side views on an ISO sheet. See below.

Bridges for parts that would fall out (DXF and SVG). When a plate with text is cut by a laser or a plotter, the middle of letters like o, a and b falls out. Tick “Pontes para manter as partes internas presas” in the export window of the DXF, or of the SVG with the top view, and small bridges hold such parts to the material round them, as on a stencil: “Largura da ponte” (0.5 to 3 mm) and “Pontes por parte” (1 to 4) are set beside it. A bridge never touches another outline or another bridge and never leaves a gap too narrow to cut; parts that would only hold each other are tied to the plate too. If a part gets no bridge at the chosen width, the message after the export says how many. Nothing changes unless the box is ticked.

STL into your own folder (Chrome and Edge). There the first STL export of a design opens your system's save dialog, so you pick the folder and the name yourself and can replace an existing file. After that every STL export of the design writes into that same file without a dialog; the export window shows which file, and Save as… next to the export button picks another. The dialog remembers its own folder, apart from the one for designs, so the slicer files can stay with the slicer. After the page is reloaded the design forgets its STL file and the next export asks again. Firefox and Safari download the file as before. If you would rather have every STL as a plain download, so that the browser numbers a name it has already used (name (1).stl, name (2).stl) as Tinkercad does, switch on “Salvar STL como um download” in the settings under “Aparência”.

A hole you have not grouped is taken out of every body it reaches when you export, as the view shows it. So there is no need to group before each export. With a selection, only the selected holes count. A hole cannot be exported on its own; layerling points that out.

STEP only carries exact CAD bodies. An imported mesh is made exact for the file, as “Make exact” does (see "Making an imported mesh exact" below), which can make the export take up to a minute; a mesh that is mostly free-form, such as a figure, is left out, as is anything else that cannot be written exactly. The message after the export names those bodies and says why. For the printer, use STL or 3MF, which carry everything.

SVG for a laser or plotter

With “Arestas visíveis de cima” under “Vista”, the SVG shows the design as you see it from above, like the top view of a drawing: every edge you can see is a line, and edges hidden by other parts are left out. Each line has the colour of its body, so a laser or plotter program that sorts by colour puts each colour on a layer of its own. Whether a layer is cut, scored or engraved, you choose there.

Every area a colour shows has a closed outline, and where two bodies meet, both get the line. The areas are filled even-odd, so filling a colour to engrave it leaves its holes and the places of other bodies free. A part reaching through another gets the line where it comes out. The SVG is at 1:1 in millimetres, with the front of the design at the bottom of the page, in the same place as the silhouette. A design with too many edges for this view, such as a plate with hundreds of holes, gets its filled silhouette instead, and the message after the export says so.

A drawing for the workshop

Choose the format 2D (hover over it and it says Drawing) and, below the file name, PDF or SVG. With something selected, only the selection is drawn, otherwise the whole visible design; holes you have not grouped still cut the parts they reach.

layerling draws the front, top and right-side views in first-angle layout (the right side to the left of the front view, the top view below it) on the smallest ISO sheet that fits, from A4 to A0, or a larger one if the part needs it. It is always at 1:1. Each view carries its overall width and height, and edges you cannot see are dashed. Round bores that run parallel to a view direction get a centre cross and a label (F1, T1, R1), and a table at the bottom lists their diameter and position, measured from the lower-left corner of the view. The title block in the lower-right corner holds the name, scale, units, date and sheet number. The words on the sheet follow the interface language.

Print at 100 % or "actual size", or the lengths will not match. What the drawing does not do: threads, depths, tolerances and bores at an angle are not dimensioned, and the sizes come from the model as a mesh, so they are nominal. A very detailed part (over 100,000 triangles) or more than 200 bores is refused with a message; choose fewer objects then.

The projection is based on the drawing work of Cadverix-3D by WC3D.

How much filament does it take?
